It is worth noticing that at this point the original intuition of repeated multiplication has been left entirely behind. There is no sense in which anything has been multiplied by itself 1.41421 times. What survives is the structural property that adding exponents corresponds to multiplying values, and it is that property, not the counting picture, which is the real content of the idea. A famous consequence of the extension is the Gelfond-Schneider theorem of 1934: if a is algebraic and not 0 or 1, and b is algebraic and irrational, then a^b is transcendental, so 2^(square root of 2) is not the root of any polynomial with rational coefficients. A related question makes a fine non-constructive proof: can an irrational number raised to an irrational power be rational? Take 2^(square root of 2) raised again to the power square root of 2. By the power of a power rule this is 2 raised to the product of the two square roots, which is 2^2, that is 4, a rational number. Now either 2^(square root of 2) is itself rational, in which case take a and b both equal to the square root of 2 for a simpler example, or it is irrational, in which case it serves as the base and the square root of 2 as the exponent. Either way such a pair exists, even though the argument never says which case holds.

sections.heading: Scientific Notation and Orders of Magnitude
sections.body: The most widespread practical application of exponents is a compact way of writing numbers that are very large or very small. Scientific notation, sometimes called standard form, writes any number as a coefficient between 1 and 10, multiplied by a power of 10. The speed of light in vacuum, 299,792,458 metres per second, becomes 2.99792458 times 10^8. The mass of a proton, 0.00000000000000000000000000167 kilograms, becomes 1.67 times 10^(-27). Avogadro's number is 6.02214076 times 10^23, and the diameter of a hydrogen atom is about 1 times 10^(-10) metres, a length so commonly used it has its own name, the angstrom. The rules of indices do the arithmetic. To multiply two numbers in scientific notation, multiply the coefficients and add the exponents; to divide, divide the coefficients and subtract. So (3 times 10^8) times (2 times 10^(-3)) is 6 times 10^5, and (6 times 10^12) divided by (3 times 10^4) is 2 times 10^8. If the coefficient strays outside the range 1 to 10, renormalise by shifting one power: 45 times 10^6 becomes 4.5 times 10^7. Engineering notation is a variant that restricts exponents to multiples of three, so that they line up with the metric prefixes kilo, mega, giga, tera and milli, micro, nano, pico. Related to this is the idea of an order of magnitude, which is simply the power of ten nearest the size of a quantity. Two things differing by one order of magnitude differ by a factor of about ten. Saying that a city has a population on the order of 10^6 communicates the scale without pretending to precision. Order-of-magnitude estimation, sometimes called Fermi estimation after the physicist Enrico Fermi, who famously estimated the yield of the first atomic test by dropping scraps of paper and watching how far the blast wave carried them, is a genuine intellectual skill: chains of rough estimates multiply, and because the errors are as likely to be high as low they tend to partially cancel, so a five-step estimate is often correct within a factor of ten. Several measurement scales are explicitly logarithmic for this reason. The Richter and moment magnitude scales for earthquakes add 1 for each factor of about 31.6 in released energy; the decibel scale adds 10 for each factor of 10 in power; the pH scale subtracts 1 for each factor of 10 increase in hydrogen ion concentration; and stellar magnitudes, inherited from Hipparchus, run backwards with five magnitudes corresponding to a factor of 100 in brightness. A practical caution attends all of this. Significant figures do not survive careless arithmetic in scientific notation. Writing a measurement as 2.99792458 times 10^8 claims nine significant figures, which is a claim about the instrument as much as about the number, and multiplying it by a value known to two figures produces a result good to two figures however many digits the calculator displays. The exponent carries scale and the coefficient carries precision, and confusing the two is how a rough estimate acquires spurious authority.

sections.heading: Exponential Growth and Decay, Doubling Times and Half-Lives
sections.body: A quantity grows exponentially when it changes by a fixed proportion in each equal interval, so that the rate of change is proportional to the current amount. The standard model is N(t) = N0 times r^t, where N0 is the starting quantity, r is the growth factor per period, and t counts periods. If a bacterial culture doubles every 20 minutes, then r is 2 and t is measured in twenty-minute intervals; after 8 hours, 24 intervals have passed and the population is 2^24 times its starting value, about 16.8 million fold. Compound interest is the same formula with r equal to 1 plus the rate: money at 5 per cent annual interest grows by a factor of 1.05 each year, so 1,000 units becomes 1,000 times 1.05^10, which is about 1,629 after ten years, noticeably more than the 1,500 that simple interest would give. Decay is identical with r less than 1. Radioactive material follows N(t) = N0 times (1/2)^(t/T), where T is the half-life, the time for half the material to decay. Carbon-14 has a half-life of about 5,730 years, which is why radiocarbon dating is useful out to roughly ten half-lives, about 50,000 years, beyond which too little remains to measure. Iodine-131, used in medicine, has a half-life of 8 days, so after 80 days about one thousandth remains. Two mental shortcuts are worth memorising. The rule of 72 says that a quantity growing at p per cent per period doubles in approximately 72 divided by p periods; at 6 per cent that is 12 periods, and the exact answer is 11.9. The rule works because the natural logarithm of 2 is 0.693, and 69.3 is adjusted upward slightly to 72 both for arithmetic convenience, since 72 has many divisors, and because it improves accuracy in the 6 to 10 per cent range where it is most used. The second shortcut is that ten doublings is a factor of 1,024, close enough to 1,000 for estimation, which is the reason a kilobyte was historically 1,024 bytes. The defining feature of exponential behaviour, and the one that makes it dangerous to intuition, is that it eventually outpaces any polynomial growth, however large the polynomial's degree. A process growing at 1 per cent per day will overtake one growing by a fixed large amount per day, given enough time. In the real world nothing grows exponentially forever, because resources are finite; the exponential phase is always the early part of a curve that eventually flattens, most often modelled by the logistic function. Recognising exponential behaviour in data is worth a word. If a quantity is exponential, plotting its logarithm against time gives a straight line, and the slope of that line is the growth rate. This semi-logarithmic plot is the standard diagnostic, used heavily during epidemics, and it separates genuine exponential growth from growth that merely looks fast. A straight line on ordinary axes means constant absolute increase; a straight line on logarithmic axes means constant proportional increase, and only the second is exponential.

sections.heading: The Number e and the Natural Exponential Function
sections.body: Among all possible bases, one is singled out by calculus. Consider what happens to compound interest as the compounding becomes more frequent. One unit of money at 100 per cent annual interest compounded once a year becomes 2. Compounded twice, it becomes (1 + 1/2)^2, which is 2.25. Four times a year gives (1 + 1/4)^4 = 2.4414. Monthly gives (1 + 1/12)^12 = 2.6130. Daily gives 2.71457. Compounded every second it is 2.718282, and the sequence converges to a specific irrational number, approximately 2.718281828459045, denoted e. Formally, e is the limit of (1 + 1/n)^n as n grows without bound, and equivalently the sum of the infinite series 1 + 1/1! + 1/2! + 1/3! + ... which converges very fast: eight terms already give six correct decimal places. The constant was first noticed by Jacob Bernoulli in 1683 studying exactly this compound interest problem, though the notation e and much of the theory are due to Leonhard Euler in the 1720s and 1730s. What makes e special is a property of the function e^x: it is its own derivative. The rate of change of e^x at any point equals the value of e^x at that point. No other base has this property exactly; the derivative of a^x is a^x times the natural logarithm of a, and that logarithm equals 1 precisely when a equals e. Because of this, e^x is the natural solution to any situation where a quantity's rate of change is proportional to its size, which describes population growth, radioactive decay, the cooling of a hot object toward ambient temperature by Newton's law of cooling, the charging of a capacitor through a resistor, and the concentration of a drug being cleared by the liver. In these settings the model is written N(t) = N0 times e^(kt), with k positive for growth and negative for decay. Converting between this form and the base-r form is straightforward: r^t equals e^(t ln r), so a doubling every 20 minutes corresponds to k equal to ln 2 divided by 20, about 0.0347 per minute. The number e is irrational, proved by Euler in 1737, and transcendental, proved by Charles Hermite in 1873, meaning it satisfies no polynomial equation with rational coefficients. It appears in places with no obvious connection to growth, such as the probability that a random permutation of n objects leaves none in its original position, which tends to 1 over e, about 0.368, as n increases. A caution about notation is worth stating, since it causes real confusion. On calculators and in programming languages the letter e is used in a second, entirely unrelated way, as the marker in scientific notation, so that 1.5e3 means 1.5 times 10^3, which is 1500, and has nothing to do with 2.71828. The function exp(x) is the unambiguous way of writing e to the power x in code and in print, and it is worth preferring where any confusion is possible.

sections.heading: Logarithms: Running the Operation Backwards
sections.body: Every operation in arithmetic invites the question of how to undo it, and the inverse of exponentiation is the logarithm. The logarithm of x to base a, written log_a x, is the exponent to which a must be raised to give x. So log_2 8 is 3, because 2^3 is 8; log_10 1000 is 3; log_10 0.01 is -2; and log_a 1 is 0 for every valid base, since a^0 is 1. The base must be positive and not equal to 1, and only positive arguments have real logarithms, because a^x is always positive. Three bases dominate practice. Base 10, the common logarithm, is written log or lg and matches decimal notation, so that the common logarithm of a number is essentially its order of magnitude. Base e, the natural logarithm, is written ln, and is the one calculus prefers because the derivative of ln x is simply 1 over x. Base 2, sometimes written lb or lg in computing contexts, counts doublings and is the natural measure for information, since a bit is one binary decision and n bits distinguish 2^n possibilities. Every law of indices has a mirror-image law of logarithms, and the mirror is exactly the correspondence that makes logarithms useful: log(xy) = log x + log y, log(x/y) = log x minus log y, and log(x^n) = n log x. Multiplication has become addition, division has become subtraction, and raising to a power has become multiplication. This is why John Napier's publication of logarithm tables in 1614, and Henry Briggs's base-10 tables of 1617 and 1624, were transformative: they let astronomers and navigators replace laborious multi-digit multiplication with table lookup and addition, a saving Laplace described as doubling the life of the astronomer. The slide rule, invented by William Oughtred around 1622 and in continuous professional use until pocket calculators arrived in the mid-1970s, is simply two logarithmic scales sliding against one another so that adding lengths multiplies numbers. One further identity, the change of base formula, lets any logarithm be computed from any other: log_a x equals log_b x divided by log_b a. This is how a calculator offering only ln and log can evaluate log_2 1000, as ln 1000 divided by ln 2, which is about 9.966. Solving equations where the unknown sits in an exponent is the commonest everyday use: to solve 3^x = 50, take logarithms of both sides to get x ln 3 = ln 50, so x equals ln 50 divided by ln 3, about 3.561. Because logarithms compress multiplicative ranges into additive ones, they also make otherwise unmanageable data legible. A dataset spanning body masses from a shrew at 2 grams to a blue whale at 150 tonnes covers eight orders of magnitude, and no linear plot can show both; plotted logarithmically it becomes an orderly scatter, and many biological relationships that look like a featureless cloud on linear axes reveal themselves as straight lines with a characteristic slope, which is the basis of allometric scaling laws. The habit of thinking in logarithms is, in the end, the habit of thinking in ratios rather than differences.

sections.heading: Powers in Other Bases: Binary, Hexadecimal and Computing
sections.body: Positional number systems are themselves built from powers, and seeing this makes several computing conventions obvious rather than arbitrary. In decimal, the numeral 3,507 means 3 times 10^3 plus 5 times 10^2 plus 0 times 10^1 plus 7 times 10^0. Every position is a power of the base, counting from zero at the right, and digits after a decimal point continue into negative powers, so 0.25 is 2 times 10^(-1) plus 5 times 10^(-2). Change the base and everything else follows. In binary, base 2, the only digits are 0 and 1 and the positions are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 and so on, so the binary numeral 1011 means 8 plus 0 plus 2 plus 1, which is 11 in decimal. In hexadecimal, base 16, the digits run 0 to 9 then A to F standing for 10 to 15, and positions are 1, 16, 256, 4,096. The hexadecimal numeral 2F is 2 times 16 plus 15, which is 47. Hexadecimal is popular in computing precisely because 16 is 2^4, so each hex digit maps to exactly four binary digits with no arithmetic required, making it a compact way of writing bit patterns. Octal, base 8, served the same purpose with three bits per digit and survives mainly in Unix file permissions. This is also the origin of the sizes that pervade computing. A byte of 8 bits has 2^8 = 256 possible values, which is why a colour channel runs 0 to 255 and why the original ASCII character set with 7 bits held 128 characters. A 16-bit integer spans 2^16 = 65,536 values, a 32-bit unsigned integer reaches 4,294,967,295, and the transition from 32-bit to 64-bit addressing raised the theoretical memory limit from about 4 gigabytes to about 18.4 exabytes. The Year 2038 problem arises because signed 32-bit Unix timestamps overflow 2^31 seconds after the start of 1970. A persistent ambiguity is worth knowing: the prefix kilo means 1,000 in the metric system but was long used in computing for 1,024, which is 2^10. Since 1998 the International Electrotechnical Commission has recommended the distinct binary prefixes kibi, mebi and gibi for the powers of 1,024, so that a kibibyte is 1,024 bytes and a kilobyte is 1,000. Adoption is partial, which is why a disk sold as 1 terabyte typically shows as roughly 931 gibibytes in an operating system: the same quantity counted with a different power. Powers of two also explain why certain algorithms are fast. Binary search halves a sorted list at each step, so searching a million items takes about log base 2 of a million steps, which is 20, rather than a million. Doubling the size of the list adds one step rather than doubling the work, and this logarithmic behaviour is the single most valuable property an algorithm can have. The same reasoning underlies binary representations of every kind: any whole number can be written uniquely as a sum of distinct powers of two, which is why weights of 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 grams can balance any whole number of grams up to 31.

sections.heading: Complex Exponents and Euler's Formula
sections.body: The final extension takes the exponent out of the real numbers altogether. What could e raised to an imaginary power mean? The route is the power series. The exponential function can be written as e^x = 1 + x + x^2 over 2 factorial + x^3 over 3 factorial + and so on, a series that converges for every real x. Nothing in the series requires x to be real, so define e^z for a complex z by the same series. Substituting z equal to i times theta, where i is the square root of -1, and using the fact that i^2 is -1, i^3 is -i and i^4 is 1, the terms separate into two familiar series: the even-powered terms reproduce the series for cosine, and the odd-powered ones reproduce i times the series for sine. The result is Euler's formula, published in 1748: e^(i theta) = cos theta + i sin theta. Setting theta equal to pi gives e^(i pi) = -1, usually written as e^(i pi) + 1 = 0, an identity connecting five fundamental constants that is routinely voted the most beautiful equation in mathematics. Geometrically, e^(i theta) is the point on the unit circle at angle theta radians from the positive real axis, so multiplying a complex number by e^(i theta) rotates it by theta. Because multiplication of exponentials adds exponents, rotations compose by adding angles, which is exactly how rotations should behave. This one observation reorganises trigonometry: the angle addition formulas for sine and cosine drop out of expanding e^(i(A+B)) = e^(iA) e^(iB), and De Moivre's theorem, that (cos theta + i sin theta)^n = cos n theta + i sin n theta, becomes a special case of the power of a power rule. The practical payoff is enormous. Alternating current analysis, signal processing, quantum mechanics and Fourier analysis all replace oscillating sines and cosines with complex exponentials, because differentiating an exponential is trivial while differentiating products of trigonometric functions is not. There is a cost in tidiness. In the complex plane the exponential is periodic with period 2 pi i, since e^(z + 2 pi i) equals e^z, so the logarithm is no longer single-valued: every nonzero complex number has infinitely many logarithms differing by multiples of 2 pi i. Choosing one, the principal branch, is a convention, and the laws of indices hold only up to that choice. This is the deep reason why the naive manipulations that break for negative bases break at all. The multi-valuedness produces one of mathematics' better curiosities. Since i can be written as e^(i pi over 2), raising it to the power i gives e^(i times i times pi over 2), which is e^(-pi over 2), approximately 0.2079. So i to the power i, an imaginary number raised to an imaginary power, is a perfectly ordinary real number, and indeed infinitely many of them, one for each choice of branch, all real. Euler noted this in 1746 and remarked on how strange it seemed.

sections.heading: Simplifying Expressions in Practice
sections.body: Most of the routine work with indices is simplification: taking a tangle of powers, roots and fractions and reducing it to a single clean expression. The reliable approach is procedural rather than inspirational, and following a fixed order avoids the errors that come from trying to do several things at once. The target form is usually a single fraction with each distinct base appearing exactly once, all exponents positive, and no radicals in the denominator, although which of these conventions applies depends on the setting. Consider a worked example: simplify (8 x^4 y^(-2))^(2/3) divided by (2 x y)^2. Handling the numerator first, the power of a product rule distributes the 2/3 across every factor, giving 8^(2/3) times x^(4 times 2/3) times y^(-2 times 2/3), that is 4 x^(8/3) y^(-4/3), since 8^(2/3) is the cube root of 8 squared, which is 4. The denominator expands to 4 x^2 y^2. Dividing, the numerical parts cancel to 1, the x terms give x^(8/3 minus 2) which is x^(2/3), and the y terms give y^(-4/3 minus 2) which is y^(-10/3). Making the exponent positive by moving the factor to the denominator, the answer is x^(2/3) divided by y^(10/3). Two habits pay for themselves repeatedly. The first is to write every root as a fractional exponent before doing anything else, because the laws of indices then apply uniformly and there is no need to remember separate rules for radicals. The second is to check the result numerically by substituting easy values, such as x equal to 8 and y equal to 1, into both the original and the simplified expression; a mismatch reveals an error in seconds that could otherwise survive to the end of a long calculation.
steps: Rewrite every radical as a fractional exponent, so a square root becomes an exponent of one half and an nth root becomes one over n.
Deal with any brackets by distributing the outer exponent across each factor inside, multiplying exponent by exponent, and remember that this never works across a sum or difference.
Evaluate any purely numerical powers, such as 8 to the two thirds or 16 to the three quarters, to keep the numbers small.
Collect like bases in the numerator and again in the denominator, using the product rule to add their exponents.
Combine the numerator and denominator with the quotient rule, subtracting the denominator exponent from the numerator exponent for each shared base.
Rewrite any negative exponent as a positive one by moving that factor across the fraction bar, from numerator to denominator or the reverse.
Rationalise the denominator if the conventions of the problem require it, by multiplying top and bottom by whatever radical factor clears it.
Substitute one or two convenient numerical values for the variables into both the original and final expressions and confirm they agree.

sections.heading: Common Errors and Persistent Misconceptions
sections.body: A small number of mistakes account for the overwhelming majority of errors with indices, and each has an identifiable cause worth naming. The most common by a wide margin is distributing a power across a sum: writing (a + b)^2 as a^2 + b^2, or the square root of (a^2 + b^2) as a + b. The underlying error is over-generalising a rule that genuinely does hold for products and quotients to an operation where it does not. The permanent cure is a numerical counterexample held in memory: (3 + 4)^2 is 49, not 25. The same error appears in disguised forms, such as claiming that log(x + y) equals log x + log y, which is equally false. Second is misreading a negative exponent as producing a negative number. Since 2^(-3) is one eighth, a positive base always gives a positive result no matter what the exponent is. Third is confusing the roles of base and exponent when adding: a^m plus a^n does not simplify to a^(m+n) or anything else neat. The product rule applies to multiplication only, and a^3 plus a^3 is 2a^3, not a^6. Fourth is mishandling coefficients under a power: (3x)^2 is 9x^2, not 3x^2, because the exponent applies to everything inside the bracket. Conversely 3x^2 leaves the 3 alone, because there is no bracket. Fifth is the unary minus problem, where -3^2 is -9 while (-3)^2 is 9; spreadsheet software has historically disagreed with mathematical convention here, with some versions of one popular program evaluating -3^2 as 9. Sixth is the exponent tower ambiguity, where 2^3^2 means 2^9 by the right-associative convention, giving 512. Seventh is the belief that a^0 should be 0. Eighth is treating the laws as valid over negative bases with fractional exponents, which produces the classic fallacy that -1 equals the square root of (-1)^2 equals the square root of 1 equals 1. Beyond manipulation, there is a conceptual misconception worth confronting: many people reason about exponential processes as though they were linear, which leads to systematic underestimation. Asked how many people an epidemic doubling every three days will infect in a month, most estimates fall an order of magnitude or more short, because intuition extrapolates the early, flat-looking part of the curve. The corrective is to think in doublings rather than in totals: thirty days is ten doublings, which is a factor of about a thousand, regardless of where you started. Two habits reduce the error rate more than any amount of rule memorisation. The first is to test any doubtful identity with small numbers before trusting it: substituting 2 and 3 takes ten seconds and settles the question definitively, because a claimed identity must hold for every value, so a single counterexample destroys it. The second is to write out one step of expansion when unsure. Anyone tempted to write (a + b)^2 as a^2 + b^2 will be cured by writing (a + b)(a + b) and multiplying out honestly. Both habits shift the work from recalling a rule to deriving it, which is slower but far more reliable, and with repetition the derivation becomes the recall.

sections.heading: Edge Cases, Ambiguities and Honest Limits
sections.body: Several corners of the subject are genuinely contested or undefined rather than merely difficult, and it is better to know which is which. The most famous is 0^0. The product-rule argument that a^0 equals 1 divides by a and so is silent when a is zero. Combinatorially, a^b counts the functions from a set of size b to a set of size a, and there is exactly one function from the empty set to the empty set, the empty function, so 0^0 should be 1. Algebraically, the binomial theorem, the power series for e^x, and polynomial notation all require 0^0 = 1 to work at x equal to zero without special cases, so essentially all of discrete mathematics adopts that value, and most programming languages return 1. In analysis, however, the two-variable function x^y has no limit as both x and y approach zero: along the path y = 0 the value is 1, along x = 0 it is 0, and along suitable curves it can be made to approach any positive number. So 0^0 is called an indeterminate form in the context of limits, which is a statement about limits rather than a contradiction of the definition. Both conventions are defensible; the discipline decides. Next, 0 raised to a negative power is undefined outright, because it demands division by zero. Negative bases with fractional exponents are undefined over the reals whenever the reduced fraction has an even denominator, and even when a real value exists, most calculators and programming languages will refuse or return a complex result, because they evaluate a^b internally as e^(b ln a) and the logarithm of a negative number is not real. Very large towers raise practical rather than theoretical difficulties: 9^9^9 has roughly 369 million digits and cannot be written out, though its last digits and its logarithm are computable. Repeated exponentiation, called tetration, grows so fast that ordinary notation fails, which is why Knuth's up-arrow notation and Conway's chained arrows were invented. Finally, floating-point arithmetic imposes real limits on computation. Double precision holds numbers only up to about 1.8 times 10^308 and with about 15 to 16 significant digits, so large exponentials overflow to infinity and repeated multiplication accumulates rounding error. Numerical work therefore often computes in logarithms and exponentiates only at the end, a technique that trades a small loss of precision for the ability to handle quantities that would otherwise be unrepresentable. It is worth ending on what remains genuinely open rather than merely awkward. Whether certain specific numbers formed from exponentials are irrational is unknown: nobody has proved whether e plus pi is irrational, though at least one of e plus pi and e times pi must be, since if both were rational then e and pi would be roots of a quadratic with rational coefficients, contradicting their transcendence. Whether pi to the power e is transcendental is likewise open, while e to the power pi is known to be transcendental by Gelfond-Schneider. These gaps mark the honest edge of what is currently provable about a subject that otherwise looks completely settled.

guides.title: Percentages and Percent Problems
guides.summary: How percentages work and how to solve every standard percent problem: conversions, increase and decrease, reverse percentages, interest, error, and the traps that make percent claims misleading.

sections.heading: Why Percent: The Language of Comparison
sections.body: A percentage is a fraction with a fixed denominator of one hundred, and that single design decision is why the idea conquered the world. The word comes from the Latin per centum, by the hundred, and the symbol grew from an abbreviation of the Italian per cento scribbled by Renaissance merchants until the letters fused into the two circles and slash we write today. The problem percentages solve is comparison across different sizes. If one school has 340 students pass out of 425 and another has 1,180 pass out of 1,475, the raw numbers are nearly impossible to compare at a glance; expressed as 80 percent in both cases, the comparison is instant. By forcing every proportion onto the same scale of hundredths, percentages make rates portable: a bank can quote the same interest rate to a saver with one hundred dollars and a corporation with one hundred million, a pollster can compare support for a policy in a village and a nation, and a doctor can weigh a treatment's benefit measured in Finland against its risk measured in Brazil. That portability explains where percentages show up: interest and inflation, tax and discounts, battery charge and exam marks, alcohol strength and humidity, unemployment and election swings, drug efficacy and materials tolerances. Anyone who cannot manipulate percentages fluently is locked out of the quantitative side of citizenship, because public argument about money, risk, and policy is conducted almost entirely in this dialect. The concept is old. Roman tax law levied a centesima rerum venalium, a one-hundredth on goods sold at auction, and by the fifteenth century Italian arithmetic texts taught percentage calculation as core merchant skill, alongside the double-entry bookkeeping that depended on it. Yet for all its familiarity, percent is a subtle instrument, and this guide takes the subtleties seriously. A percentage is never a number in isolation; it is always a percentage of something, and identifying that something, the base, is the single most important habit in the whole subject. Fifty percent of a small number is small; a two hundred percent increase of almost nothing is still almost nothing; a fall of fifty percent followed by a rise of fifty percent does not return you to where you started. Most percentage confusion in news reports, advertising, and even scientific abstracts traces back to a hidden, shifted, or mismatched base, and most percentage skill consists of dragging the base into the open. The guide builds from the ground up: converting between fractions, decimals, and percents; computing a percent of a quantity; recognizing the three canonical problem types and one procedure that solves them all; handling increase, decrease, and chains of changes with multipliers; reversing a change to recover an original value; the special conventions of money, interest, growth, and measurement error; the ways percentages are used honestly and dishonestly in statistics; mental shortcuts that make you fast without a calculator; and the recurring mistakes that a two-line check will catch. The mathematics never rises above multiplication and division, but the discipline of applying it precisely is genuine and learnable.

sections.heading: From Fractions and Decimals to Percent
sections.body: Percentages, fractions, and decimals are three notations for the same underlying object, a ratio, and fluency means moving among them without friction. The definitions do all the work. Writing p percent means the fraction p over one hundred, so 45 percent is 45/100, which reduces to 9/20 and equals the decimal 0.45. To convert a percent to a decimal, divide by one hundred, which shifts the decimal point two places left: 7 percent is 0.07, 62.5 percent is 0.625, 250 percent is 2.5. To convert a decimal to a percent, multiply by one hundred, shifting the point two places right: 0.03 is 3 percent, 1.2 is 120 percent. To convert a fraction, either divide numerator by denominator and then shift, or scale the denominator to one hundred when that is easy: 3/4 becomes 75/100, so 75 percent; 7/8 is 0.875, so 87.5 percent. Going the other way, a percent becomes a fraction by putting it over one hundred and simplifying, and a percent containing a fraction is handled the same way: 33 and one-third percent is (100/3)/100, which is exactly 1/3. That last example flags an important honesty point: some simple fractions have no terminating percent form. One third is 33.333 repeating percent, one sixth is 16.666 repeating percent, one seventh is about 14.2857 percent, and rounding them too early is a real source of error in chained calculations, so carry fractions or full calculator precision until the final step. A core vocabulary of equivalences is worth memorizing because it converts many percent problems into instant fraction arithmetic: 50 percent is one half, 25 percent is one quarter, 75 percent is three quarters, 20 percent is one fifth, 10 percent is one tenth, 5 percent is one twentieth, 12.5 percent is one eighth, 33 and a third percent is one third, and 66 and two thirds percent is two thirds. With these in hand, 25 percent of 88 is simply 88 divided by 4, which is 22, no calculator required. Percentages above one hundred are legitimate and common: 100 percent of a quantity is all of it, 200 percent is twice it, and a company whose revenue is 340 percent of last year's has grown to 3.4 times its former size. Percentages can also be smaller than one: 0.5 percent is half of one percent, the decimal 0.005, and finance sharpens this further with the basis point, one hundredth of a percentage point, so a central bank raising rates by 25 basis points has moved them by 0.25 percentage points. Related notations extend the same idea to other denominators: per mille, symbol with two lower circles, means per thousand and appears in blood alcohol limits and salinity; parts per million and parts per billion carry the pattern into chemistry and pollution measurement, where one part per million is 0.0001 percent. The single most common conversion blunder is the stray factor of one hundred, writing 5 percent as 0.5 or 0.05 percent as 0.05; the antidote is to sanity-check against a known anchor, remembering that 50 percent must come out as one half, so the conversion rule that maps 50 to 0.5 is the one that divides by one hundred.

sections.heading: Finding a Percentage of a Quantity
sections.body: The workhorse operation of the whole subject is computing p percent of a quantity Q, and the mechanism is a single multiplication: convert the percent to a decimal or fraction and multiply. Twelve percent of 340 is 0.12 times 340, which is 40.8. The word of in a percent sentence almost always signals multiplication, and internalizing that translation converts English into arithmetic. Why multiplication? Because p percent of Q means p hundredths of Q: split Q into one hundred equal parts and take p of them. That splitting picture also yields the two-step mental route: one percent of 340 is 3.4, and twelve of those parts is 12 times 3.4, again 40.8. Three worked examples show the range of the operation. A restaurant bill of 64 dollars with a 15 percent tip: 0.15 times 64 equals 9.60, so the tip is nine dollars and sixty cents. A 7,850-person town where 62 percent are registered to vote: 0.62 times 7,850 equals 4,867 registered voters. An alloy that is 4.5 percent copper, in a casting of 2.2 kilograms: 0.045 times 2.2 equals 0.099 kilograms, or 99 grams of copper. Notice that the percent always acts on a stated base, and the answer inherits the base's units: dollars, people, kilograms. When the base changes, the same percent means a different amount, which is why 10 percent of a junior salary and 10 percent of an executive salary are different raises, and why any claim of the form the amount rose by X percent is empty until you know what the base was. Two useful symmetries speed computation. Multiplication commutes, so p percent of Q always equals Q percent of p; this seems like a party trick until you meet 8 percent of 25, which becomes 25 percent of 8, obviously 2. And percents distribute over addition, so 23 percent of something can be computed as 20 percent plus 3 percent, or as 25 percent minus 2 percent, whichever pieces are mentally convenient. Precision deserves a word. In money contexts, round only at the end and follow the local convention, usually to the nearest cent; in measurement contexts, the percent operation cannot add precision the inputs lack, so 4.5 percent of a mass known to two significant figures is only meaningful to about two significant figures. In exact discrete contexts, a percent of a count may come out fractional, 62 percent of 45 students is 27.9 students, and the sensible statement is that about 28 students are in the group, with the fraction a signal that the original percent was itself rounded. Finally, keep the distinction between of and off. Thirty percent of the price is a part of the price; thirty percent off the price is a reduction, leaving seventy percent of it. Retailers rely on shoppers blurring that line, and the difference between paying 30 percent of and paying 30 percent off a two hundred dollar coat is the difference between sixty dollars and one hundred forty dollars.

sections.heading: The Three Faces of a Percent Problem
sections.body: Every basic percent question is one equation wearing three disguises. The equation is part equals rate times base, where the base is the whole quantity the percent refers to, the rate is the percent expressed as a decimal, and the part is the piece of the base being described. Given any two of the three, you can solve for the third, and the three canonical problem types are simply the three choices of unknown. Type one asks for the part: what is 24 percent of 250? Multiply: 0.24 times 250 gives 60. Type two asks for the rate: 60 is what percent of 250? Divide part by base: 60 over 250 is 0.24, so 24 percent. Type three asks for the base: 60 is 24 percent of what number? Divide part by rate: 60 over 0.24 is 250. The entire skill lies in parsing the sentence correctly, and the reliable translation dictionary is small: is (or are, was, equals) marks the verb of the equation, of attaches to the base, what marks the unknown, and a percent sign marks the rate. Read the question 15 is what percent of 80 through the dictionary and it transcribes itself as 15 = x times 80, giving x = 0.1875, so 18.75 percent. The proportion view gives an equivalent method that many people find sturdier: part over base equals percent over one hundred, one proportion with three known slots and one unknown, solved by cross multiplication. The question 60 is 24 percent of what becomes 60 over B equals 24 over 100, so 24B equals 6,000 and B is 250, the same answer by a different road. Real problems drape context over these skeletons, and the dangerous step is identifying the base when the sentence buries it. In a class where 18 students walk to school and that is 40 percent of the class, the class size is the base, so the class has 18 divided by 0.40, which is 45 students. A rated 900-watt microwave that actually draws 60 percent more power than its label is drawing 0.60 times 900 more, that is 540 extra watts, base equal to the label. If a museum's 12,600 visitors this month represent 84 percent of last month's visitors, last month is the base: 12,600 divided by 0.84 gives 15,000. A disciplined procedure removes the guesswork, and it is worth following in full until it becomes reflex.
steps: Read the whole problem once and write down the actual question being asked, in your own words, before touching any numbers.
Identify the base: ask percent of what, and underline the quantity that follows the word of or that the percent plainly refers to.
Label each given number as part, rate, or base, and mark the missing one as the unknown x.
Convert the rate to a decimal by dividing by one hundred, keeping fractions exact when the percent repeats, as with a third.
Write the single equation part = rate times base with your labels in place, and solve for x with one multiplication or one division.
Check the answer for size sanity: a part must be smaller than its base when the rate is under one hundred percent, and larger when the rate is over.
Substitute the answer back into the original sentence and read it aloud; if the sentence is now obviously true, the parsing was correct.

sections.heading: Percent Increase and Decrease
sections.body: Change is where percentages earn their keep, and the defining formula is: percent change equals the change divided by the original value, times one hundred. The original value, the starting point, is always the base; that convention is the entire content of the definition, and forgetting it is the most common error in the subject. If rent rises from 800 to 920, the change is 120, the base is 800, and the increase is 120 over 800, which is 0.15, so 15 percent. If a laptop falls from 1,250 to 1,000, the change is 250 on a base of 1,250, a 20 percent decrease. Notice the asymmetry hiding in that pair: going from 1,000 back up to 1,250 is a rise of 250 on a base of 1,000, which is 25 percent. The same price gap is a 20 percent fall one way and a 25 percent rise the other, because the base switches. This is not a paradox but a bookkeeping fact, and it has teeth: a stock that drops 50 percent must then rise 100 percent, not 50, to recover, and an investor who hears both numbers without checking bases will misjudge the round trip badly. In general, a fall of f percent needs a rise of 100f over (100 minus f) percent to undo it, so a 20 percent fall needs 25 percent, a 50 percent fall needs 100 percent, and a 90 percent fall needs a 900 percent recovery. Percent change also behaves badly near zero and across zero: a town of 12 people that grows by 12 has grown 100 percent while remaining tiny, and a company whose profit moves from a loss of 2 million to a gain of 1 million has no meaningful percent change at all, because the base is negative; honest reporting in such cases states the absolute change instead. Applying a known percent change forward is the reverse operation: increase 640 by 35 percent by computing the change, 0.35 times 640 equals 224, and adding, giving 864; decrease 640 by 35 percent by subtracting, giving 416. Doing this in two steps works but is slow and error-prone in chains, which is why the multiplier form described elsewhere in this guide, multiplying by 1.35 or by 0.65 in one step, is the professional habit. Interpreting reported changes needs one more distinction: the size of a percent change says nothing about the size of what changed. A headline that violent incidents rose 40 percent could describe a move from 5 to 7 incidents; a 2 percent shift in a national vote can move millions of ballots. Always ask for the underlying counts, from what to what, before letting a percent change carry weight. When comparing several changes, keep the time periods equal as well: 6 percent growth over three years is not comparable to 6 percent growth in one year, and annualizing, expressing every change as an equivalent per-year rate, is the standard way to put them on a common footing.

sections.heading: The Multiplier Method and Successive Changes
sections.body: The single most powerful upgrade to percent skill is to stop thinking of a change as an amount added or subtracted and start thinking of it as a multiplication. Increasing a quantity by 18 percent means ending with 100 percent of it plus 18 percent of it, that is 118 percent of it, so multiply by 1.18. Decreasing by 18 percent leaves 82 percent, so multiply by 0.82. Every percent change owns a multiplier: add the change to one for growth, subtract from one for decline, with 1 itself meaning no change. The translation is mechanical, up 7 percent is 1.07, down 35 percent is 0.65, up 250 percent is 3.5, down 100 percent is 0, and it pays off the moment changes come in sequence, because successive percentage changes multiply. A price raised 20 percent and then raised 10 percent has been multiplied by 1.2 and then by 1.1, a combined multiplier of 1.32, an overall rise of 32 percent, not 30. The naive addition of successive percents is always wrong except when one of them is zero, and the error compounds with size: up 50 then up 50 is 1.5 times 1.5 equals 2.25, a 125 percent rise, not 100. Mixed directions produce the famous trap: up 10 percent then down 10 percent is 1.1 times 0.9 equals 0.99, a net one percent loss, and the order does not matter because multiplication commutes, down then up lands on the same 0.99. Symmetric percentage swings always lose ground, since (1 plus x)(1 minus x) equals 1 minus x squared, which is why volatile investments that alternate gains and losses of equal percent grind downward, a phenomenon traders call volatility drag. Worked realistically: a jacket listed at 150 is marked down 30 percent in a sale and the till then adds 8 percent sales tax; the price paid is 150 times 0.7 times 1.08, which is 113.40, and note that applying the tax before the discount gives 150 times 1.08 times 0.7, exactly the same number, another gift of commutativity that surprises most shoppers. Chains of equal changes become powers: a population growing 3 percent a year for ten years multiplies by 1.03 to the tenth power, about 1.344, a 34.4 percent decade of growth, and this power form is the bridge from percentages to exponential growth, compound interest, and decay. The multiplier view also cleans up combined rates of different kinds: a country whose economy grows 2 percent while prices inflate 5 percent has real output changing by 1.02 divided by 1.05, about 0.971, a 2.9 percent real decline in purchasing terms, a calculation nearly impossible to do correctly in added-percent language. Finally, multipliers expose fraudulent stacking. A store that raises a price 25 percent one week and advertises 20 percent off the next has multiplied by 1.25 times 0.8, exactly 1: the discount is fiction. Whenever you meet more than one percentage acting on the same quantity, refuse to add them; convert each to its multiplier, multiply the multipliers, and read the true combined change from the result.

sections.heading: Reverse Percentages: Undoing a Change
sections.body: Reverse percentage problems give you the value after a change and ask for the value before it, and they are the problems people get wrong most confidently. A coat costs 68 after a 15 percent discount; what was the original price? The seductive wrong move is to add 15 percent back: 68 times 1.15 is 78.20, and it is incorrect. The mechanism exposes the error: the discount was 15 percent of the original price, not 15 percent of the sale price, so adding 15 percent of the smaller number cannot rebuild the larger one. The correct move runs the multiplier backward. The sale price is the original times 0.85, so the original is 68 divided by 0.85, which is 80; check it forward, 80 times 0.85 is indeed 68. The rule in one line: to undo a percentage change, divide by its multiplier. After an increase of p percent, divide by 1 plus p over one hundred; after a decrease, divide by 1 minus p over one hundred. Worked examples cement the pattern. A salary of 41,200 after a 3 percent raise was 41,200 divided by 1.03, which is 40,000. A town of 5,394 after losing 7 percent of its people had 5,394 divided by 0.93, which is 5,800. A price of 129.60 that includes 8 percent sales tax carries a pre-tax price of 129.60 divided by 1.08, which is 120, and this tax-extraction move is a daily necessity for anyone reconciling receipts, since the tax itself is then 9.60, not 8 percent of 129.60. Value-added tax at 20 percent hides the same trap at larger scale: the VAT inside a 240 gross price is not 48 but 240 minus 240 over 1.2, which is 40. The division can always be recast as algebra for those who prefer it: let x be the original, write x times 0.85 equals 68, and solve, which is the same division wearing formal clothes. Layered changes reverse in reverse order, dividing out the most recent multiplier first, though because multiplication commutes the order affects only the bookkeeping, not the answer: an item at 226.80 after a 20 percent markup followed by a 10 percent markdown began at 226.80 divided by 0.9 divided by 1.2, which is 210. A subtler variant gives the change amount rather than the final value: if a 12 percent raise added 54 dollars a week, the original wage was 54 divided by 0.12, which is 450, the plain type-three problem of finding a base. How do you recognize a reverse problem in the wild? The tell is that the known number sits after the change, phrases like after the discount, including tax, following the increase, now that it has grown. Whenever you see them, name the unknown original, write the forward multiplication that produced the known value, and divide. And always run the forward check at the end; it takes five seconds, and it catches the add-it-back error every single time because the wrong answer fails to reproduce the given value.

sections.heading: Percentage Points Versus Percent
sections.body: Two different units hide behind the percent sign, and confusing them moves elections, sells newspapers, and misprices risk. A percentage point is the absolute unit of the percent scale itself: the gap between 40 percent and 45 percent is five percentage points. A percent change, by contrast, is relative to the starting value: moving from 40 percent to 45 percent is a rise of 5 over 40, which is 12.5 percent. Both sentences describe the same event, and they sound almost identical, which is exactly why the distinction matters. The mechanism is that a percentage, once measured, is just a number, and like any number it can change either absolutely, measured in points, or relatively, measured in percent of itself. Consider an interest rate lifted from 2 percent to 3 percent. In points, that is a one-point rise, and it is also a 50 percent increase in the rate, and a borrower's interest cost really does rise by half. A headline writer choosing between rates rose one point and rates soared 50 percent is choosing between technically equivalent claims with wildly different emotional loads, and outlets choose accordingly. The reverse manipulation is just as common: a support level collapsing from 4 percent to 2 percent can be softened to down two points, hiding that half the support vanished. Finance defends itself with a third unit, the basis point, one hundredth of a percentage point, so that a bond yield moving from 3.25 percent to 3.75 percent has moved 50 basis points, with no ambiguity about base. Medicine and public health live or die on the same distinction, under the names absolute and relative risk. Suppose a disease strikes 2 people in 100 without treatment and 1 in 100 with it. The relative risk reduction is 50 percent, a number that sounds transformative; the absolute risk reduction is one percentage point, meaning one hundred people must be treated for one to benefit, a statistic called number needed to treat. Drug advertising overwhelmingly quotes the relative figure, regulators increasingly require the absolute one, and a reader who knows the difference can translate: any relative risk claim is uninterpretable without the baseline risk it multiplies. The same discipline sorts out compound comparisons in social statistics. If unemployment falls from 10 percent to 8 percent, that is two points, a 20 percent relative fall in unemployment, and simultaneously a rise in employment from 90 to 92 percent, a 2.2 percent relative rise in employment; all four numbers are correct, and each will be preferred by a different advocate. There is no rule that one framing is honest and the other deceptive; the honesty lies in stating base and unit explicitly. Writing conventions help: percentage point and its abbreviations pp or pts mark the absolute unit, percent alone should be reserved for relative statements, and careful documents give both, as in support fell three points, from 31 percent to 28 percent, a decline of about a tenth. When you meet a bare percent-change claim about a quantity that is itself a percentage, stop and ask which unit is in play; the answer usually reveals what the writer wanted you to feel.

sections.heading: Money Problems: Discount, Markup, Tax, and Tip
sections.body: Commerce is percentages with a cash register, and each transaction type has its own conventions worth knowing cold. Discounts state a percent off a list price, so the price paid is the list times one minus the rate: 35 percent off 84 is 84 times 0.65, which is 54.60. Stacked promotions multiply rather than add, an extra 10 percent off already-reduced prices applies its 0.9 to the sale price, so 30 percent plus an extra 10 percent is 0.7 times 0.9, a true 37 percent off, not 40, and retailers count on the difference. Sales taxes and value-added taxes are percentages added at the till, price times one plus the rate, and extracting them from a tax-inclusive total requires division by that same multiplier, never multiplication of the total by the rate. Tipping customs quote 15 to 20 percent of the pre-tax bill in North American practice, computed fastest as 10 percent plus half again for 15, or twice 10 percent for 20. The seller's side of the counter runs on two related but distinct percentages that professionals refuse to confuse: markup and margin. Markup is profit expressed as a percent of cost; margin is the same profit expressed as a percent of selling price. An item bought for 40 and sold for 60 carries a 50 percent markup, 20 over 40, but only a 33.3 percent margin, 20 over 60. The conversion formulas follow from the definitions: margin equals markup over one plus markup, and markup equals margin over one minus margin, both with rates as decimals. A shop instructed to achieve a 25 percent margin must therefore mark up by a third, not a quarter, and pricing errors from this confusion are among the most common small-business mistakes. Commission structures pay sellers a percent of sales, sometimes tiered, 3 percent of the first hundred thousand and 5 percent beyond, which is computed piecewise like a tax schedule. Income tax brackets work the same way and generate a persistent public misunderstanding: a marginal rate applies only to income inside its bracket, so moving into a higher bracket taxes the additional dollars more, never the whole income, and a raise can never reduce take-home pay through bracket arithmetic alone. The effective tax rate, total tax over total income, is always below the top marginal rate. Currency exchange quotes are ratios rather than percents, but the fees ride as percentages, an exchange spread of 2.5 percent silently converts both directions, and a round trip through two 2.5 percent conversions costs 1 minus 0.975 squared, about 4.9 percent. Inflation is a percentage applied to everything at once: at 5 percent annual inflation, money loses purchasing power by the multiplier 1 over 1.05, about 4.8 percent per year, and a wage that rises 3 percent under 5 percent inflation has fallen about 1.9 percent in real terms, computed as 1.03 over 1.05. Everywhere in money problems the two questions that keep you honest are the same: percent of what, and applied in which order? Multipliers answer both mechanically, and receipts, contracts, and pay slips all yield to a patient line-by-line translation into multipliers.

sections.heading: Simple and Compound Interest
sections.body: Interest is the price of money, quoted as a percent per unit of time, and the two regimes for computing it, simple and compound, produce dramatically different worlds. Simple interest pays only on the original principal. The formula is I equals P times r times t, interest equals principal times annual rate times time in years, so 2,000 lent at 6 percent simple interest for three years earns 2,000 times 0.06 times 3, which is 360, and the balance grows linearly, the same 120 every year. Simple interest survives in short-term consumer loans, some bonds' coupon arithmetic, and legal judgments, but it is the exception. Compound interest pays interest on interest: each period's interest joins the principal and itself earns from then on. The balance formula is A equals P times the quantity one plus r over n, raised to the power n times t, where n is the number of compounding periods per year. The same 2,000 at 6 percent compounded annually for three years grows to 2,000 times 1.06 cubed, which is 2,382.03, and the extra 22.03 over the simple-interest result is interest earned by earlier interest. Compounding frequency matters, though less than intuition suggests: at 6 percent nominal, annual compounding yields 6.000 percent effective, monthly compounding yields one plus 0.06 over 12 to the twelfth power minus one, about 6.168 percent, daily about 6.183 percent, and the mathematical limit of continuous compounding, e to the 0.06, about 6.184 percent. That effective annual rate, the true one-year percentage growth including compounding, is the honest number for comparing products, and disclosure rules in many countries require quoting it, as APY on savings or APR-style effective rates on loans, precisely because a nominal 24 percent compounded monthly is really 26.8 percent effective. The doubling behaviour of compound growth follows a famous shortcut, the rule of 72: money at p percent per period doubles in roughly 72 over p periods. At 6 percent, doubling takes about twelve years; at 9 percent, eight years; at 2 percent, thirty-six. The rule is an approximation to the exact time, the logarithm of 2 divided by the logarithm of one plus p over one hundred, and it is accurate within a few percent across ordinary rates, which makes it the fastest sanity check in personal finance. Compounding also runs in reverse as discounting: a promise of 10,000 in eight years, valued at 5 percent, is worth 10,000 divided by 1.05 to the eighth power today, about 6,768, and this present-value operation underlies every bond price, mortgage, pension valuation, and the entire machinery of comparing money across time. On the borrowing side, compound interest is the engine of debt spirals: a credit card balance at 24 percent effective, left unpaid, multiplies by 1.24 yearly, doubling in just over three years, and minimum payments engineered near the interest accrual can hold a balance nearly immortal. The practical morals are symmetric. For savers, start early, because in A equals P times growth to the power t, the exponent t is where fortunes hide. For borrowers, compare effective rates, not nominal ones, and treat any rate above the rule-of-72 horizon of your repayment plan as an emergency.

sections.heading: Growth and Decay Beyond Money
sections.body: Any quantity that changes by a fixed percent per period, rather than a fixed amount, follows the same mathematics as compound interest, and recognizing that pattern in the wild is one of the most transferable skills percentages teach. The signature is the multiplier raised to a power: after t periods of change at rate r per period, the quantity has been multiplied by one plus r, or one minus r for decline, to the power t. Populations are the classic case. A city growing 2.5 percent a year multiplies by 1.025 annually, so over twenty years it grows by 1.025 to the twentieth, about 1.639, a 64 percent increase, and nothing about the arithmetic cares whether the units are people, bacteria, or subscribers. Decay mirrors growth with multipliers below one. A new car losing 15 percent of its value each year is worth 0.85 to the power t of its price after t years, about 44 percent after five years; accountants formalize this as declining-balance depreciation, in contrast to straight-line depreciation, which subtracts a fixed amount, the simple-interest of value loss. Radioactive decay is percent decay in continuous time, and scientists prefer to quote it by half-life, the time for half the substance to remain. Half-life and percent-per-period interconvert through logarithms: carbon-14's half-life of about 5,730 years corresponds to losing about 0.0121 percent per year, and after any time t the remaining fraction is one half raised to t over the half-life, which is how radiocarbon dating turns a measured 25 percent remaining into an age of two half-lives, about 11,460 years. Doubling time is the optimist's half-life, and the rule of 72 translates between rate and horizon in a breath: anything growing at 3 percent per year doubles in about 24 years, which is how a modest-sounding growth rate quietly implies a city, an economy, or a resource demand twice its size within a career. Epidemiology made this arithmetic front-page material: an epidemic whose cases grow 26 percent per day multiplies by 1.26 daily, roughly 10 times in ten days and 100 times in twenty, and the difference between 26 percent and 13 percent daily growth is not half as bad, it is the difference between a hundredfold and a tenfold explosion over the same three weeks. Two honesty rules keep exponential percent claims meaningful. First, no real system grows by a fixed percent forever; bacteria exhaust the dish, products saturate their markets, epidemics run out of susceptible hosts, so the constant-percent model is a description of a phase, and extrapolating it far beyond observed data is the oldest quantitative folly there is. Second, the choice of period can disguise a rate: 1 percent per week is not 52 percent per year but 1.01 to the fifty-second power, about 68 percent per year, and converting all rates to a common period with multipliers, never by scaling the percent linearly, is the only safe comparison. When a claim's growth is quoted per month, per quarter, or per day, translate before judging, and when someone adds percent-per-period rates across periods, reach for the multipliers, because the exponential world is multiplicative all the way down.

sections.heading: Percent in Measurement and Science
sections.body: Laboratories, workshops, and factories use percentages to express two different things, composition and error, and each has precise conventions. Composition first. A mixture's strength can be quoted as percent by mass, grams of solute per hundred grams of mixture, or percent by volume, millilitres per hundred millilitres, and the two differ whenever densities differ, which is nearly always. Physiological saline at 0.9 percent by mass contains 9 grams of salt per litre of solution; a spirit at 40 percent alcohol by volume contains 400 millilitres of ethanol per litre, but only about 33 percent alcohol by mass, because ethanol is lighter than water. Labels that omit which convention they use are ambiguous by that margin, so chemistry writes the basis explicitly, and for trace amounts hands off to parts per million and parts per billion, where one ppm equals 0.0001 percent, the natural dialect for contaminants, dissolved gases, and air quality. Error is the second job. Percent error measures how far a result strays from an accepted value: the difference between measured and true, divided by the true value, times one hundred, quoted as an absolute magnitude in most classroom conventions. Measuring gravity at 9.63 metres per second squared against the accepted 9.81 gives an error of 0.18 over 9.81, about 1.8 percent. Percent difference, used when neither value is privileged, divides the gap by the average of the two instead. Relative uncertainty expresses an instrument's honesty as a percent of its reading, a multimeter rated at plus or minus 0.5 percent of reading plus a fixed count, a machinist's tolerance of plus or minus 0.1 percent on a shaft diameter, and the general rule for combining such uncertainties is that when quantities multiply or divide, their percent uncertainties add, at least as a conservative estimate; more precisely, independent errors add in quadrature, the square root of the sum of squares. That rule explains a workshop truth: a density computed from a mass known to 1 percent and a volume known to 3 percent is uncertain by about 3.2 percent, dominated by the worst input, so precision effort belongs on the weakest measurement, not the strongest. Percentages also express efficiency, output over input times one hundred, bounded above by 100 for any real machine: a petrol engine converts around 25 to 35 percent of fuel energy to motion, a home gas boiler 90-plus percent to heat, a photovoltaic panel about 20 to 23 percent of sunlight to electricity, and quoting efficiencies makes technologies comparable across wildly different scales. Yield in chemistry is the same idea, actual product over theoretical maximum. Grades and specifications lean on percentages, too: stainless steel 18/8 is 18 percent chromium and 8 percent nickel by mass, milk is sold at 2 percent fat, ore bodies are mined or abandoned on grades measured in percent metal. Two cautions carry across all scientific uses. Percentages inherit the significant figures of their inputs, so an efficiency computed from rough data should not be paraded with four decimals; and percent error near a true value of zero explodes meaninglessly, which is why offsets near zero are reported in absolute units instead.

sections.heading: Percentages in Data: Rates, Bases, and Misleading Claims
sections.body: Statistics speaks percent, and most statistical deception is percent deception, so a short course in the standard traps is a civic vaccination. The master principle is that every percentage has a base, and the base is where the bodies are buried. A store advertising that 90 percent of customers recommend it may have surveyed twenty loyalists; a party claiming crime doubled may be describing two incidents becoming four. Small bases make percentages theatrical and unstable, which is why polls publish sample sizes and margins of error, typically around plus or minus three percentage points for a thousand respondents, and why any percent computed from fewer than a hundred cases deserves to be reported alongside its raw counts. The second trap is base switching between comparisons. If men's wages average 100 and women's 80, women earn 20 percent less than men, but men earn 25 percent more than women; both are true, the chosen framing is rhetoric. Percentages of different bases can never be added or averaged naively: a company with 60 percent share of a small market and 10 percent of a huge one does not have 35 percent of anything; the honest combination weights each percent by its base. That weighting failure has a spectacular pathological form, Simpson's paradox, where a treatment can show a higher success rate than its rival inside every subgroup yet a lower rate overall, because the subgroup sizes differ; the classic real case is the University of California, Berkeley's 1973 admissions data, where the university admitted a lower percentage of women overall even though most individual departments admitted women at equal or higher rates, women having applied disproportionately to the most selective departments. The paradox dissolves the moment you look at the subgroup bases, which is the general cure for percent puzzles. Third, distinguish percent of a total from percent change over time, and never let a chart's truncated axis inflate a small change: a bar chart running from 95 to 100 can make a one-point difference look like a collapse. Fourth, conditional percentages reverse badly. The percentage of burglars who wear gloves is not the percentage of glove-wearers who are burglars; formally, the probability of A given B is not the probability of B given A, and the base-rate fallacy, ignoring how rare a condition is, wrecks intuition about testing. A screening test that is 99 percent accurate applied to a disease afflicting one person in a thousand still generates about ten false positives for every true positive, so a positive result means roughly a 9 percent chance of disease, not 99; the arithmetic is just percentages taken over the correct bases, a thousand people, one sick, ten falsely flagged. Fifth, percentages over 100 are fine for growth but impossible for shares: any claim that parts of a whole sum to more than 100 percent signals overlapping categories, multiple responses, or sloppiness. The defensive reading habit that defeats all five traps is identical: rebuild the underlying counts. Ask what the base is, how big it is, whether it changed between comparisons, and whether the percent is a share, a change, or a conditional rate; a claim that survives this reconstruction is usually sound.

sections.heading: Mental Arithmetic with Percent
sections.body: Percent fluency in daily life is mostly the art of decomposition: every awkward percentage is a sum of easy ones, and every easy one is an instant operation. The atoms are these. Ten percent of anything is the number with its decimal point moved one place left, so 10 percent of 74 is 7.4. One percent moves the point two places, giving 0.74. Fifty percent halves, 25 percent halves twice, 20 percent is a tenth doubled, 5 percent is a tenth halved. From the atoms, build molecules by addition and subtraction: 15 percent is 10 plus 5, so 15 percent of 380 is 38 plus 19, which is 57; 35 percent is 25 plus 10, or three tenths plus half a tenth; 90 percent of a price is the price minus a tenth, so 90 percent of 62 is 62 minus 6.2, which is 55.8; 17.5 percent, the old British VAT rate, was famously computed as 10 plus 5 plus 2.5, each term half the one before, so 17.5 percent of 240 is 24 plus 12 plus 6, which is 42. The commutativity trick rescues ugly bases: p percent of q equals q percent of p, so 16 percent of 25 becomes 25 percent of 16, which is 4, and 78 percent of 50 becomes 50 percent of 78, which is 39, transformations that turn apparent long division into reflex. For chained changes, keep multipliers in your head rather than percents: a 30 percent discount then 10 percent tax is 0.7 then 1.1, and since 0.7 times 1.1 is 0.77, the total is 77 percent of list, a 23 percent saving, computed before the cashier finishes scanning. Reverse problems yield to fraction sense: dividing by 0.8 is multiplying by five quarters, so a price of 96 after 20 percent off began at 96 plus a quarter of 96, which is 120; dividing by 0.75 is adding a third; dividing by 0.9 is adding a ninth. Estimation deserves equal training, because most real decisions need two significant figures, not four. Round the base to a friendly number, compute, then correct: 23 percent of 412 is close to a quarter of 400, about 100, minus a bit, and the exact 94.76 confirms the estimate was within safe range. Learn the tip anchors of your country, double-the-tax where sales tax is near 8 to 10 percent, and the doubling shortcut for 20 percent. For rates over time, the rule of 72 turns compound growth into division: 8 percent growth doubles in about nine periods. Two calibration habits finish the toolkit. First, bracket every answer: 43 percent of 90 must land between 40 percent, 36, and 50 percent, 45, so an answer of 38.7 is plausible while 48 is not, and this envelope-checking catches slip errors faster than re-computation. Second, translate percentages into natural frequencies when judging risk, since 0.3 percent means three people in a thousand, a picture the mind weighs far more sensibly than a decimal. None of this is a parlour trick; it is the difference between being a spectator and a participant whenever numbers are being used at you.

sections.heading: Common Errors and How to Check Your Work
sections.body: The same handful of percent mistakes accounts for nearly all wrong answers, in classrooms and in professional life alike, and each has a mechanical cure. Error one: using the wrong base. Percent change divides by the original value, not the new one, and discounts and taxes apply to the values their contracts name, not to whatever number is nearest. The cure is to write percent of what explicitly before computing anything, every single time; the habit costs three seconds and eliminates the largest error class outright. Error two: adding percentages that act in sequence or that sit on different bases. Successive changes multiply, up 20 then up 10 is times 1.32, and shares of different wholes cannot be combined without weighting. Whenever two percent signs approach each other, convert both to multipliers or to raw counts before doing arithmetic. Error three: the add-it-back reversal, undoing a 15 percent discount by adding 15 percent; undoing multiplies by the inverse, dividing by 0.85, and the forward check, does my original produce the given final value, catches this infallibly. Error four: the misplaced factor of one hundred, treating 5 percent as 0.5 in one line and 0.05 in the next; anchor on 50 percent equals one half to verify which conversion you are using. Error five: confusing percentage points with percent change, reporting a move from 10 percent to 12 percent as 2 percent when it is two points and a 20 percent relative rise; state the unit aloud. Error six: expecting symmetric changes to cancel, when down 30 then up 30 is 0.7 times 1.3, a 9 percent net loss. Error seven: percent of a percent slippage, as when 40 percent of members vote and 60 percent of voters approve, which is 24 percent of members approving, not 60 or 100 minus something; multiply the fractions. Error eight: precision theatre, quoting 33.333 percent from data good to one significant figure, or letting a spreadsheet's eight decimals imply knowledge nobody has. Against all of these, a general checking discipline works better than vigilance. First, estimate before computing, using round numbers to fix the answer's order of magnitude, so a slip that produces 4.6 where 46 was expected announces itself. Second, bracket with easy percents on either side of the target rate. Third, run every reversal forward and every forward computation backward when stakes are high; multiplication and division check each other. Fourth, rebuild counts from percentages when a claim smells wrong, because 85 percent of 40 cases being 34 people is easier to audit than the bare rate. Fifth, mind the impossible: shares of one whole must sum to 100 percent within rounding, no probability or share exceeds 100, and a quantity that fell by more than 100 percent has gone negative, which for prices, masses, and populations means someone has made exactly the error you are hunting. Percentages reward this kind of humble bookkeeping. The concept is nothing but a fraction of one hundred, yet it routes through nearly every consequential number a person meets, and the difference between fluency and confusion is not talent but the small, repeatable habits of naming the base, multiplying the multipliers, and checking the answer against common sense.

guides.title: Ratios, Rates and Proportional Reasoning
guides.summary: A complete treatment of ratios, rates, proportions and percentages: what they mean, the methods for solving proportion problems, how proportional relationships behave in graphs, scaling, science and money, and the classic reasoning errors to avoid.

sections.heading: Why Proportional Reasoning Matters
sections.body: Proportional reasoning is the ability to think in terms of multiplicative relationships rather than additive ones, and it is arguably the single most useful mathematical skill an adult carries out of school. It is what you use when you double a recipe, dilute a cleaning concentrate, convert dollars to euros, read a map, compare the price of a 400 gram box against a 650 gram box, adjust a medicine dose to body weight, mix fuel for a two-stroke engine, or judge whether a statistic in a news story is alarming or trivial. Educational researchers who followed how people actually reason, notably Jean Piaget in the mid twentieth century and a long line of mathematics education studies since, consistently find that proportional thinking develops late and incompletely: a large fraction of adults, when asked a question like the classic orange juice problem, comparing two mixtures with different amounts of concentrate and water, fall back on comparing differences rather than ratios and get a confidently wrong answer. The stakes of that failure are not academic. A nurse who reasons additively about a dose, a builder who reasons additively about a mortar mix, or an investor who confuses a percentage of a percentage with a simple sum can each do real damage. The core mental shift this whole subject asks for can be stated in one sentence: two situations are proportionally alike when one is a stretched or shrunk copy of the other, meaning every quantity has been multiplied by the same factor, and the questions worth asking are always about that common factor. Three families of tools carry the idea. Ratios express the internal structure of a situation, such as two parts cement to five parts sand. Rates connect two different kinds of quantity, such as kilometres per hour or price per kilogram, and pin down the multiplicative factor as a single number with units. Proportions are equations declaring that two ratios are equal, and solving them is how a known situation is scaled to an unknown one. Around these sit percentages, which are simply ratios with 100 as the fixed reference, and the graphical picture, where direct proportion appears as a straight line through the origin. This guide builds the subject from definitions upward: what ratios are and how to manipulate them, what makes a rate a unit rate, why the cross-multiplication rule is legitimate rather than magic, the standard solution methods and when each shines, how proportion governs scale drawings and models, the crucial and widely misunderstood way that area and volume scale differently from length, direct and inverse proportion as functions, applications across cooking, medicine, finance, maps and machines, and finally the well-documented ways proportional reasoning goes wrong. The mathematics never rises above multiplication and division, but the discipline of knowing what to multiply, what to divide, and when a relationship is not proportional at all is a lifelong instrument, and it rewards being learned properly once.

sections.heading: What a Ratio Is
sections.body: A ratio is a comparison of two or more quantities by division rather than by subtraction. When a fruit punch is made from 2 cups of grape juice and 3 cups of apple juice, the ratio of grape to apple is written 2:3, read two to three, and the claim it makes is multiplicative: there is two thirds as much grape as apple, however large the batch. The same relationship can be written as the fraction 2/3, as the decimal 0.667 to three places, or in words, and part of fluency is moving freely among these forms. Order matters absolutely: the ratio of apple to grape is 3:2, a different statement, and a distressing number of practical errors are nothing more than reversed ratios, which is why careful workers always name the parts in the order written, cement to sand to aggregate, and keep that order for the whole calculation.
