Ratios come in two flavours that must not be confused. A part-to-part ratio compares one component with another, like 2:3 for grape to apple. A part-to-whole ratio compares a component with the total, and since the punch has 5 cups altogether, grape to whole is 2:5, meaning grape is two fifths, or 40 percent, of the drink. Converting between the flavours is routine but essential: given part-to-part a:b, the parts are a/(a+b) and b/(a+b) of the whole; given the fraction of the whole, the complementary part is what remains. Fractions and percentages are thus part-to-whole ratios in standard clothing. Ratios extend naturally to three or more terms, as in the bricklayer's 1:2:9 for cement to lime to sand, and the same rules apply term by term. Two ratios are called equivalent when one can be obtained from the other by multiplying every term by the same nonzero number: 2:3, 4:6, 20:30 and 200:300 all express the identical relationship, because the comparison a ratio makes is unchanged by resizing both quantities together. This is the deepest fact about ratios and the licence for everything done with them; a ratio is really the whole family of equivalent pairs, and any convenient member of the family may represent it. Units deserve care. A ratio between quantities of the same kind, cups with cups or metres with metres, is a pure number and survives any change of units, provided both terms are expressed in the same unit first: a plan drawn at 1 centimetre to 2 metres is the ratio 1:200 only after converting the 2 metres to 200 centimetres. Comparing quantities of different kinds, distance with time or money with mass, is the business of rates, treated separately, and keeping the distinction between a unitless ratio and a unit-carrying rate is a habit that prevents an entire genus of mistakes. Finally, notation: the colon form a:b, the fraction form a/b, and the phrase a to b are interchangeable, and continued ratios like 1:2:9 have no single fraction form, only the family of triples.

sections.heading: Simplifying, Comparing and Scaling Ratios
sections.body: Because a ratio is unchanged when all its terms are multiplied or divided by the same number, every ratio has a simplest form, obtained by dividing all terms by their greatest common divisor. The ratio 18:24 simplifies by dividing both terms by 6 to give 3:4; the three-term ratio 12:18:30 simplifies by 6 to 2:3:5. Ratios involving fractions or decimals are cleared first: the ratio 1.5:2.25 becomes 150:225 by multiplying by 100, then 2:3 by dividing by 75, and the ratio two thirds to one half becomes 4:3 after multiplying both terms by 6, the least common multiple of the denominators. Simplest form is for communication; for computation, other equivalent forms are often more useful, and choosing the convenient representative is a skill in itself. Two standard normalisations recur. Writing a ratio as n:1 or 1:n, by dividing both terms by one of them, turns it into a single number that can be compared at a glance: a school with 540 students and 24 teachers has a student-teacher ratio of 22.5:1, immediately comparable with another school's 19:1. Writing ratios with a common total, or common corresponding term, supports mixing and comparison problems: to compare paint mixes of 3:5 and 2:3 red to white, rewrite them with a common second term as 9:15 and 10:15, and it is now visible that the second mix is redder. The same technique answers the classic concentration questions that defeat additive thinkers. Which lemonade is more lemony, one made with 3 lemons for 7 cups of water or one with 4 lemons for 9 cups. Convert both to lemons per cup, 3/7 which is about 0.429 and 4/9 which is about 0.444, and the second wins, though the difference is small enough that the additive comparison, one more lemon but two more cups, gives no reliable verdict at all. Scaling a ratio to a required total is the everyday operation of the kitchen and the building site. A mortar of 1:5 cement to sand has 6 parts in total; to mix 30 litres, each part is 30 divided by 6, that is 5 litres, giving 5 litres of cement and 25 of sand. A recipe serving 4 scaled to serve 10 is multiplied throughout by the factor 10/4, which is 2.5, and the multiplicative habit matters: every ingredient is multiplied by 2.5, and nothing is ever adjusted by adding the difference. When a ratio must be scaled so that one particular term reaches a target, divide the target by that term to get the factor, then apply it to the rest: if the 3:4:2 ratio of flour to liquid to fat must use exactly 600 grams of flour, the factor is 200, and the liquid and fat follow as 800 and 400 grams. All of these manipulations are one idea, resizing the family of equivalent ratios to whichever member the problem makes convenient, and practising until that idea is reflexive is most of what ratio fluency means.

sections.heading: Rates and Unit Rates
sections.body: A rate is a ratio between quantities of different kinds, and because the kinds differ, a rate carries units and its numerical value depends on them. Speed in kilometres per hour, price in dollars per kilogram, fuel economy in litres per 100 kilometres, flow in litres per minute, density in grams per cubic centimetre, wage in dollars per hour and dosage in milligrams per kilogram of body weight are all rates, and the word per, meaning for each, is their signature. The most useful standard form is the unit rate, the amount of the first quantity corresponding to exactly one unit of the second, found by dividing: a car covering 288 kilometres in 3.2 hours has a unit rate of 288 divided by 3.2, which is 90 kilometres per hour. Unit rates make comparison trivial, which is why grocery shelf labels in many countries are legally required to show price per 100 grams or per litre: a 400 gram box at 3.20 in some currency costs 0.80 per 100 grams, while a 650 gram box at 4.94 costs 0.76 per 100 grams, so the bigger box is genuinely cheaper per unit, a conclusion invisible from the sticker prices alone. Every rate has a reciprocal companion with the quantities swapped, and choosing the convenient direction is a quiet but important skill. Speed's companion is pace, minutes per kilometre, which runners prefer because it adds naturally over the segments of a race. Fuel economy illustrates the trap: miles per gallon and litres per 100 kilometres run in opposite directions, one rewards large numbers and the other small, and improvements that look linear in one measure are not linear in the other; going from 10 to 12 miles per gallon saves more fuel over a fixed distance than going from 30 to 35, a fact known in the literature as the MPG illusion. Dimensional analysis, also called the factor-label method, is the professional technique for computing with rates: treat units as algebraic symbols that cancel, and chain conversion factors written as fractions equal to one. To convert 90 kilometres per hour to metres per second, multiply by 1000 metres per kilometre and by one hour per 3600 seconds; the kilometres and hours cancel, leaving 90 times 1000 divided by 3600, which is 25 metres per second. The method is self-checking, because if the leftover units are not the ones required, the setup is wrong, and it scales to any length of chain, from currency conversions through medication drip rates to engineering calculations. Two cautions complete the picture. First, rates average badly: driving 100 kilometres at 50 kilometres per hour and 100 more at 100 does not average to 75, because the slow half takes longer; the correct average speed is total distance over total time, 200 over 3, about 66.7. Second, a rate is only meaningful while the relationship stays steady; a heart rate or a flow rate quoted from a ten-second sample assumes the next minute resembles the last ten seconds, an assumption worth stating rather than smuggling.

sections.heading: Proportions: When Two Ratios Are Equal
sections.body: A proportion is an equation asserting that two ratios are equal, written a:b = c:d or a/b = c/d, and read a is to b as c is to d. The four numbers are traditionally called terms, with a and d the extremes and b and c the means, vocabulary inherited from Euclid's theory of proportion in Book V of the Elements, worked out around 300 BCE largely to handle magnitudes that could not be expressed as whole-number ratios. The central manipulative fact is the cross-multiplication rule: a/b = c/d exactly when ad = bc, provided b and d are not zero. This is no mystery once seen as algebra. Multiply both sides of a/b = c/d by the product bd; on the left the b cancels leaving ad, on the right the d cancels leaving bc, so the equality of fractions and the equality of cross-products are the same statement in two costumes. In classical language, the product of the means equals the product of the extremes. The rule turns any proportion with one unknown into a one-step equation. If 5 kilograms of apples cost 12 units of currency, the cost x of 8 kilograms satisfies 5/12 = 8/x when built part to part, or 12/5 = x/8 when built as price per kilogram; either way cross-multiplication gives 5x = 96, so x is 19.2. The discipline that keeps such setups honest is insisting that corresponding quantities occupy corresponding positions: both numerators of one kind, both denominators of the other, so the equation says kilograms are to cost as kilograms are to cost. Writing the units into the proportion and checking they match across the equals sign catches nearly every setup error before arithmetic begins. A proportion can be read in two directions, and good solvers consciously choose. The between reading compares across the two situations: 8 kilograms is 1.6 times 5 kilograms, so the cost is 1.6 times 12. The within reading stays inside one situation: cost is 2.4 times mass in these units, and that internal multiplier, 2.4, must hold in the second situation too. Both are legitimate; whichever multiplier is a nicer number is the better road. Related classical ideas still earn their keep. The mean proportional, or geometric mean, of a and d is the number m with a/m = m/d, so m squared equals ad; it appears in similar-triangle geometry, in the side of a square equal in area to a rectangle, and in average growth rates over several periods. Proportions also transform legally in several ways worth recognising: a/b = c/d implies b/a = d/c by inversion, a/c = b/d by alternation, and the addition rule that a plus b over b equals c plus d over d, each provable by the same multiply-and-cancel algebra and each occasionally the shortcut that makes a hard-looking problem trivial. What a proportion never licenses is adding the same amount to all terms; equality of ratios lives entirely in multiplication.

sections.heading: Methods of Solution: Unitary, Scale Factor and Build-Up
sections.body: Proportion problems admit several honest methods, and the mark of a strong reasoner is not loyalty to one but the habit of picking the cheapest for the numbers at hand. The unitary method reduces to one unit and rebuilds. If 7 identical notebooks cost 16.80, one notebook costs 16.80 divided by 7, which is 2.40, and 12 cost 12 times 2.40, which is 28.80. Its strength is transparency, every step has a physical meaning, and it generalises smoothly to awkward compound cases: if 6 workers tile a floor in 10 days, one worker would notionally need 60 worker-days, so 15 workers need 4 days, an inverse-proportion twist the method absorbs without new machinery. The scale-factor method finds the single multiplier between situations and applies it wholesale. A photograph 15 centimetres wide printed 36 centimetres wide has been scaled by 36/15, which is 2.4, so a height of 10 centimetres becomes 24; when the factor is clean, this is the fastest route there is. The within-rate method extracts the internal constant of one situation, price per kilogram, students per class, grams of flour per egg, and carries that constant across; it is the natural method whenever the internal rate is the quantity you would want anyway, and it is how spreadsheets and scientific work are actually organised. Cross-multiplication, setting a/b equal to c/d and solving ad = bc, is the universal fallback that always works and never illuminates; use it when the numbers are ugly or the structure is unclear, but form the habit of asking afterwards what the multiplier was, because that question is where understanding lives. Build-up reasoning, doubling and halving toward the target, suits mental arithmetic: to scale a 4-person recipe to 10, take the whole, add the whole again to reach 8, then add half of the original to reach 10, multiplying by 2.5 in honest instalments. Estimation deserves a place of its own, because proportion problems are unusually easy to sanity-check: before solving, bracket the answer, since 8 kilograms at the price of 5 must cost more than the 5 and less than double it; after solving, verify that the answer sits the right side of the nearest easy multiple. For multi-step problems the golden rule is to keep units attached and visible at every stage, letting dimensional cancellation audit the logic: a hospital drip problem that runs millilitres per hour through drops per millilitre to drops per minute is three chained rates, and writing each as a labelled fraction makes the chain check itself. Finally, recognise when no method applies because the relationship is not proportional at all: a taxi fare with a fixed flag-fall, a phone plan with an included allowance, a person's height against age. The first diagnostic question of the subject is always the same: if one quantity doubles, does the other honestly double. Only a yes licenses any of these tools.

sections.heading: Fractions, Decimals and Percentages as Ratios
sections.body: Percent means per hundred, from the Latin per centum, and a percentage is nothing more exotic than a ratio whose second term has been standardised to 100. Saying 35 percent of a town's voters supported a measure asserts the part-to-whole ratio 35:100, equivalently the fraction 35/100, equivalently the decimal 0.35. The three notations are one idea at three levels of convenience: fractions are best for exact structure, decimals for calculation, percentages for communication, and fluency means converting on sight. To move a decimal to a percentage multiply by 100, so 0.075 is 7.5 percent; to move a percentage to a decimal divide by 100, so 140 percent is 1.4; a fraction converts through division, so 5/8 is 0.625 and hence 62.5 percent. The percentages worth memorising as fractions are the workhorses: 50 percent is a half, 25 a quarter, 20 a fifth, 10 a tenth, 5 a twentieth, one third is 33.3 percent repeating, and two thirds is 66.7 percent to one place. Every percentage statement has three roles, the part, the whole and the rate, and every problem hides exactly one of them. Finding the part is multiplication: 18 percent of 250 is 0.18 times 250, which is 45. Finding the rate is division of part by whole: 45 out of 250 is 0.18, hence 18 percent. Finding the whole, the reverse percentage problem, is division of the part by the rate, and it is the one people botch: if 45 people are 18 percent of a club, the club has 45 divided by 0.18, which is 250 members. The most reliable mental technique is the 10 percent anchor: one tenth of the whole is easy, and from it 5 percent, 15 percent, 35 percent are assembled by halving and adding, so 35 percent of 240 is three tens plus a half-ten, 72 plus 12, which is 84. A second elegant trick is commutativity: a percent of b equals b percent of a, so 8 percent of 25 is 25 percent of 8, which is 2, a much easier mental object. Percentages of quantities other than 100 confuse mainly because the reference keeps moving, and the discipline that dissolves the confusion is naming the whole aloud before computing: percent of what. Two further conventions matter in adult life. Percentage points measure the arithmetic difference between two percentages, while percent measures relative change, so a rate rising from 4 percent to 6 percent has risen 2 percentage points but 50 percent, and journalism that muddles the two misleads sincerely. And per mille, written with the symbol resembling a doubled percent sign, means per thousand, used for blood alcohol and gradients, while parts per million serves chemistry and pollution measurement; all are the same construction, a ratio pinned to a standardised denominator, chosen large enough that the numbers stay comfortable. Seen this way, the whole percentage apparatus is a single habit: standardise the comparison, then multiply.

sections.heading: Percentage Change, Markup, Discount and Compounding
sections.body: Change expressed as a percentage always refers to the starting value, and holding onto that anchor resolves every classic confusion. An increase of 20 percent means the new value is the old multiplied by 1.20; a decrease of 20 percent means multiplication by 0.80. This multiplier form is the professional habit, because it chains: a price raised 20 percent and later cut 20 percent has been multiplied by 1.20 and then by 0.80, which is 0.96 overall, a net 4 percent loss, not a return to the start, since the second percentage was taken of a larger base. The same algebra explains why a 50 percent loss needs a 100 percent gain to recover, and why alternating gains and losses of equal size grind a portfolio downward. Reverse problems yield to the same tool run backwards: if a jacket costs 84 after a 30 percent discount, then 84 is 0.70 of the original, so the original was 84 divided by 0.70, which is 120; if a bill of 92 includes 15 percent tax, the pre-tax amount is 92 divided by 1.15, which is 80. Dividing by the multiplier, never subtracting the percentage from the final figure, is the entire secret of reverse percentage problems, and it is exactly where additive intuition sabotages people. Commerce runs on these operations under special names. Markup is the percentage added to cost to reach selling price; margin is profit as a percentage of the selling price, a different denominator, so a 50 percent markup is only a 33.3 percent margin, and confusing the two misprices goods. Repeated proportional change is compounding, the multiplier applied again and again: money at 5 percent annual interest grows by the factor 1.05 each year, reaching 1.05 to the power of 10, about 1.629, after a decade, so 1000 becomes roughly 1629, while simple interest, which adds 50 each year to the original base only, reaches just 1500. The gap widens with time and rate, which is why compound growth dominates long horizons and why credit card debt at around 20 percent annually can double in under four years if unpaid, a consequence of the doubling-time approximation known as the rule of 72: dividing 72 by the percentage growth rate estimates the number of periods to double, so 72 divided by 6 gives about 12 years at 6 percent. The same mathematics with multipliers below one describes depreciation and decay: a car losing 15 percent of its value yearly is worth 0.85 to the power of 5, about 44 percent, of its price after five years. Two habits keep all of this trustworthy. State the base of every percentage explicitly, because increased by 40 percent is meaningless until of what is answered; and convert every chain of changes into a product of multipliers before judging it, because percentages, unlike the multipliers behind them, do not add, subtract or cancel, however strongly the notation invites it.

sections.heading: Sharing in a Ratio and Mixture Problems
sections.body: Dividing a quantity in a given ratio is the oldest applied use of the subject, running from inheritance law in ancient texts to profit shares in modern partnerships, and one clean procedure covers every case. To share an amount in the ratio a:b:c, add the terms to find the total number of parts, divide the amount by that total to find the size of one part, and multiply out. Sharing 720 among three people in the ratio 2:3:4 gives 9 parts of 80 each, hence shares of 160, 240 and 320, and the check is that the shares must sum to the original amount. The inverse questions are just as common and slightly more instructive. If the largest share in a 2:3:4 split is 320, then 4 parts equal 320, one part is 80, and the whole was 720. If the difference between two shares is known, say the middle person received 80 more than the smallest, then the difference in parts, 3 minus 2, equals one part, so a part is 80 again; differences in parts are as usable as totals. Ratios also update under change, and these problems train genuine algebra: two quantities in ratio 3:5 that become 2:3 after 4 is added to each can be written as 3k and 5k with the equation 3k plus 4 over 5k plus 4 equal to 2 over 3, giving k equal to 4 and original values 12 and 20. Mixture problems are sharing run in reverse: instead of splitting a whole into parts, parts are combined and the ratio of the blend is required. Mixing 2 litres of 60 percent juice with 3 litres of 20 percent juice gives 1.2 plus 0.6, that is 1.8 litres of pure juice in 5 litres, a 36 percent blend; the general rule is that the blend concentration is the weighted average of the ingredient concentrations, weighted by their amounts, and it must land between the two ingredient strengths, nearer the larger contributor, which provides an instant sanity check. Merchants and pharmacists long used the shortcut called alligation to answer the reverse question, what ratio of two ingredients produces a target strength: the answer is that the amounts must be in inverse proportion to the distances of the ingredient strengths from the target. To blend 60 percent and 20 percent juices into 36 percent, the distances are 24 and 16, so the strong and weak juices mix in the ratio 16:24, which simplifies to 2:3, exactly the mixture above. The same arithmetic prices blended coffee, sets alloy compositions, and dilutes stock solutions in the laboratory, where the standard dilution formula, concentration times volume before equals concentration times volume after, is one more disguise of the same proportionality. In all of these, the invariant worth watching is the amount of pure substance, the thing that neither mixing nor splitting creates or destroys; track it and every mixture problem becomes bookkeeping.

sections.heading: Scale Drawings, Maps and Models
sections.body: A scale drawing is a proportional copy: every length on the drawing is the corresponding real length multiplied by one fixed number, and that number, or its ratio form, is the scale. Map and plan scales are written as unitless ratios like 1:50000, meaning one unit on the map represents 50000 of the same unit in the world, so 1 centimetre stands for 50000 centimetres, which is 500 metres, and a measured map distance of 6.4 centimetres means 3.2 kilometres on the ground. Architectural plans use gentler scales, commonly 1:50 or 1:100 for rooms and 1:20 or 1:10 for details, while model engineering has its own dialects: a model railway in OO gauge is 1:76, and a die-cast car at 1:43 is a copy in which every real metre has shrunk to about 23 millimetres. Working with scale is two-directional and the arithmetic must be kept straight: from drawing to world multiply by the scale factor, from world to drawing divide, and the commonest error is doing the right operation in the wrong direction, which announces itself if the answer's plausibility is checked, since a house cannot be 4 centimetres wide nor a drawing 8 metres. Constructing a scale drawing is proportional reasoning as a physical act: choose a scale that fits the object onto the paper with room for annotation, convert every measured length by the same factor, and preserve every angle exactly, because scaling changes lengths but never angles. That angle-preserving property is the geometric heart of the matter: two figures related by a scale factor are called similar, and similar triangles, whose corresponding sides are proportional, are the engine behind almost all indirect measurement. Thales of Miletus is credited by ancient sources with measuring the height of the Great Pyramid around 600 BCE by comparing its shadow with the shadow of a staff: at the same moment, height stands to shadow in the same ratio for every upright object, so a staff of known height and measurable shadow calibrates the ratio, and the pyramid's shadow reveals its height by one multiplication. The same triangle logic finds river widths from two sightings, tree heights from a mirror on the ground, and star distances from the parallax of the Earth's orbit; surveying, navigation and astronomy are, at this level, applied proportion. Scales also chain: a photograph of a 1:100 plan enlarged 150 percent is a 1:66.7 representation, the product of the factors, and photocopier percentage settings are exactly scale factors, with 71 percent approximating the side ratio needed to reduce A3 to A4, since that ratio is one over the square root of two. Reading any scale representation, the disciplined questions are always the same three: what is the scale, which direction is this conversion going, and is the resulting size believable for the thing represented.

sections.heading: The Square-Cube Law: How Area and Volume Scale
sections.body: The single most important refinement to scaling intuition is this: when lengths scale by a factor k, areas scale by k squared and volumes by k cubed. A floor plan at 1:100 compresses every length by 100, so each square metre of floor becomes one ten-thousandth of a square metre on paper; a model at one quarter size holds not a quarter but one sixty-fourth of the original's volume. The reason is visible in a square and a cube: doubling the side of a square tiles it with four copies of the original, doubling the side of a cube stacks eight, and every area or volume, however curved, is a limit of little squares or cubes that all obey the same rule. The consequences are everywhere once seen. A pizza of 30 centimetres diameter has 2.25 times the area of a 20 centimetre one, since 1.5 squared is 2.25, so it is the better buy at anything less than 2.25 times the price. A recipe scaled up by half in every linear dimension of its tin needs about 3.4 times the batter, since 1.5 cubed is 3.375, and it will bake differently because its surface, through which heat enters, grew only 2.25 times while its interior grew 3.4. Paint requirements follow areas, so a statue twice as tall needs four times the paint; weight follows volume, so it weighs eight times as much. That mismatch between the square and the cube, named the square-cube law and articulated by Galileo Galilei in his Discourses of 1638, governs the sizes of living things. An animal scaled up by k gains muscle and bone cross-section, hence strength, by k squared, but weight by k cubed, so strength relative to weight falls as one over k; this is why an ant can lift many times its body weight while an elephant cannot jump, why the giants of fairy tales would break their own legs, and why large animals need disproportionately thick bones, as Galileo himself illustrated with drawings of scaled femurs. Heat balance obeys the same law in reverse: an organism generates heat roughly with its volume and loses it through its surface, so small animals, with large surface relative to volume, lose heat fast and must eat constantly, while whales and elephants shed excess heat with difficulty; the biological rules of Bergmann and Allen about body size and limb length in cold climates are corollaries. Engineering lives with the law daily: a ship design enlarged 10 percent gains about 33 percent displacement; a scaled-up bridge is proportionally weaker unless redesigned; wind-tunnel models must be corrected because air forces do not scale with the model. For the practical reasoner the lesson is compact: ask of every scaling problem whether the quantity of interest is a length, an area or a volume, and raise the length factor to the first, second or third power accordingly, because intuition unassisted almost always guesses the first power and is almost always wrong.

sections.heading: Direct Proportion and the Line Through the Origin
sections.body: Two quantities are directly proportional when one is a constant multiple of the other: y equals kx for some fixed nonzero constant k, called the constant of proportionality, written y is proportional to x. The definition carries three equivalent signatures, and recognising any one of them establishes the relationship. Algebraically, the quotient y over x is the same for every data pair; doubling x doubles y, tripling x triples y, and x equal to zero forces y equal to zero. Graphically, the points lie on a straight line through the origin, and the slope of that line is exactly k. In a table, the entries in one row are the entries of the other row all multiplied by the same number. Each signature is a working test. Given a table of measurements, divide each y by its x: constant quotients, allowing for measurement noise, mean direct proportion, and the common quotient is the physical rate. Given a graph, straightness alone is not enough, because a line that misses the origin, like a taxi fare with a fixed starting charge, is linear but not proportional: fare may be 3 plus 2 per kilometre, and doubling the distance does not double the fare. The through-the-origin condition is precisely what makes ratio reasoning legal, and treating merely linear relationships as proportional is one of the most frequent quantitative errors in practical work. The constant k always has a meaning and usually a name. In distance equals speed times time, k is the speed. In mass equals density times volume, it is density, about 1 gram per cubic centimetre for water and 19.3 for gold, the disparity Archimedes exploited, according to the Roman architect Vitruvius, to test the king's crown in the third century BCE. In Hooke's law, published by Robert Hooke in 1678, the stretch of a spring is proportional to the applied force within the elastic limit, and k describes the spring's stiffness. In Ohm's law, stated by Georg Ohm in 1827, current is proportional to voltage at fixed resistance. Circumference equals pi times diameter makes pi itself a constant of proportionality, arguably humanity's most celebrated one. Working with a direct proportion has a fixed rhythm: establish proportionality by test or by trusted theory, determine k from one reliable data pair by division, then answer every further question by multiplication, checking the units of k, which are always the units of y per unit of x. The rhythm extends to proportionality against transformed variables, where y is proportional not to x but to some power of it: the area of a circle is proportional to the square of its radius, the volume of a sphere to the cube, and Kepler's third law of 1619 makes the square of a planet's orbital period proportional to the cube of its mean distance from the Sun. Plotting y against the appropriate power of x straightens such laws into lines through the origin, a technique that remains a standard instrument of experimental science.

sections.heading: Inverse Proportion and Other Relationships
sections.body: Two quantities are inversely proportional when their product is constant: y equals k divided by x, so doubling one halves the other. The everyday cases are shared work and shared totals. If a journey of 240 kilometres is fixed, speed and travel time are inversely proportional, since their product must be 240: at 60 kilometres per hour the trip takes 4 hours, at 80 it takes 3. If a job amounts to a fixed quantity of work, measured in worker-days, then workers and days are inversely proportional: 6 workers for 10 days is 60 worker-days, so 15 workers finish in 4 days, subject to the honest caveat that real tasks stop scaling when workers begin queueing for the same doorway, a fact project managers know as the lesson of Brooks's law in software engineering. The graph of an inverse proportion is not a line but a hyperbola, falling steeply at first and flattening forever, never touching either axis, because neither quantity can reach zero while their product stays fixed; plotting y against 1 over x straightens it into a line through the origin with slope k, the standard laboratory trick for confirming the relationship. Physics supplies canonical examples. Boyle's law, published by Robert Boyle in 1662, states that the pressure and volume of a fixed amount of gas at constant temperature are inversely proportional, pressure times volume constant, which is why a bubble expands as it rises. The intensity of light, sound or gravity from a compact source follows an inverse square law, falling with the square of distance because the same output spreads over a sphere whose area grows as distance squared: step twice as far from a lamp and receive a quarter of the light; Newton's law of universal gravitation of 1687 has the same shape. Recognising which relationship the data obeys is a diagnostic craft. Compute products: constant products mean inverse proportion. Compute quotients: constant quotients mean direct proportion. If neither is constant, test scalings, does doubling x quadruple y, suggesting proportionality to the square, or add a fixed amount, suggesting a linear-with-intercept law. And many relationships are none of these: a person's height against age rises then stops, a drug's effect against dose can reverse, and no amount of ratio work applies. The gravest practical error in this territory is extrapolating a genuine proportion beyond its domain of validity: Hooke's spring law fails past the elastic limit, work scaling fails when coordination costs bite, and a bacterial culture doubling every 20 minutes cannot do so for a week, or a single cell would outweigh the planet. A proportional model is a local law plus a domain, and stating the domain, over what range of x has this k been verified, is part of stating the law. The disciplined summary: identify the invariant, product or quotient or neither, fit the constant from data, and never trust the model further than the data reaches.

sections.heading: Proportional Reasoning in Science, Money and Daily Life
sections.body: The reach of this subject is best seen by walking through the places adults actually use it. In the kitchen, scaling a recipe is multiplication by a single factor, with the caveats that pan area scales with the square of linear size, cooking times do not scale proportionally because heat must diffuse deeper, and strong flavours like salt and chilli are safer scaled below the factor and corrected at the end. In health care, dosage is a rate, commonly milligrams per kilogram of body weight per day: a 15 milligram per kilogram dose for a 22 kilogram child is 330 milligrams, and if the syrup supplies 250 milligrams per 5 millilitres, the volume required is 330 over 50, which is 6.6 millilitres. Drip rates chain three ratios, millilitres per hour, drops per millilitre, seconds per drop, and unit cancellation audits the chain; clinical protocols drill exactly this arithmetic because additive errors here injure people. In money, exchange rates are rates: at 1.32 dollars per pound, 250 pounds is 330 dollars, and the return conversion divides. Unit pricing, interest multipliers, tax and tip calculations, and the difference between percentage points and percent are all the machinery of earlier sections earning rent. In travel, fuel consumption converts distance to litres and litres to cost in one dimensional chain, and average speed over a journey is total distance over total time, never the average of the speeds. In the workshop, mixtures rule: two-stroke fuel at 50:1 needs 100 millilitres of oil for 5 litres of petrol, mortar at 1:5 turns a bag of cement into a predictable volume of mix, and epoxy resins demand their stated ratio by weight or volume within a few percent or they cure badly. In science, most named laws of the school curriculum are proportionality statements, from density through Ohm and Boyle to Hooke and Kepler, and the experimental method of plotting transformed variables to hunt for straight lines through the origin is proportional reasoning as laboratory practice. In maps, models and images, scale factors and the square-cube law govern everything from hiking distances to why film miniatures must be shot in slow motion, since the physics of a small splash betrays its true size. In statistics and citizenship, per-capita rates are what make countries comparable, crime or income totals mean little between a nation of 5 million and one of 300 million, and base rates decide whether a screening result matters: a test with a 5 percent false positive rate applied to a condition afflicting 1 person in 1000 produces roughly 50 false alarms per true case, so most positives are false even from an accurate test, a proportional fact that surprises trained professionals. The pattern across every example is identical: identify the invariant rate or ratio, attach its units, and let multiplication and division do all the work.

sections.heading: Failure Modes: The Classic Errors and How to Avoid Them
sections.body: Proportional reasoning fails in well-documented ways, and knowing the catalogue is the most efficient vaccination. The deepest error is additive thinking, reaching for a difference where the situation demands a factor. Asked to enlarge a 3 by 5 photograph so the short side becomes 6, additive thinkers make the long side 8, adding 3, instead of 10, doubling; the tell is that their rectangles subtly change shape. The mistake has been reproduced in decades of classroom studies, and its cure is the habit of asking times what, never plus what, whenever two situations are copies at different sizes. Its mirror image is just as damaging: applying proportional machinery where the relationship is not proportional. Linear-with-intercept situations, taxi fares, phone plans, oven preheating, are not proportional because they fail the origin test; many others, like height against age or stopping distance against speed, are not even linear, stopping distance growing roughly with the square of speed because kinetic energy does. The two-question screen, does zero give zero, does doubling double, catches most abuse in seconds. Percentage errors form their own family. Percentages are added and subtracted as though they commute, but a 20 percent rise then a 20 percent fall lands at 96 percent of the start; successive discounts of 30 and 20 percent are 44 percent off, not 50, because 0.7 times 0.8 is 0.56. Reverse percentage problems are solved by subtracting the percentage from the final value instead of dividing by the multiplier. Percent is confused with percentage points, and a rate is quoted without its base, of what, which makes the number strictly meaningless. Ratio-specific slips include reversing the order of terms, mixing part-to-part with part-to-whole so that 2:3 becomes two fifths in one line and two thirds in the next, and comparing ratios by cross-differences instead of converting to a common denominator or unit rate. Averaging rates arithmetically instead of weighting by exposure produces the average-speed fallacy, and aggregating ratios across groups invites Simpson's paradox, the startling but rigorous fact, analysed by Edward Simpson in 1951, that a treatment can show a better success rate in every subgroup yet a worse rate overall when the groups are pooled, because the groups differ in size and difficulty; the famous 1973 Berkeley admissions data behaved exactly this way. Extrapolation beyond the verified domain, discussed with inverse proportion, rounds out the list. The defensive habits are few and cheap. Write units on every quantity and insist they cancel correctly. Name the base of every percentage and the order of every ratio aloud. Convert chained percentage changes to multiplied factors before judging them. Bracket every answer with an estimate before computing, and test the finished answer for plausibility against the brackets. And when a claim compares two groups, ask for the rates, the bases and the subgroups before believing anything, because most statistical deception is nothing more than proportional reasoning carefully left undone.

guides.title: Fractions and Rational Arithmetic
guides.summary: What a fraction actually is, why each of the four operations works the way it does, and how rational numbers connect to decimals, ratios, percentages and continued fractions, with worked examples and the errors that most often go wrong.

sections.heading: What a Fraction Is, and Why the Idea Was Needed
sections.body: Counting numbers answer the question how many. They fail immediately at the question how much. Three people share two loaves; a plank must be cut seven eighths of the way along; a recipe for six is being made for four. Each of these requires a number that lies between the whole numbers, and the fraction is the oldest and still the most exact answer to that requirement. A fraction written as a over b consists of a numerator a and a denominator b, with b not zero. The denominator names the size of the parts, telling you how many equal pieces a whole has been divided into, and the numerator counts how many of those pieces you have. Three quarters means a whole cut into four equal pieces, of which three are taken. The word denominator shares a root with nominate, to name, and numerator with number, to count, which is a genuinely useful memory hook because it captures the asymmetry: the bottom names, the top counts. That is only one of at least four correct interpretations, and fluency requires all of them. The part-whole view just described is the one taught first. The measurement view treats three quarters as a length measured in quarter units, which is how a ruler works and why fractions feel natural to carpenters. The quotient view treats a over b as the result of dividing a by b, so three quarters is three loaves shared among four people, and this is the interpretation that makes fractions and division the same subject. The operator view treats a fraction as a machine that acts on a quantity: three quarters of forty is thirty. The ratio view, closely related, treats it as a comparison of two quantities. Learners who know only the part-whole view get stuck the moment a numerator exceeds a denominator, because there is no such thing as five quarters of a single pie in that picture, whereas the measurement and quotient views handle it without complaint. The set of all such numbers is called the rational numbers, written with the symbol Q for quotient, and it consists of every number expressible as a ratio of two integers with a non-zero denominator. It includes the integers themselves, since 5 equals 5 over 1, and it is closed under addition, subtraction, multiplication and division by anything other than zero, meaning those operations never take you outside the set. That closure is exactly what the whole numbers lack and precisely why the rationals were invented. Historically this took a very long time to settle. Egyptian mathematics of the Rhind Papyrus, around 1650 BCE, worked almost exclusively with unit fractions, those with numerator one, writing two thirds as a special symbol and everything else as sums of distinct unit fractions. Babylonian scribes used base 60 place value with sexagesimal fractions, which is why an hour still has 60 minutes. The modern horizontal bar came through Arabic mathematics, notably al-Hassar in the twelfth century, and entered Europe with Fibonacci's Liber Abaci of 1202.

sections.heading: Equivalence: Why Many Names Describe One Number
sections.body: The single most important structural fact about fractions is that each rational number has infinitely many written forms. One half, two quarters, three sixths, fifty hundredths and 1000 over 2000 are not five numbers that happen to be equal; they are five names for one number. Almost every difficulty learners have with fractions traces back to treating the written form as the thing itself. The rule is that multiplying or dividing both numerator and denominator by the same non-zero number leaves the value unchanged. Formally, a over b equals ka over kb for any non-zero k. The reason is not arbitrary. Multiplying by k over k is multiplying by 1, since any non-zero quantity divided by itself is 1, and multiplying by 1 changes nothing. Geometrically, cutting every existing piece into k smaller pieces multiplies both the number of pieces you hold and the number in the whole by the same factor, so the shaded proportion of the diagram is untouched. The cross-multiplication test follows directly: a over b equals c over d exactly when ad equals bc, for positive denominators. Checking whether 12 over 18 equals 30 over 45 means comparing 12 times 45, which is 540, with 18 times 30, which is also 540, so they are equal. This test is fast and mechanical and is worth having as a reflex, but it is worth understanding why it works: multiplying both sides of the equation by bd clears both denominators simultaneously. Every rational number has exactly one preferred name, called lowest terms or simplest form, in which the numerator and denominator share no common factor greater than 1. Reaching it means dividing both by their greatest common divisor. For 84 over 126, the greatest common divisor is 42, and dividing gives 2 over 3. Finding the greatest common divisor by inspection works for small numbers; for larger ones the Euclidean algorithm, described in Euclid's Elements around 300 BCE and still the standard method after more than two millennia, is reliable and fast. Divide the larger by the smaller and keep the remainder, then repeat with the smaller number and that remainder until the remainder is zero; the last non-zero remainder is the greatest common divisor. For 84 and 126: 126 divided by 84 leaves 42; 84 divided by 42 leaves 0; so the answer is 42. Simplest form matters for more than tidiness. It makes comparison and recognition possible, it keeps numbers small enough to compute with by hand, and in computer arithmetic it prevents numerators and denominators from growing explosively through repeated operations, which is a real problem in exact rational arithmetic systems and is why they normalise after every step.

sections.heading: Comparing and Ordering: Which Fraction Is Bigger
sections.body: Deciding which of two fractions is larger is not visually obvious, because two numbers are varying at once and they pull in opposite directions. Increasing the numerator increases the value; increasing the denominator decreases it, because the same whole is being cut into more and therefore smaller pieces. That second relationship is genuinely counter-intuitive and is the source of the persistent error in which a learner judges one fifth to be larger than one third because five exceeds three. Several reliable methods exist and it is worth knowing more than one. Common denominators are the most general: rewrite both fractions with the same denominator, then compare numerators directly, because once the pieces are the same size counting them settles it. To compare 5 over 8 with 7 over 12, use 24: 5 over 8 becomes 15 over 24 and 7 over 12 becomes 14 over 24, so 5 over 8 is larger. Cross multiplication is the same computation with the writing suppressed: compare 5 times 12, which is 60, with 8 times 7, which is 56, and since 60 exceeds 56 the first fraction wins. This shortcut is valid only when both denominators are positive, and reversing the inequality when a denominator is negative is a standard trap. Benchmarking is faster and often sufficient. Compare each fraction to a landmark, usually one half or one. A fraction exceeds one half exactly when twice its numerator exceeds its denominator, so 7 over 12 is just above a half because 14 exceeds 12, and 5 over 11 is just below because 10 is less than 11. If one candidate is above the benchmark and the other below, the question is settled without arithmetic. Two more techniques are worth carrying. When numerators are equal, the larger denominator gives the smaller fraction, immediately. When both fractions are one unit fraction short of a whole, as with 7 over 8 and 11 over 12, the one with the larger denominator is closer to 1 and therefore larger, because the missing piece is smaller. Converting to decimals also works and is often quickest with a calculator, though it can mislead when rounding hides a small difference, and it obscures exactness. Ordering has a property worth stating explicitly: between any two distinct rational numbers there is always another rational number, for instance their average. This is called density, and it means the rationals have no gaps in the sense of adjacency, no fraction has a next fraction. Yet, remarkably, they still leave room for the irrationals, a fact that took mathematicians until the nineteenth century to make precise. Between one third and one half, for example, sits five twelfths, and between one third and five twelfths sits three eighths, and the process never terminates however many times it is repeated.

sections.heading: Addition and Subtraction: Why the Denominators Must Match
sections.body: Adding fractions is the operation learners find hardest, and the reason is that the obvious guess is wrong. One half plus one third is not two fifths. The guess fails because addition counts things, and counting only works when the things being counted are the same size. Halves and thirds are different sizes, so there is nothing to count until they are rewritten in a common unit. The principle is identical to one everybody already applies without thinking. Three metres plus forty centimetres is not forty-three of anything; you must first convert to a shared unit, giving 300 plus 40 equals 340 centimetres. Fractions behave exactly the same way, with the denominator playing the role of the unit. Once both are expressed in twelfths, one half is 6 over 12, one third is 4 over 12, and the sum is 10 over 12, which reduces to 5 over 6. The general rule follows: a over b plus c over d equals ad plus bc, all over bd. This works because multiplying the first fraction by d over d and the second by b over b converts both to denominator bd without changing either value. Using bd always works but often gives larger numbers than necessary; the least common multiple of b and d, called the least common denominator, keeps the arithmetic small. For denominators 8 and 12 the product is 96 but the least common multiple is 24, and working in 24ths is noticeably less painful. The least common multiple can be found by dividing the product by the greatest common divisor, so for 8 and 12 it is 96 divided by 4, which is 24. A worked example is worth following in full. To compute 3 over 8 plus 5 over 12, first find the least common denominator, 24. Then 3 over 8 becomes 9 over 24, since 8 times 3 is 24 and so the numerator is multiplied by 3. And 5 over 12 becomes 10 over 24. The sum is 19 over 24, which cannot be reduced because 19 is prime and does not divide 24. Subtraction is identical with a minus sign: 3 over 8 minus 5 over 12 gives 9 over 24 minus 10 over 24, which is negative 1 over 24. Mixed numbers, such as two and three quarters, are a compact notation for a whole number plus a fraction, and they hide an invisible plus sign that causes real confusion once algebra arrives, where two adjacent symbols mean multiplication. For calculation, the safest route is usually to convert to an improper fraction first: two and three quarters becomes 11 over 4, because two wholes are 8 quarters. Subtracting mixed numbers directly requires borrowing, exactly as in whole-number subtraction. To compute five and one third minus two and two thirds, rewrite five and one third as four and four thirds, then subtract to get two and two thirds. Converting to improper fractions, 16 over 3 minus 8 over 3 equals 8 over 3, avoids the borrowing entirely and is usually less error-prone.

sections.heading: Multiplication: Why It Is Easier Than Addition
sections.body: Multiplying fractions is the one operation whose rule is simpler than the corresponding rule for whole numbers, and the fact that it is easier than addition genuinely surprises people. The rule is: multiply the numerators, multiply the denominators. So 2 over 3 times 4 over 5 equals 8 over 15, and no common denominators are needed at all. The reason lies in the operator meaning of a fraction. Multiplying by 2 over 3 means taking two thirds of something, and taking two thirds of four fifths can be pictured directly. Draw a rectangle, shade four fifths of it by dividing it vertically into five strips and shading four. Now divide the same rectangle horizontally into three bands and take two of them. The doubly shaded region is 2 times 4 equals 8 small cells out of 3 times 5 equals 15 in total, which is 8 over 15. The grid picture is not a mnemonic; it is the reason the rule is what it is, and it also shows why multiplication of fractions is an area computation. A consequence that upsets intuition is that multiplying can make a number smaller. Whole-number experience trains the expectation that multiplication increases, but multiplying by any number between 0 and 1 shrinks: one half of one half is one quarter. Precisely, multiplying by a fraction greater than 1 increases the value, multiplying by exactly 1 leaves it unchanged, and multiplying by a fraction between 0 and 1 decreases it. Keeping this straight prevents a great many estimation errors. Cancelling before multiplying is the practical technique that keeps numbers manageable. Because the final result will be reduced anyway, common factors can be removed across the diagonal beforehand. To compute 8 over 15 times 5 over 12, note that 5 divides into both 5 and 15, leaving 8 over 3 times 1 over 12, and 4 divides into both 8 and 12, leaving 2 over 3 times 1 over 3, which is 2 over 9. Doing it the other way gives 40 over 180, the same answer after a harder reduction. The validity of cancelling across the diagonal follows from the fact that multiplication combines everything into a single numerator and denominator before reduction, so it does not matter when the common factors are removed. Multiplication of fractions also makes the word of concrete. Three quarters of 200 grams is 3 over 4 times 200, which is 150 grams. Scaling a recipe designed for 6 to serve 4 means multiplying every quantity by 4 over 6, which reduces to 2 over 3. And repeated multiplication gives powers: 2 over 3 cubed is 8 over 27, since both numerator and denominator are cubed. These are the same operation wearing different clothes.

sections.heading: Division: Invert and Multiply, and Why That Works
sections.body: The instruction to invert the second fraction and multiply is probably the most widely memorised and least widely understood rule in school arithmetic. It is correct, it is easy to apply, and there are at least three good explanations of why it holds, each illuminating a different aspect. The first explanation uses the meaning of division as measurement: how many of these fit into that. Asking what 3 divided by one quarter equals is asking how many quarter-units fit into 3 whole units. The answer is plainly 12, and multiplying 3 by 4 gives 12, so dividing by one quarter is the same as multiplying by 4. Generalising, dividing by 1 over n means asking how many nth parts fit in, which is n times as many as there are wholes. Dividing by 2 over 3 means asking how many two-thirds fit in, which is half as many as the number of thirds, giving the multiplier 3 over 2. The second explanation uses reciprocals. Every non-zero rational number a over b has a multiplicative inverse, b over a, with the property that their product is 1, since ab over ba equals 1. Division is defined as multiplication by the inverse, in exactly the same way that subtraction is addition of the negative. So dividing by 2 over 3 is by definition multiplying by 3 over 2. Under this account the rule is not a trick at all but the definition unpacked. The third explanation is algebraic and is the one that convinces sceptics. Write the division as a compound fraction, a over b divided by c over d, and multiply the whole thing top and bottom by d over c. The bottom becomes c over d times d over c, which is 1, so the bottom disappears, and the top becomes a over b times d over c. Since multiplying by a form of 1 changes nothing, the two expressions are equal. A worked example: 3 over 4 divided by 2 over 5 equals 3 over 4 times 5 over 2, which is 15 over 8, or one and seven eighths. A sanity check confirms it: two fifths is less than one, so dividing by it should produce something bigger than three quarters, and 15 over 8 duly exceeds 1. That check, does the answer move in the direction it should, catches most slips. Two cautions. Division by zero is undefined, and this is not squeamishness: if 3 divided by 0 equalled some number q, then q times 0 would have to equal 3, but anything times 0 is 0. Nothing can be assigned consistently, which is why calculators error rather than guessing. Second, division does not commute: 3 over 4 divided by 2 over 5 is not equal to 2 over 5 divided by 3 over 4, and the two answers, 15 over 8 and 8 over 15, are reciprocals of each other, which is a useful thing to notice.

sections.heading: Fractions, Decimals and When a Decimal Terminates
sections.body: Every fraction can be written as a decimal simply by carrying out the division, and the results fall into exactly two kinds. Some terminate, like 3 over 8 equals 0.375. Others repeat forever in a fixed cycle, like 1 over 3 equals 0.333... or 1 over 7 equals 0.142857142857..., where the block 142857 recurs indefinitely. There is no third possibility, and the reason is worth understanding because it is a complete and provable rule rather than an observation. Long division of a by b can only ever produce remainders in the range 0 to b minus 1. If a remainder of 0 turns up, the process stops and the decimal terminates. If not, then after at most b minus 1 steps some remainder must repeat, by the pigeonhole principle, and once a remainder repeats the whole sequence of digits from that point repeats identically. This also bounds the period: the repeating block of 1 over 7 cannot be longer than 6 digits, and it is exactly 6. The criterion for termination is precise. Write the fraction in lowest terms; the decimal terminates exactly when the denominator's prime factorisation contains no primes other than 2 and 5. The reason is that a terminating decimal is a fraction whose denominator is a power of 10, and 10 factorises as 2 times 5. So 3 over 8 terminates because 8 is 2 cubed; 7 over 40 terminates because 40 is 2 cubed times 5; 1 over 6 does not, because 6 contains a factor of 3. The insistence on lowest terms matters: 3 over 6 looks as though it should repeat, but it reduces to 1 over 2, which terminates. Converting the other way is mechanical. A terminating decimal is read directly: 0.375 is 375 over 1000, which reduces by 125 to 3 over 8. A repeating decimal takes an algebraic trick. To convert 0.272727..., let x be that number, multiply by 100 to get 100x equal to 27.272727..., subtract the original to get 99x equal to 27, and divide to get x equal to 27 over 99, which reduces to 3 over 11. The multiplier is 10 raised to the length of the repeating block. This method proves, incidentally, that 0.999... equals exactly 1, since letting x be 0.999... gives 10x equal to 9.999..., so 9x equals 9 and x equals 1. That result is genuinely true rather than an approximation, and it disturbs people because decimal notation, unlike fraction notation, is not quite unique. The practical trade-off is exactness against convenience. Fractions are exact; decimals are easy to compare and to feed into machines, but any repeating decimal must be truncated to be stored, introducing error. Financial and engineering software that must not accumulate rounding error therefore often keeps numbers as exact integer pairs or as scaled integers rather than as binary floating point, in which even 0.1 is not representable exactly.

sections.heading: Percentages, Ratios and Proportions
sections.body: Percentages, ratios and proportions are not separate topics from fractions; they are fractions specialised for particular jobs, and seeing them as one subject removes most of the difficulty. A percentage is a fraction with denominator fixed at 100. The word comes from the Latin per centum, by the hundred, and the notation is simply a shorthand for that denominator, so 37 per cent is 37 over 100, which is 0.37. Fixing the denominator makes comparison instant, which is the whole point: judging whether 17 over 43 exceeds 23 over 58 is work, whereas 39.5 per cent against 39.7 per cent is not. Converting between forms is one operation. Fraction to percentage, multiply by 100: 3 over 8 becomes 37.5 per cent. Percentage to fraction, put it over 100 and reduce: 37.5 per cent becomes 375 over 1000, which is 3 over 8. The most common percentage error is confusing percentage points with per cent change. If a rate rises from 4 per cent to 6 per cent, that is a rise of 2 percentage points but a relative rise of 50 per cent, and headlines exploit the ambiguity routinely. A second common error is assuming percentage changes cancel. A price cut by 20 per cent then raised by 20 per cent does not return to its start: 100 becomes 80, and 80 raised by 20 per cent is 96. The multipliers are 0.8 and 1.2, and their product is 0.96, a net 4 per cent loss. Successive percentage changes multiply, they do not add, and this single fact explains a great deal of misleading advertising. A ratio compares quantities and is written with a colon, as in 3:2. It differs from a fraction in what the parts refer to. If a mixture is 3 parts cement to 2 parts sand, the ratio is 3:2, but the fraction of the mixture that is cement is 3 over 5, because the total has 5 parts. Confusing part-to-part with part-to-whole is the standard mistake, and it appears everywhere from concrete mixes to odds. In betting, odds of 3 to 1 against mean a probability of 1 over 4, not 1 over 3. A proportion is a statement that two ratios are equal, and solving one is the workhorse of practical arithmetic. If 3 kilograms of flour cost 4.50, what do 7 kilograms cost? Set up 3 over 4.50 equals 7 over x, cross-multiply to get 3x equal to 31.50, and divide to get 10.50. Scaling recipes, converting units, reading maps, mixing chemicals, calculating drug doses by body weight and enlarging drawings are all this one operation. The essential discipline is to keep units consistent on each side and to sanity check the direction: more flour must cost more, so an answer smaller than 4.50 would signal that the ratio was inverted.

sections.heading: The Rational Numbers as a Number System
sections.body: Stepping back from calculation, it is worth seeing what kind of mathematical object the rationals form, because the abstract description explains why the rules are what they are rather than leaving them as a list to memorise. The rationals form what algebraists call a field: a set with addition and multiplication obeying a short list of laws. Addition and multiplication are each commutative, meaning order does not matter, and associative, meaning grouping does not matter. There is an additive identity, 0, and a multiplicative identity, 1. Every element has an additive inverse, its negative, and every element except 0 has a multiplicative inverse, its reciprocal. Multiplication distributes over addition. The rationals are the smallest field containing the integers, which is why they are sometimes called the field of fractions of the integers, and the same construction can be run on other systems to produce, for example, rational functions from polynomials. They are also an ordered field, meaning the order relation behaves well with the arithmetic: if x is less than y then x plus z is less than y plus z for any z, and x times z is less than y times z for any positive z. That last clause carries an important warning, because multiplying an inequality by a negative number reverses it, a rule that is not a convention but a consequence. What the rationals lack is completeness. There are sequences of rationals that get arbitrarily close together yet converge to no rational number. The classic example is the sequence of decimal approximations to the square root of 2. The Pythagoreans discovered, probably in the fifth century BCE, that no fraction squares to exactly 2, and the proof is short enough to give. Suppose the square root of 2 equals a over b in lowest terms. Then a squared equals 2b squared, so a squared is even, so a is even, say a equals 2k. Substituting gives 4k squared equals 2b squared, so b squared equals 2k squared, so b is also even. But then a and b share a factor of 2, contradicting lowest terms. The assumption must therefore be false. Legend has it the discovery was scandalous, and the story that the Pythagorean Hippasus was drowned for revealing it is almost certainly a later embellishment, though the intellectual shock was real. Filling the gaps requires the real numbers, constructed rigorously only in the 1870s by Richard Dedekind, using cuts in the rationals, and by Georg Cantor, using convergent sequences. Cantor also showed something still more surprising: the rationals are countable, meaning they can be listed in a sequence, while the reals are not, so in a precise sense almost every real number is irrational.

sections.heading: Fractions in Measurement, Trade and Everyday Life
sections.body: Fractions survive in daily life wherever a system of measurement is built on repeated halving, and that turns out to be most traditional systems, because halving is the one division that can be done reliably by eye and by folding. The imperial and US customary systems are the clearest case. An inch divides into halves, quarters, eighths, sixteenths, thirty-seconds and sixty-fourths, and a tape measure is graduated accordingly. This looks primitive beside millimetres until you notice what it buys: any of those subdivisions can be found by folding or by stepping dividers, without arithmetic, and adding sixteenths is easy because the denominators are already compatible. A carpenter reading five and three sixteenths adds and subtracts such quantities all day without converting anything. The drawback appears when denominators must be mixed, and the standard method is to convert everything to the finest denominator present, add, then reduce: three eighths plus five sixteenths becomes six sixteenths plus five sixteenths, which is eleven sixteenths. Cooking works the same way, with cups divided into halves, thirds and quarters, and scaling recipes is proportional reasoning under another name. Halving a recipe calling for three quarters of a cup means computing three eighths, which is not a standard measure, so a cook converts to tablespoons: a cup is 16 tablespoons, so three eighths of a cup is 6 tablespoons. That conversion is a change of denominator, no different in principle from finding a common denominator to add. Music is fractional through and through. A whole note divides into two halves, four quarters, eight eighths; a time signature of 3 over 4 states three quarter-note beats per bar. Musical intervals are frequency ratios, and the simplest ratios sound most consonant: an octave is 2:1, a perfect fifth 3:2, a perfect fourth 4:3, a major third 5:4. The Pythagorean discovery that harmony corresponds to simple whole-number ratios is one of the oldest links between mathematics and physical experience. It also produces a famous problem: twelve perfect fifths, each 3 over 2, should close the circle back to seven octaves, but 3 over 2 to the twelfth power is about 129.746 while 2 to the seventh is 128, a discrepancy of roughly 1.36 per cent called the Pythagorean comma. Equal temperament resolves it by abandoning exact ratios altogether and spacing semitones at the twelfth root of 2, an irrational number, so every fifth is very slightly flat. Financial systems retain fractions too. Stock prices were quoted in eighths of a dollar on US exchanges until decimalisation in 2001, a legacy of Spanish silver dollars physically cut into eight pieces of eight. Bond markets still quote in thirty-seconds. Interest rates move in basis points, one hundredth of a percentage point, which is a fraction with denominator 10000.

sections.heading: Continued Fractions and the Best Approximations
sections.body: There is a way of writing numbers that fractions make possible and decimals do not, and it produces the most efficient rational approximations that exist. A continued fraction expresses a number as an integer plus one over an integer plus one over an integer, and so on. It looks awkward written out but is generated by an entirely mechanical procedure: take the whole part, subtract it, invert the remainder, and repeat. Take 415 over 93. The whole part is 4, leaving 43 over 93. Inverting gives 93 over 43, whose whole part is 2, leaving 7 over 43. Inverting gives 43 over 7, whose whole part is 6, leaving 1 over 7. Inverting gives 7, and the process ends. The sequence of whole parts, 4, 2, 6, 7, is the continued fraction expansion, and it terminates precisely because the number is rational. In fact the algorithm is the Euclidean algorithm in disguise, which is why it always halts for rationals. Truncating the expansion partway gives a convergent, and convergents have a remarkable property: each is the best rational approximation to the number among all fractions with denominator no larger. Nothing else gets closer without a bigger denominator. This makes continued fractions the right tool whenever a simple fraction must stand in for an awkward number. The most famous instance is pi, whose expansion begins 3, 7, 15, 1, 292. Truncating after the first term gives 22 over 7, accurate to about 0.04 per cent, known to Archimedes in the third century BCE. Truncating after 15 and 1 gives 355 over 113, which matches pi to seven decimal places, an error below three parts in ten million; it was found by the Chinese mathematician Zu Chongzhi in the fifth century and is astonishingly good for such a small denominator. The reason is the unusually large next term, 292, which signals that truncating just before it loses very little. Continued fractions also expose structure that decimals conceal. The golden ratio has the expansion 1, 1, 1, 1 and so on forever, all ones, which makes it in a precise sense the hardest number to approximate by fractions, a fact connected to the appearance of Fibonacci numbers in plant spirals. The square root of 2 is 1 followed by 2 repeating forever. Every quadratic irrational, meaning a solution of a quadratic equation with integer coefficients, has an eventually periodic expansion, a theorem proved by Lagrange in 1770, and this gives a clean criterion that decimal expansions cannot supply. The practical uses are real. Gear ratios, calendar design and musical temperament all reduce to approximating an awkward ratio with small whole numbers. The Gregorian calendar's rule of 97 leap days in 400 years approximates the tropical year, and the Metonic cycle of 19 years to 235 lunar months, known in Babylon and to Meton of Athens by 432 BCE, is a convergent of the ratio between the two.

sections.heading: Working a Problem: A Reliable Procedure
sections.body: Most fraction errors are procedural rather than conceptual, in the sense that the person knows the rules but applies them in a disorderly way and loses track. A fixed routine, applied even when it feels unnecessary, removes the majority of mistakes, and the discipline of estimating before computing is the single most valuable habit in the list because it catches errors of a whole order of magnitude that careful arithmetic will never notice. The routine below assumes pencil and paper and no calculator, which is the situation in which it matters. Every step is cheap; skipping steps to save time is a false economy that costs more in re-checking. It is also worth noticing that the same routine handles every question in the subject, because scaling a recipe, converting a measurement, working out a discount and solving a proportion are all the same four operations wearing different clothes. The differences between them lie entirely in the translation step at the start and the interpretation step at the end, which is why those two steps deserve more attention than the arithmetic sandwiched between them.
steps: Read the problem and decide which operation is wanted, translating the words first: of means multiply, per and each usually mean divide, and total or altogether means add.
Convert every mixed number to an improper fraction before doing anything else, so that two and three quarters becomes 11 over 4 and no invisible plus signs remain.

Estimate the answer with whole numbers or benchmarks before computing, so that 7 over 8 plus 11 over 12 is recognised as a little less than 2, and any later answer near one half is instantly known to be wrong.
For addition or subtraction, find the least common denominator by factorising both denominators, then rewrite both fractions with it, multiplying numerator and denominator by the same factor.
For multiplication, cancel common factors across the diagonal first, then multiply straight across, which keeps every intermediate number small.
For division, rewrite as multiplication by the reciprocal of the second fraction, then proceed exactly as for multiplication.
Carry out the arithmetic, writing each rewriting on its own line rather than in the head; most slips happen at the moment a step is done mentally to save writing.
Reduce the result to lowest terms by finding the greatest common divisor of numerator and denominator, using the Euclidean algorithm if the numbers are large.
Convert back to a mixed number if the context calls for it, since a joiner wants two and five eighths of an inch, not 21 over 8.
Check the answer against the estimate, check that the units are what the question asked for, and check the direction of the result: dividing by something less than 1 must have made it bigger.

sections.heading: Common Misconceptions and Where They Come From
sections.body: The errors learners make with fractions are strikingly consistent across countries and decades, which suggests they are not carelessness but the predictable result of over-generalising from whole numbers. Naming them makes them far easier to unlearn. The most widespread is adding numerators and denominators separately, so that one half plus one third is reported as two fifths. This comes from applying the pattern of whole-number addition to a symbol that looks like two numbers stacked. The cure is not repetition of the rule but the unit argument: you cannot count halves and thirds together any more than you can add three metres to forty centimetres without converting. Interestingly, the operation that adds tops and bottoms separately is not meaningless; it gives the mediant, which always lies between the two fractions and is genuinely useful in the study of Farey sequences and in some voting-share calculations, so the instinct is not stupid, merely misapplied. The second is judging fractions by denominator size, concluding that one eighth exceeds one fifth because 8 exceeds 5. The underlying error is treating the denominator as a count rather than as a divisor, and the fix is the sharing picture: a cake split eight ways gives smaller slices than one split five ways. The third is believing multiplication always makes things bigger and division always smaller. Both fail whenever the second number lies between 0 and 1. The fix is the measurement reading: multiplying by one half means taking half, and dividing by one half means asking how many halves fit in. The fourth is cancelling across a sum, writing something like the 3 in (3 plus 4) over 3 and striking it out to leave 4. Cancellation is valid only for factors, never for terms, because it is really division of the whole numerator and the whole denominator by the same quantity. Testing with numbers settles it instantly: (3 plus 4) over 3 is 7 over 3, not 4. The fifth concerns the whole. A fraction is meaningless without knowing what it is a fraction of, and comparing one half of a small pizza with one third of a large one is not a fraction question. Much misleading statistics exploits exactly this, quoting percentage changes without stating the base. Finally, mixed numbers cause trouble when algebra arrives, because two and a half written as adjacent symbols means addition while 2x means multiplication. This is a genuine defect in the notation rather than a failure of the learner, and it is one reason mathematicians beyond school level almost always write improper fractions instead. What unites all six errors is the assumption that a fraction is two numbers rather than one. Every cure consists of returning to a physical model, a shared cake, a length on a ruler, a rectangle of area, in which the fraction is a single quantity and the wrong answer is visibly absurd. Rules memorised without such a model are fragile and decay within months; rules attached to a picture survive.

sections.heading: Exact Rational Arithmetic in Computing
sections.body: Computers do not naturally handle fractions, and understanding why explains a class of bugs that regularly reaches production software and occasionally the news. Standard computer arithmetic uses binary floating point, standardised as IEEE 754 in 1985 and revised in 2008 and 2019. A double-precision number stores a sign, an 11-bit exponent and a 53-bit significand, representing a value as a binary fraction times a power of two. This is fast, has a huge range, and is exact for any number expressible with a denominator that is a power of 2. It is not exact for anything else, and crucially that includes 0.1, because one tenth in binary repeats forever exactly as one third does in decimal. The stored value is very slightly more than 0.1, which is why in most languages 0.1 plus 0.2 prints as 0.30000000000000004 and why testing floating-point results for exact equality is a mistake. The consequences are not merely cosmetic. Repeated addition accumulates error, and a well-documented case occurred in 1991 when a Patriot missile battery at Dhahran failed to intercept an incoming Scud; its internal clock counted tenths of a second in a 24-bit fixed-point representation, and after about 100 hours of continuous operation the accumulated rounding error had grown to roughly a third of a second, enough to misplace the target by over half a kilometre. Twenty-eight people died. Financial systems face a quieter version of the same problem, which is why currency is normally stored as an integer number of the smallest unit, cents or pennies, or in a decimal type, rather than as a floating-point number of pounds. Exact rational arithmetic is the alternative. A rational is stored as a pair of arbitrary-precision integers and every operation is performed by the rules of fraction arithmetic, with the result reduced by the greatest common divisor after each step. Python's fractions.Fraction, Java's BigDecimal for the decimal case, and the rational types built into computer algebra systems such as Mathematica, Maxima and SageMath all work this way. The arithmetic is exact: a sum of thirds really equals 1, and no error ever accumulates. The cost is performance and growth. Rational arithmetic is perhaps one to two orders of magnitude slower than hardware floating point, and worse, numerators and denominators grow.
