Adding fractions with unrelated denominators multiplies them, so a long chain of additions can produce integers with thousands of digits even when the value stays small, which is why reduction after every operation is mandatory rather than optional. The practical rule is to use exact rationals where correctness is the binding constraint, in symbolic computation, in accounting, and in geometric predicates where a sign error crashes an algorithm, and floating point where speed matters and a known small error is acceptable.

sections.heading: Limits of the Rationals and What Comes Next
sections.body: Fractions are powerful enough to have carried mathematics for thousands of years and remain sufficient for most practical measurement, yet they have definite limits, and knowing where those limits fall is part of understanding the tool. The first limit is that many perfectly ordinary geometric quantities are not rational. The diagonal of a unit square is the square root of 2, the circumference of a unit-diameter circle is pi, and the growth constant of continuous compounding is e. None can be written as a ratio of integers. The square root of 2 was proved irrational by the Pythagoreans; pi was shown irrational by Johann Lambert in 1761 and transcendental, meaning it is not the root of any polynomial with rational coefficients, by Ferdinand von Lindemann in 1882, which settled the ancient problem of squaring the circle with compass and straightedge in the negative. In practice this limit is soft rather than hard, because a rational approximation can be made as close as desired, and 355 over 113 is closer to pi than any physical measurement of a real circle will ever be. The second limit is more structural. The rationals have gaps in the sense that a sequence can march steadily toward a target that is not in the set, which means limits, continuity and calculus cannot be built on them. The nineteenth-century construction of the real numbers by Dedekind and Cantor exists precisely to fill those gaps, and everything from integration to differential equations depends on the completeness that results. The third limit is that some equations still have no solution. The rationals cannot solve x squared equal to negative 1, which requires the complex numbers, developed through the sixteenth-century work of Cardano and Bombelli on cubic equations and made respectable only in the nineteenth century. There is also a subtler point about what fractions cannot express in the first place. A fraction compares two quantities of the same kind, and there are important quantities, notably probabilities of continuous events and irrational proportions in nature, where the fraction model gives an approximation rather than a description. Physical measurement is always uncertain, so quoting a measurement as an exact fraction is often a false precision; the honest form carries an uncertainty. None of these limits diminishes the fraction's standing. The rationals remain the natural home of exact computation, the foundation on which the reals are built, the language of proportion in trade, cooking, music and construction, and the first place where a learner meets the idea that a number can have many names. Getting comfortable with that one idea, that 2 over 4 and 1 over 2 are not two numbers but one, is genuinely the hinge on which most later mathematics turns.

guides.title: Decimals and Decimal Arithmetic
guides.summary: A thorough treatment of decimal numbers: what place value actually means, how the four arithmetic operations work on decimals and why the rules are what they are, the relationship between decimals and fractions, repeating expansions, rounding, scientific notation, and the errors that decimals introduce in measurement and in computers.

sections.heading: What a Decimal Really Says
sections.body:
A decimal is not a different kind of number from a fraction or a whole number. It is a notation, a way of writing a number down, and understanding what the notation asserts is the whole of the subject. When somebody writes 3.472, they are making a compact claim about a sum: three units, plus four tenths, plus seven hundredths, plus two thousandths. Written out, that is 3 plus 4/10 plus 7/100 plus 2/1000. The decimal point is simply a marker announcing where the whole units stop and the fractional parts begin, and every position to its right is worth one tenth of the position to its left.

This is the same idea that already governs the digits to the left of the point. In 3472, the digits mean three thousands, four hundreds, seven tens and two units, and each position is worth ten times the one to its right. Decimal notation does nothing new; it simply continues an existing pattern past the units column instead of stopping there. The positions running rightward are tenths, hundredths, thousandths, ten-thousandths, hundred-thousandths, millionths, and so on indefinitely, corresponding to 10 to the power minus one, minus two, minus three and downward. A number like 3.472 can therefore be written as 3 times 10 to the power 0, plus 4 times 10 to the power minus 1, plus 7 times 10 to the power minus 2, plus 2 times 10 to the power minus 3, and every operation performed on decimals is ultimately justified by that expansion.

The power of the notation is that it makes comparison, ordering and arithmetic almost mechanical. To decide whether 0.4 or 0.35 is larger, no common denominator has to be found; one simply compares the tenths digit, sees 4 against 3, and stops. Doing the same with 2/5 and 7/20 requires converting both to twentieths. That convenience is the reason decimals dominate money, measurement, science and computing, while fractions survive mainly where exactness matters more than convenience.

The word decimal comes from the Latin decimus, meaning tenth, and the whole system rests on the choice of ten as the base, an accident of human anatomy rather than a mathematical necessity. Other bases work identically. In base two, the positions after the point are halves, quarters, eighths and sixteenths, and 0.101 in binary means one half plus zero quarters plus one eighth, which is 0.625 in our ordinary notation. Recognising that base ten is a convention and not a law is the key to understanding why some perfectly ordinary numbers, like one third, refuse to terminate in decimal form, and why computers, which work in base two, cannot represent one tenth exactly at all.

sections.heading: Place Value, Zero and Why Trailing Zeros Are Not Always Idle
sections.body:
Place value is the machinery that makes decimal arithmetic possible, and it depends absolutely on having a symbol for nothing. Without zero there is no way to distinguish 502 from 52, or 0.05 from 0.5, because the notation carries meaning in position and a position must be occupied to be read. The positional system with a true zero reached Europe through the work of Arab mathematicians, notably Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi in the ninth century, drawing on Indian mathematics where Brahmagupta had set out rules for zero as a number in 628. Fibonacci's Liber Abaci of 1202 pushed it into European commerce, though decimal fractions specifically were popularised much later, by the Flemish engineer Simon Stevin in his 1585 pamphlet De Thiende, and the modern decimal point was fixed in place largely through John Napier's work on logarithms in the early seventeenth century.

Two habits confuse learners, and both concern zeros. A zero written to the left of all significant digits in the whole part, as in 007, changes nothing about the value; it is padding. Likewise a zero written after the last significant digit to the right of the point, as in 2.50, does not change the value: 2.50 equals 2.5 exactly, because five tenths and zero hundredths is the same quantity as five tenths. The leading zero written before the point in 0.75 is likewise not a value; it is a typographic convention that stops a reader missing the point altogether, and in careful technical writing it is mandatory for exactly that reason.

But trailing zeros are not always idle, and this is where mathematics meets measurement. In pure arithmetic 2.5 and 2.50 are the same number. In a laboratory or a workshop they are different statements. Writing a length as 2.5 metres implies the measurement is good to the nearest tenth, so the true value lies somewhere between 2.45 and 2.55. Writing 2.50 metres implies it is good to the nearest hundredth, so the true value lies between 2.495 and 2.505, a claim ten times more precise. The digits that carry this information are called significant figures, and a trailing zero after the decimal point is always significant. Discarding it destroys real information about how well the quantity is known.

Reading a decimal aloud correctly reinforces the structure. The number 0.406 should be read as four hundred six thousandths, or as zero point four zero six, but never as zero point four hundred and six, which invites the reader to mistake the fractional part for a whole number. Similarly the final position names the whole fractional part: since the last digit of 0.406 sits in the thousandths column, the whole fraction is 406/1000. That single observation converts any terminating decimal to a fraction instantly.

sections.heading: Comparing and Ordering Decimals
sections.body:
Comparing decimals looks trivial and is one of the most reliably misunderstood operations in elementary mathematics, because a habit learned from whole numbers actively misleads. With whole numbers, more digits means a bigger number: 1000 beats 99 without any thought. Applied to decimals this rule fails immediately. The number 0.9 is larger than 0.85, which is larger than 0.7999, even though the digit counts run the other way. Researchers who study arithmetic learning call this the longer-is-larger misconception, and it persists into adulthood in a surprising fraction of the population.

A second and opposite error, sometimes called shorter-is-larger, arises when a learner over-corrects by reasoning that more decimal places means smaller pieces, so a number with more places must be smaller. That yields the false conclusion that 0.3 is bigger than 0.45. Both errors come from treating the digit string as an object rather than reading the place values it encodes.

The reliable method is to compare position by position from the left, exactly as one would compare words alphabetically. First compare the whole-number parts. If they differ, the comparison is settled. If they are equal, compare the tenths digits; if those are equal, compare the hundredths, and so on, stopping at the first position where the digits differ. Whichever number has the larger digit at that first point of difference is the larger number, regardless of what follows. To compare 5.4029 with 5.41, the whole parts match at 5 and the tenths match at 4, but the hundredths are 0 against 1, so 5.41 is larger, even though 5.4029 has more digits.

A practical aid is to pad the shorter number with trailing zeros until both have the same number of decimal places, since appending zeros never changes a value. To compare 0.7 with 0.6982, rewrite 0.7 as 0.7000; now both are four-place decimals, and comparing 7000 ten-thousandths against 6982 ten-thousandths is an ordinary whole-number comparison. This padding trick is worth teaching explicitly because it converts an unfamiliar problem into a familiar one and eliminates both misconceptions at once.

Ordering a list follows the same rule applied repeatedly. To arrange 0.5, 0.05, 0.55, 0.505 and 0.055 in increasing order, pad everything to three places, giving 0.500, 0.050, 0.550, 0.505 and 0.055, then read them as 500, 50, 550, 505 and 55 thousandths, which sort as 50, 55, 500, 505, 550. The original order is therefore 0.05, 0.055, 0.5, 0.505, 0.55.

Negative decimals reverse the sense of the comparison, as with all negative numbers. Between minus 0.3 and minus 0.25, the one closer to zero is the larger, so minus 0.25 exceeds minus 0.3, even though 0.3 exceeds 0.25. The safe procedure is to compare magnitudes first and then reverse the result.

sections.heading: Addition and Subtraction: Why the Points Must Line Up
sections.body:
The rule everyone remembers for adding decimals is to line up the decimal points. The rule is correct, but stated that way it sounds arbitrary, and students who learn it as a ritual routinely misapply it. The real rule is that you may only add digits that represent the same thing, and lining up the points is simply the mechanical way of guaranteeing that tenths sit above tenths and hundredths above hundredths. It is the identical principle that makes you line up the units column when adding whole numbers; nobody would add 47 and 5 by placing the 5 under the 4.

Consider adding 12.7 and 3.45. Written with the points aligned, the tenths column holds 7 and 4, the hundredths column holds nothing and 5. Padding 12.7 to 12.70 makes the structure explicit, because the empty hundredths position genuinely holds zero hundredths. Now the hundredths give 0 plus 5, or 5. The tenths give 7 plus 4, which is 11 tenths; since ten tenths make one unit, write 1 in the tenths place and carry 1 into the units. The units give 2 plus 3 plus the carried 1, which is 6. The tens give 1. The answer is 16.15. Every carry in decimal arithmetic is the same event: ten of something in one column has been exchanged for one of the next thing to the left, exactly as ten pennies become a dime.

Subtraction works identically, with borrowing as the reverse exchange. To compute 8.3 minus 4.756, pad the first number to 8.300 so both have three decimal places. Working right to left, the thousandths column asks for 0 minus 6, which requires borrowing: take one hundredth from the hundredths column, but that column is also zero, so borrow again from the tenths. The tenths 3 becomes 2, the hundredths become 10, then one hundredth is passed down so the hundredths become 9 and the thousandths become 10. Now 10 minus 6 is 4, 9 minus 5 is 4, 2 minus 7 requires borrowing from the units, giving 12 minus 7 equals 5, and 7 minus 4 is 3. The result is 3.544.

Two habits protect against error. First, always pad to a common number of decimal places before starting; the great majority of misalignment mistakes disappear. Second, estimate before computing. Since 8.3 minus 4.756 is roughly 8 minus 5, the answer should be near 3, and an answer of 3.544 passes, whereas 4.544 or 0.354 would not. Estimation costs a couple of seconds and catches misplaced points, the single most damaging class of decimal error, because a misplaced point is wrong by a factor of ten rather than by a little.

sections.heading: Multiplication: Counting the Decimal Places
sections.body:
Multiplying decimals is taught with a rule that seems, at first encounter, to have nothing to do with the rule for addition: ignore the decimal points, multiply as though both numbers were whole, then place the point in the answer so that it has as many decimal places as the two factors had together. Unlike addition, the points do not need to line up, which strikes many learners as inconsistent. It is not; it follows directly from what the notation means.

The justification uses powers of ten. The number 3.4 is 34 divided by 10, and 0.25 is 25 divided by 100. Their product is therefore 34 times 25, divided by 10 times 100, which is 850 divided by 1000, or 0.850, that is 0.85. The one-decimal-place factor contributed a division by 10 to the power one, the two-place factor contributed a division by 10 to the power two, and the exponents added because that is what happens when powers with the same base are multiplied. One decimal place plus two decimal places gives three decimal places in the raw product, and 850 with the point three places from the right is 0.850. The rule is nothing more than bookkeeping for the exponents.

A worked example fixes the method. To find 12.5 times 0.04, first multiply 125 by 4 to get 500. The factors carry one and two decimal places respectively, three in total, so place the point three from the right in 500, which requires padding to 0.500, giving 0.5. A sanity check confirms it: 0.04 is about one twenty-fifth, and a twenty-fifth of 12.5 is 0.5.

Two behaviours surprise people. Multiplying by a number less than one makes the result smaller, not larger, which contradicts the intuition built from whole numbers that multiplication always increases. Multiplying 60 by 0.5 gives 30 because taking a half of something is exactly what multiplying by 0.5 means. Conversely, multiplying by a number between zero and one is the same as taking a fraction of the quantity, and this equivalence is what makes percentages tractable: 18 per cent of 250 is 0.18 times 250, which is 45.

Multiplying and dividing by powers of ten deserve separate attention because they are so common. Multiplying by 10 shifts every digit one place to the left relative to the point, which in practice looks like moving the point one place to the right: 4.62 times 10 is 46.2. Multiplying by 100 moves it two places, by 1000 three places. Dividing does the reverse: 4.62 divided by 100 is 0.0462, with zeros inserted as placeholders. Describing this as moving the decimal point is a convenient fiction, since strictly the digits move and the point stays put, but the fiction is harmless as long as the direction is right, and estimating first will catch it when it is not.

sections.heading: Division: Turning the Divisor into a Whole Number
sections.body:
Division by a decimal is the operation that most often defeats mental arithmetic, and the standard technique is a genuinely elegant piece of reasoning rather than a trick. The problem is that long division is comfortable only when the divisor is a whole number. The solution is to convert the problem into an equivalent one that has a whole-number divisor, exploiting the fact that multiplying both the dividend and the divisor by the same number leaves the quotient unchanged. This is exactly the property of fractions that lets 6/4 be rewritten as 3/2.

To compute 8.4 divided by 0.35, multiply both numbers by 100. The divisor 0.35 becomes 35, a whole number, and the dividend 8.4 becomes 840. The problem is now 840 divided by 35, which is 24. The answer to the original problem is therefore also 24. In practice this is described as moving the decimal point in the divisor to the right until it disappears, then moving it the same number of places in the dividend, and the description is accurate provided one remembers why: both numbers were multiplied by the same power of ten.

Dividing by a whole number requires only that the decimal point in the quotient be placed directly above the point in the dividend, after which the division proceeds exactly as with whole numbers. To compute 7.35 divided by 5, place the point above, then divide: 7 divided by 5 is 1 remainder 2; bring down the 3 to make 23; 23 divided by 5 is 4 remainder 3; bring down the 5 to make 35; 35 divided by 5 is 7 exactly. The quotient is 1.47.

When the division does not terminate, the dividend can be extended indefinitely with zeros, because appending zeros after the point does not change its value. Computing 1 divided by 8 begins by writing 1 as 1.000: 10 divided by 8 is 1 remainder 2, 20 divided by 8 is 2 remainder 4, 40 divided by 8 is 5 remainder 0, so the answer is 0.125 exactly. Computing 1 divided by 3 gives 3 remainder 1 at every stage forever, producing 0.3333 without end.

The same counter-intuition that appears in multiplication appears here in mirror image: dividing by a number smaller than one makes the result larger. Dividing 5 by 0.1 gives 50, because the question being asked is how many tenths fit into five, and the answer is fifty. Reading division as a question about how many of the divisor fit into the dividend is the most reliable way to keep the direction straight, and it makes the result obvious in cases where the rule alone would leave doubt.

sections.heading: Converting Between Decimals and Fractions
sections.body:
Every terminating decimal is a fraction whose denominator is a power of ten, and reading that fraction off the notation takes no calculation at all. The position of the final digit names the denominator. In 0.4 the last digit sits in the tenths place, so the number is 4/10, which reduces to 2/5. In 0.375 the last digit sits in the thousandths place, so the number is 375/1000; dividing top and bottom by 125 gives 3/8. In 2.06 the fractional part ends in hundredths, so the number is 2 and 6/100, or 2 and 3/50, or as an improper fraction 103/50. The whole procedure is: write the digits after the point as the numerator, write 1 followed by as many zeros as there are decimal places as the denominator, then reduce.

Going the other way, from fraction to decimal, is simply division: 3/8 means 3 divided by 8, which long division gives as 0.375. But an important structural question lurks behind it. Which fractions terminate and which do not? The answer is exact and provable. A fraction in lowest terms terminates as a decimal if and only if its denominator, after reduction, has no prime factors other than 2 and 5. The reason is that a terminating decimal is by definition a fraction over some power of ten, and ten factorises as 2 times 5, so any power of ten has only 2s and 5s in its prime factorisation. A denominator of 8, which is 2 cubed, terminates. A denominator of 20, which is 2 squared times 5, terminates. A denominator of 3, 6, 7, 9, 11 or 12 does not, because each contains a prime factor other than 2 or 5.

This test is quick and worth internalising. One seventh cannot terminate because 7 is neither 2 nor 5, and indeed 1/7 equals 0.142857142857 repeating with a six-digit cycle. One sixth cannot terminate because 6 contains a 3, and 1/6 equals 0.16666 repeating. But 7/56 looks non-terminating until it is reduced to 1/8, which terminates at 0.125; the test applies only after reduction to lowest terms.

A useful working set of equivalences is worth memorising outright, because it removes most everyday conversion work: 1/2 is 0.5, 1/4 is 0.25, 3/4 is 0.75, 1/5 is 0.2, 1/8 is 0.125, 3/8 is 0.375, 5/8 is 0.625, 7/8 is 0.875, 1/3 is approximately 0.333, 2/3 is approximately 0.667, 1/10 is 0.1, 1/16 is 0.0625 and 1/100 is 0.01. Tradespeople working in imperial units effectively memorise the sixteenths table for exactly this reason, since a rule marked in sixteenths must constantly be reconciled with a caliper reading in thousandths. A sixteenth is 0.0625, an eighth 0.125, a thirty-second 0.03125, and a sixty-fourth 0.015625, each exactly half the one before, so the whole table can be reconstructed from a single remembered value by repeated halving rather than memorised outright.

sections.heading: Repeating Decimals and How to Convert Them Back
sections.body:
When a fraction fails the terminating test, its decimal expansion does not simply wander; it repeats, and it must repeat. The reason is a counting argument. Dividing by a denominator n can produce only n possible remainders, namely 0 through n minus 1. If a remainder of 0 ever appears, the division terminates. If not, then within at most n steps some earlier remainder must reappear, because there are only finitely many to choose from, and once a remainder repeats, the entire subsequent sequence of digits repeats identically. This guarantees that every fraction has an expansion that either terminates or eventually falls into a cycle, and it bounds the cycle length at n minus 1 digits.

The bound is achieved surprisingly often. One seventh repeats with period six, the maximum for a denominator of seven: 0.142857 recurring. One thirteenth has period six as well: 0.076923 recurring. One seventeenth achieves the maximum period of sixteen. Denominators like these, whose reciprocals have the longest possible cycle, are called full reptend primes, and 7, 17, 19, 23 and 29 are among them. The digits of 1/7 have the further curiosity that the six cyclic shifts of 142857 are exactly the expansions of 2/7 through 6/7, so 142857 multiplied by any of 1 through 6 gives a rearrangement of the same digits.

Notation for repetition varies. A bar over the repeating block is standard in most textbooks, a dot over the first and last digits of the block is common in Britain, and writing several cycles followed by an ellipsis is unambiguous in plain text. The repeating block is called the repetend or period.

Converting a repeating decimal back to a fraction uses a small piece of algebra that is worth doing once slowly. Let x equal 0.4444 recurring. Multiply both sides by 10, since the repeating block is one digit long, giving 10x equals 4.4444 recurring. Subtract the first equation from the second: the infinite tails are identical and cancel exactly, leaving 9x equals 4, so x is 4/9. For a two-digit block, multiply by 100. Let x equal 0.272727 recurring; then 100x equals 27.272727 recurring, subtraction gives 99x equals 27, and x is 27/99, which reduces to 3/11.

Mixed cases, where some digits precede the repeating block, need two multiplications. Let x equal 0.16666 recurring. Multiply by 10 to move past the non-repeating digit, giving 10x equals 1.6666 recurring, then by 100 giving 100x equals 16.6666 recurring. Subtracting yields 90x equals 15, so x is 15/90, which is 1/6. The same machinery proves the result that unsettles most people on first meeting: 0.9999 recurring equals exactly 1, since letting x be 0.999 recurring gives 10x minus x equals 9, so x equals 1. This is not an approximation or a convention; the two notations name the same number.

sections.heading: Irrational Numbers and Expansions That Never Repeat
sections.body:
The classification of decimal expansions turns out to divide all real numbers into exactly two classes, and the boundary is one of the most important in mathematics. If a decimal expansion terminates, the number is a fraction. If it repeats, the number is also a fraction, since the algebraic subtraction method converts any repeating expansion into a ratio of whole numbers. Taken together, these mean that any number whose decimal expansion is eventually predictable is rational, expressible as a ratio of two integers. The contrapositive is the interesting part: a number whose decimal expansion neither terminates nor ever settles into a repeating cycle cannot be written as a fraction at all. Such numbers are called irrational.

That irrational numbers exist was proved in ancient Greece, traditionally attributed to the Pythagoreans in the fifth century BCE, and the proof concerns the square root of two, the length of the diagonal of a unit square. The argument is by contradiction. Suppose the root of two could be written as a fraction a over b in lowest terms. Squaring gives a squared equals 2 b squared, so a squared is even, so a is even, so a equals 2c for some whole number c. Substituting gives 4c squared equals 2 b squared, so b squared equals 2 c squared, so b is even too. But a and b were assumed to have no common factor, and both being even contradicts that. The supposition fails, so no such fraction exists. The root of two begins 1.41421356 and continues forever without pattern.

Other familiar irrationals include pi, the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter, proved irrational by Johann Lambert in 1761 and beginning 3.14159265; the base of natural logarithms e, approximately 2.71828183, proved irrational by Euler; and the golden ratio, exactly one plus root five all divided by two, approximately 1.61803399. The square root of any whole number that is not a perfect square is irrational.

The practical consequence is that irrational numbers can never be written down exactly in decimal notation, only approximated. Every calculator display of pi is a truncation. This is not a defect of decimals specifically; it is a fact about the numbers. Fractions cannot capture them either, which is precisely what irrationality means, and other notations that do capture them exactly, such as writing the symbol for the root of two, do so by naming the number rather than by expressing its size digit by digit.

Counter-intuitively, the irrationals vastly outnumber the rationals. Georg Cantor showed in the 1870s that the rationals can be put into one-to-one correspondence with the counting numbers while the reals cannot, so in a precise sense almost every real number is irrational and almost every decimal expansion is patternless. The tidy terminating decimals of everyday life are a vanishingly small and highly unrepresentative sample of the numbers that exist.

sections.heading: Rounding, Truncation and Significant Figures
sections.body:
Because most real quantities cannot be written exactly, and because more digits than are meaningful are worse than useless, decimals almost always have to be shortened. The two ways of shortening are fundamentally different and confusing them causes real errors. Truncation simply discards the unwanted digits: 3.678 truncated to two places is 3.67. Rounding chooses the nearest representable value: 3.678 rounded to two places is 3.68. Truncation always biases downward in magnitude, so a long series of truncated values accumulates a systematic error, whereas rounding scatters errors in both directions and they partially cancel.

The conventional rounding rule is to look at the first digit being discarded. If it is 5 or more, increase the last retained digit by one; if it is 4 or less, leave it. So 2.34 becomes 2.3 and 2.36 becomes 2.4 to one decimal place. Rounding can cascade: 1.996 rounded to two places gives 2.00, because the 9 in the hundredths place becomes 10, carrying into the tenths and then the units.

The exact halfway case is genuinely ambiguous, and the common rule of always rounding a trailing 5 upward introduces a small upward bias, since it treats the tie asymmetrically. Statisticians and metrologists therefore often use round-half-to-even, also called banker's rounding, in which a tie goes to whichever choice leaves the last digit even: 2.5 rounds to 2, 3.5 rounds to 4, 0.125 rounds to 0.12. Over many values the biases cancel. This is the default in the IEEE 754 standard that governs computer floating-point arithmetic, which is why a spreadsheet occasionally rounds a tie in the direction a user does not expect.

Significant figures express precision differently from decimal places, and the distinction matters. Decimal places count positions after the point; significant figures count meaningful digits from the first non-zero digit onward. The number 0.004072 has six decimal places but only four significant figures, since leading zeros merely locate the point. Rounded to two significant figures it is 0.0041; rounded to two decimal places it is 0.00.

The practical rules for carrying precision through calculations are worth stating. For multiplication and division, the result should carry no more significant figures than the least precise input: 3.6 times 2.14159 should be reported as 7.7, not 7.709724, because the first factor is known only to two figures. For addition and subtraction, the result should carry no more decimal places than the least precise input: 12.7 plus 3.451 should be reported as 16.2, not 16.151. And rounding should be done once, at the end; rounding intermediate results and then rounding again compounds the error, a mistake known as double rounding, which can shift a final digit even when each individual rounding was performed correctly.

sections.heading: Scientific Notation and Working with Very Large or Very Small Numbers
sections.body:
Decimal notation becomes unwieldy at extremes. The mass of an electron written out is 0.000000000000000000000000000000910938 kilograms, and counting the zeros is both tedious and error-prone. Scientific notation solves this by separating a number's digits from its scale. Any non-zero number is written as a coefficient between 1 and 10, not including 10, multiplied by a power of ten. The electron mass becomes 9.10938 times 10 to the power minus 31. The speed of light, 299,792,458 metres per second, becomes 2.99792458 times 10 to the power 8. Avogadro's number is 6.02214076 times 10 to the power 23, and the Planck constant is 6.62607015 times 10 to the power minus 34 joule seconds.

Converting into the notation is a matter of counting places. Move the point until exactly one non-zero digit stands before it, then record how many places it moved and in which direction. Moving left gives a positive exponent, because the original number was large; moving right gives a negative exponent. The number 47,300 becomes 4.73 times 10 to the power 4, since the point moved four places left. The number 0.00062 becomes 6.2 times 10 to the power minus 4, since the point moved four places right.

Arithmetic in scientific notation follows the exponent laws. To multiply, multiply the coefficients and add the exponents: 3 times 10 to the 5, times 2 times 10 to the 7, is 6 times 10 to the 12. To divide, divide the coefficients and subtract the exponents. If the resulting coefficient falls outside the range 1 to 10, renormalise: 5 times 10 to the 4 times 4 times 10 to the 3 gives 20 times 10 to the 7, which is rewritten as 2 times 10 to the 8. Addition and subtraction require the exponents to match first, exactly as adding fractions requires a common denominator: 3.2 times 10 to the 5 plus 4 times 10 to the 4 becomes 3.2 times 10 to the 5 plus 0.4 times 10 to the 5, which is 3.6 times 10 to the 5.

Scientific notation carries a further advantage: it makes significant figures unambiguous. Written as 4500, it is impossible to tell whether the number is known to two, three or four significant figures, because the trailing zeros might be placeholders or might be measured. Written as 4.5 times 10 to the 3, it is plainly two figures; as 4.500 times 10 to the 3, plainly four. Engineering notation is a variant restricting exponents to multiples of three, so that they line up with the metric prefixes kilo, mega, giga, milli, micro and nano, which is why a resistance is quoted as 4.7 kilohms rather than 4.7 times 10 to the 3 ohms. Calculators display these forms as E notation, where 4.7E3 means 4.7 times 10 cubed.

sections.heading: Percentages, Money and Everyday Decimal Reasoning
sections.body:
Percentages are decimals in disguise. Per cent means per hundred, so 37 per cent is 37/100, which is 0.37. Converting a percentage to a decimal means dividing by 100, that is moving the point two places left; converting the other way means multiplying by 100. This single equivalence turns most percentage problems into ordinary multiplication. Finding 15 per cent of 80 means computing 0.15 times 80, which is 12. Finding what percentage 27 is of 45 means computing 27 divided by 45, which is 0.6, then multiplying by 100 to get 60 per cent.

Percentage increase and decrease are where errors cluster, and the reliable technique is to work with a single multiplier rather than in two steps. Increasing a quantity by 8 per cent means multiplying by 1.08, since the result is the original 100 per cent plus 8 per cent more. Decreasing by 8 per cent means multiplying by 0.92. A price of 250 raised by 8 per cent is 250 times 1.08, which is 270. Successive changes multiply: a price raised 10 per cent and then reduced 10 per cent is multiplied by 1.10 and then by 0.90, giving 0.99, so it ends slightly below where it started. This asymmetry surprises people constantly and is the reason a stock that falls 50 per cent must rise 100 per cent to recover.

Reversing a percentage change requires dividing rather than subtracting. If a price after a 20 per cent discount is 60, the original was 60 divided by 0.80, which is 75, not 60 plus 20 per cent, which would be 72. The same logic recovers a pre-tax figure: if a bill including 20 per cent tax is 144, the pre-tax amount is 144 divided by 1.20, which is 120, and the tax is 24.

Money is the most common decimal application and has its own conventions. Currencies with two decimal places represent amounts in hundredths of the major unit, and because financial calculation must be exact and reproducible, money is almost never stored as a decimal fraction in software. It is stored as a whole number of the smallest unit, so 19.99 is held as 1999 cents. Anyone writing a program that handles money and stores it in ordinary floating point will eventually produce a balance that is out by a fraction of a cent, and such errors are notoriously difficult to reconcile.

Compound interest illustrates the reasoning at length. A principal of 1000 at 5 per cent annual interest becomes 1000 times 1.05, which is 1050 after one year, then 1050 times 1.05, which is 1102.50 after two, and in general 1000 times 1.05 to the power n after n years. After ten years the balance is about 1628.89, considerably more than the 1500 that simple interest would give, and the gap widens with time. The rule of 72, dividing 72 by the percentage rate, estimates the doubling time: at 5 per cent, roughly 14.4 years, against an exact figure near 14.2.

sections.heading: Why Computers Cannot Represent 0.1 Exactly
sections.body:
One of the most disorienting facts a new programmer meets is that in almost every programming language, adding 0.1 to 0.2 and comparing the result to 0.3 returns false. Printed to enough places, 0.1 plus 0.2 comes out as 0.30000000000000004. This is not a bug in the language, and it is not floating-point arithmetic being unreliable in some mysterious way. It is the direct consequence of the terminating-decimal rule applied in base two rather than base ten.

Computers store real numbers in binary. In binary, the positions after the point are halves, quarters, eighths, sixteenths and so on, all powers of two. A fraction can be written exactly in binary only if its denominator, in lowest terms, is a power of two. One half is 0.1 in binary, one quarter is 0.01, three quarters is 0.11, all exact. But one tenth has a denominator of 10, which factors as 2 times 5, and the 5 is fatal: 1/10 in binary is 0.0001100110011 with 0011 repeating forever, exactly as 1/3 repeats forever in base ten. The machine must cut the expansion off at the width of its storage, so what it actually holds is a number extremely close to 0.1 but not equal to it. Adding two such approximations produces a sum whose error is visible when printed to seventeen digits.

The governing standard is IEEE 754, first published in 1985 and revised in 2008 and 2019, which defines the formats nearly all hardware uses. Double precision uses 64 bits: one sign bit, eleven for the exponent and fifty-two for the fraction, giving roughly 15 to 17 significant decimal digits and a range from about 10 to the minus 308 up to 10 to the 308. Single precision uses 32 bits and gives only about 7 decimal digits, which is why accumulating millions of small single-precision values loses accuracy badly.

The practical consequences are specific. Never test floating-point values for exact equality; instead test whether the difference is smaller than a chosen tolerance appropriate to the problem. Never accumulate money in floating point; use integer minor units or a purpose-built decimal type. Be aware that floating-point addition is not associative, so summing a long list in a different order can give a different answer, and that adding a very small number to a very large one can lose the small one entirely, a phenomenon called absorption.

Languages provide remedies. Python's decimal module, Java's BigDecimal, and the SQL numeric type all implement base-ten arithmetic in software, storing digits explicitly so that 0.1 is exact. They are slower, often by an order of magnitude, but they are correct for financial and accounting work, where a discrepancy of one hundredth of a cent is a defect. The choice between binary and decimal representation is a genuine engineering trade-off between speed and exactness, not a matter of one being right.

sections.heading: Measurement, Units and False Precision
sections.body:
Decimals are the natural language of measurement, and the metric system was built around them deliberately. Adopted in revolutionary France in the 1790s, its defining feature is that every unit relates to every other by powers of ten, so converting between them is exactly the operation of moving a decimal point. There are 1000 millimetres in a metre, 1000 metres in a kilometre, 1000 grams in a kilogram. Converting 2.35 kilometres to metres means multiplying by 1000, which shifts the point three places right to give 2350 metres. Converting 47 millilitres to litres shifts three places left to give 0.047 litres. The standard prefixes run kilo for a thousand, mega for a million, giga for a billion, tera for a trillion in the upward direction, and milli for a thousandth, micro for a millionth, nano for a billionth and pico for a trillionth downward.

The imperial and US customary systems have no such structure, since twelve inches make a foot, three feet make a yard and 1760 yards make a mile, so decimal arithmetic in those units constantly requires conversion factors. Engineering practice in those countries generally sidesteps this by measuring in decimal inches, so a machinist works in thousandths, and a dimension is quoted as 0.750 inches rather than three quarters.

The deeper issue in measurement is that every measured value carries uncertainty, and the decimal notation used to record it makes an implicit claim about how large that uncertainty is. Writing a length as 4.7 metres claims a resolution of a tenth of a metre; writing 4.70 claims a hundredth. Recording more digits than the instrument can resolve is called false precision, and it is one of the commonest failures in reported data. A tape measure marked in millimetres cannot justify a reading of 1.4372 metres. A bathroom scale reading to the nearest 0.1 kilogram cannot support a claim that someone lost 0.03 kilograms.

False precision is generated most often by unit conversion and by calculators. Converting 5 miles to kilometres by multiplying by 1.609344 yields 8.04672 kilometres, which appears to be six significant figures, but the original measurement had only one; the honest answer is 8 kilometres. Similarly a temperature of 70 degrees Fahrenheit converts arithmetically to 21.1111 degrees Celsius, but reporting anything past 21 misrepresents the original precision.

The rigorous approach is to state the uncertainty explicitly, writing a result as 4.70 plus or minus 0.02 metres, and to propagate it through calculations. For sums and differences, absolute uncertainties add; for products and quotients, relative uncertainties add. If a rectangle measures 2.0 plus or minus 0.1 by 3.0 plus or minus 0.1 metres, the relative uncertainties are 5 per cent and about 3.3 per cent, so the area of 6.0 square metres carries roughly 8.3 per cent uncertainty, that is about 0.5 square metres.

sections.heading: Common Errors and How to Catch Them
sections.body:
Decimal arithmetic fails in a small number of characteristic ways, and knowing them turns error-checking from a vague anxiety into a checklist. The most damaging by far is the misplaced decimal point, because it produces an answer wrong by a factor of ten, a hundred or a thousand rather than by a small margin. In clinical settings this class of error has killed patients; a tenfold overdose arising from reading 0.5 milligrams as 5 milligrams is a recognised and recurring hazard, which is why prescribing guidance insists on a leading zero before a decimal point and forbids a trailing zero after one, since 5.0 milligrams misread as 50 is the mirror-image failure.

The defence against misplaced points is estimation, performed before the calculation rather than after. Round every input to one significant figure, do the arithmetic mentally, and check that the computed answer sits in the same range. If 4.7 times 0.023 is required, note that 5 times 0.02 is 0.1, so the answer should be about a tenth; a calculator showing 1.081 or 0.01081 is wrong by a factor of ten and the error is caught instantly. This habit costs seconds and catches most catastrophic errors.

Misalignment in addition and subtraction is the second family. It arises whenever numbers with different decimal-place counts are written down without padding, and it produces answers that look plausible. Padding to a common number of places before starting eliminates it.

The third family is misconceptions about magnitude. Believing longer means larger leads to ranking 0.125 above 0.5. Believing multiplication always increases leads to expecting 8 times 0.4 to exceed 8. Believing division always decreases leads to disbelief that 12 divided by 0.5 is 24. All three are corrected by reading the operation in words: multiplying by 0.4 asks for four tenths of the quantity, dividing by 0.5 asks how many halves fit inside.

The fourth family concerns rounding. Rounding intermediate values and then rounding the final result compounds error. Rounding at the wrong stage of a percentage calculation can shift a final figure by a whole unit. Applying a percentage decrease and then the same percentage increase and expecting to return to the start is an error of reasoning rather than arithmetic.

Finally, there are conversion errors of notation itself. Writing 3/4 as 0.34, taking the numerator and denominator as digits, is a persistent beginner mistake. Converting 2.5 hours to 2 hours 50 minutes rather than 2 hours 30 minutes confuses a decimal fraction with a sexagesimal one, and the same confusion appears with angles, where 12.5 degrees is not 12 degrees 50 minutes but 12 degrees 30 minutes, since a minute of arc is a sixtieth. Whenever a quantity is measured in a base other than ten, the decimal point does not mean what it usually means, and the conversion must be done explicitly.

sections.heading: Limits of the Notation and When to Use Something Else
sections.body:
For all its convenience, decimal notation has real limitations, and knowing when to abandon it is part of using it well. The first limitation is exactness. A third cannot be written exactly as a decimal; 0.333 is an approximation, and 0.333 times 3 is 0.999, not 1. Anyone doing arithmetic where exactness matters should keep the value as the fraction 1/3 for as long as possible and convert to a decimal only at the final step, if at all. In algebra, symbolic manipulation, exact geometry and much of pure mathematics, fractions and radicals are simply better tools, and a result written as root 2 over 2 is both exact and more informative than 0.7071.

The second limitation is that decimal notation hides structure. The fraction 17/68 announces its own simplification to 1/4 the moment its factors are noticed; written as 0.25 the relationship to 17 and 68 has vanished. In ratio and proportion work, in probability, and in any context where a quantity is naturally a part of a whole, fractions preserve information decimals discard. A recipe scaled by 3/4 is easier to reason about than one scaled by 0.75, because thirds and quarters of the ingredient quantities remain visible.

The third limitation is base dependence. Whether an expansion terminates is not a property of the number but of the number together with the base chosen. One third is infinite in base ten and terminates as 0.1 in base three. One tenth is finite in base ten and infinite in base two. Because computers use base two and humans use base ten, this mismatch is permanent and is the source of the floating-point surprises that affect every piece of numerical software ever written. Duodecimal advocates have argued for centuries that base twelve would be superior precisely because twelve has factors of 2, 3, 4 and 6, so thirds and quarters would both terminate, and the argument is mathematically sound while being socially hopeless.

The fourth limitation is psychological rather than mathematical. Decimals confer an air of authority that is often unearned. A figure quoted as 63.4 per cent sounds more trustworthy than one quoted as about two thirds, even when the underlying data supports only the second. Survey results, financial projections and performance metrics routinely carry three or four digits of apparent precision resting on assumptions accurate to perhaps one. Reading such a number well means asking what the measurement actually was and how many digits it could possibly support.

The remedy in every case is the same: treat the decimal expansion as one representation among several, chosen for convenience in a particular task, and be willing to switch. Use decimals for comparing, for measuring, for computing and for money. Use fractions for exactness, for structure and for ratios. Use scientific notation at extremes of scale. Use exact symbols for irrational quantities. The number itself is unchanged by any of these choices; only what the notation makes easy to see is different.

guides.title: Multiplication and Division: Algorithms and Strategies
guides.summary: A comprehensive guide to what multiplication and division mean, why the standard and alternative algorithms work, and the mental strategies, extensions to fractions, decimals and negatives, and connections onward to algebra and computing.

sections.heading: What Multiplication and Division Mean
sections.body:
Multiplication and division are the third and fourth operations children usually meet, and they are inverses of one another in the same way addition and subtraction are. Multiplication begins as repeated addition: three groups of four counters is four plus four plus four, written three times four, equal to twelve. The two numbers being multiplied are called factors, and their result is the product. Because the order of the factors does not change the product, the same twelve counters can be seen as four rows of three, which is why an array or rectangle is the most powerful mental picture of the operation. A rectangle five units wide and three units tall contains fifteen unit squares, so multiplication is also the natural way to measure area, and this area model will reappear when we justify written algorithms.

Multiplication is not only repeated addition, however, and treating it as nothing more than that later causes trouble. It is better understood as scaling: multiplying by three enlarges a quantity threefold, multiplying by one half shrinks it, and multiplying by one leaves it unchanged. Scaling explains why you can multiply lengths that are not whole numbers of counters, and why multiplying by a fraction can make a number smaller, something repeated addition cannot picture.

Division reverses multiplication, and it carries two distinct everyday meanings that share one symbol. In partitive or sharing division, you know how many equal groups you want and ask how large each is: twelve sweets shared among three children gives four each. In quotitive or grouping division, you know the size of each group and ask how many groups fit: twelve sweets in bags of four gives three bags. Both are written twelve divided by three equals four. The number being divided is the dividend, the number you divide by is the divisor, and the answer is the quotient; anything left over is the remainder.

The inverse relationship is the key that unlocks fact recall and checking. Because three times four is twelve, both twelve divided by three and twelve divided by four are known immediately, so the multiplication and division facts come in linked families sometimes called fact families. This inverse also lets you verify any division by multiplying the quotient back by the divisor and adding the remainder, which should reproduce the dividend. Holding all four interpretations together, repeated addition, array or area, scaling, and the two flavours of division, gives a flexible foundation. A learner who can move between these pictures reasons about problems rather than merely reciting a procedure, and that flexibility is what every later algorithm and strategy is built to exploit.

sections.heading: Properties, Facts, and Learning the Times Tables
sections.body:
A handful of algebraic properties govern multiplication, and knowing them turns a frightening grid of facts into a manageable network. The commutative property says the order of factors does not matter, so six times eight equals eight times six; this alone roughly halves the facts a learner must memorise. The associative property says that when multiplying three or more numbers the grouping does not matter, so two times three times five may be computed as six times five or two times fifteen, whichever is easier. The distributive property, which links multiplication with addition, says that multiplying a sum is the same as multiplying each part and adding, so seven times twelve equals seven times ten plus seven times two, that is seventy plus fourteen, ninety-four. The distributive property is the single most important idea in the whole subject, because every written multiplication algorithm and nearly every mental shortcut is an application of it.

Two special numbers behave simply. One is the multiplicative identity: any number times one is itself. Zero is the annihilator: any number times zero is zero, a fact that follows from the empty array of zero rows and quietly explains later rules about zeros in products.

The multiplication facts, commonly the products up to twelve times twelve, deserve genuine fluency because they are the atoms from which all larger calculation is assembled. Rote drilling has its place, but understanding accelerates it. The tens are automatic in base ten, appending a zero. The fives are half of the corresponding ten. The nines have the famous pattern in which the tens digit counts up while the units digit counts down, and the two digits always sum to nine, a pattern that follows from nine being one less than ten. Doubling handles the twos, fours, and eights in a chain. The square numbers, such as six times six, act as anchors from which neighbours are reached: seven times six is one more six than six times six.

For the genuinely awkward facts near the centre of the table, such as seven times eight, learners lean on the distributive property, computing seven times eight as seven times four doubled, or as five eights plus two eights. Practising facts as fact families, pairing each product with its two divisions, builds the division facts at the same time. The goal is not speed for its own sake but freeing working memory: a pupil who must reconstruct six times seven cannot simultaneously attend to the structure of a multi-digit problem, whereas one who simply knows it has attention to spare for reasoning.

sections.heading: Place Value: Why the Algorithms Work
sections.body:
Every efficient written method for multiplying and dividing whole numbers rests on the base-ten place value system, so it is worth stating that system precisely before meeting the algorithms it supports. In positional notation each digit's contribution depends on its place, with places increasing by a factor of ten from right to left: units, tens, hundreds, thousands, and so on. The number three hundred and forty-seven is not three, four, seven jammed together but three hundreds plus four tens plus seven units. Written in expanded form it is three times one hundred plus four times ten plus seven times one. This decomposition is the hinge on which the algorithms turn.

Multiplying by ten, one hundred, or any power of ten is therefore especially simple. Because every place is worth ten times the place to its right, multiplying by ten shifts every digit one place to the left and a zero fills the vacated units place, so fifty-two times ten is five hundred and twenty. It is more honest, and more useful later, to describe this as shifting digits than as adding a zero, because the add-a-zero slogan breaks down for decimals, where multiplying by ten moves the decimal point instead. Dividing by a power of ten shifts digits the other way, to the right.

The general written multiplication algorithm exploits place value together with the distributive property. To multiply by a multi-digit number you multiply by each of its digits separately, remembering that a digit standing in the tens place is really that many tens, so its partial product must be shifted one place left; a digit in the hundreds place shifts two places. The rows of partial products in long multiplication are exactly these place-scaled pieces, and the final addition reassembles the whole. Nothing mysterious happens; the layout simply keeps the powers of ten aligned in columns so they can be added.

Division likewise processes a number one place at a time, working from the largest place downward, because that is the order in which the size of the answer is determined. The reason we start long division at the left, unlike addition or multiplication which we start at the right, is that we want the leading, most significant digit of the quotient first, and each place we handle depends on what was left over from the more significant place above it.

Understanding place value also demystifies carrying and borrowing, which are simply the acts of regrouping ten of one unit into one of the next unit up, or unpacking one of the higher unit into ten of the lower. A learner who genuinely sees a written calculation as bookkeeping of tens, hundreds and thousands is far less likely to misplace a digit, and far better placed to invent or repair a method when memory fails.

sections.heading: The Standard Multiplication Algorithm
sections.body:
The standard, or long, multiplication algorithm is the compact written method most adults learned in school, and it is best understood as an organised way of computing and adding partial products. Consider a two-digit by two-digit example, forty-three times twenty-six. The distributive property expands this into four pieces: forty times twenty, forty times six, three times twenty, and three times six. Long multiplication computes these pieces in a tidy layout so that the powers of ten line up and the final sum is easy.

In the usual arrangement you write the larger number above the smaller, multiply the top number first by the units digit of the bottom number and then by its tens digit, writing each result as a row, and finally add the rows. When multiplying by the tens digit, the entire row shifts one place to the left, most simply by writing a zero in the units column before starting, because that digit represents tens, not units. Carrying appears whenever a single-digit product exceeds nine: the tens part of that product is carried into the next column and added after the next multiplication, exactly the regrouping described by place value.

Worked through, forty-three times six is two hundred and fifty-eight, and forty-three times twenty is eight hundred and sixty, written as eight-six-zero. Adding two hundred and fifty-eight to eight hundred and sixty gives one thousand one hundred and eighteen, so forty-three times twenty-six equals one thousand one hundred and eighteen. Each partial-product row is a genuine, meaningful number, and seeing them as such guards against the mechanical errors that come from treating the algorithm as a ritual.

The method scales without change to larger numbers: a three-digit multiplier simply produces three shifted rows, one for units, one for tens shifted once, and one for hundreds shifted twice. The only real sources of error are misaligned columns and forgotten or mis-added carries, both prevented by neat handwriting and by checking that each new row starts one column further left than the last. Long multiplication is not the fastest method humans have devised, but it is compact, general, and self-checking once the partial products are understood, which is why it became the schoolbook standard across the world.

Some curricula teach an expanded variant first, in which all four partial products of a two-by-two problem are written out separately rather than compressed into two rows, precisely mirroring the grid method: forty times twenty is eight hundred, forty times six is two hundred and forty, three times twenty is sixty, and three times six is eighteen, and the four are added. This expanded form is slower but makes every piece visible and carries less risk of a hidden carrying slip, so it serves as a bridge to the compressed standard layout. A subtle case worth practising is a factor containing an internal zero, such as multiplying by two hundred and five, where the tens digit is zero: the corresponding partial-product row is entirely zeros and is often simply omitted, but the placeholder shift for the hundreds digit must still be counted, or the final digit lands in the wrong column.
steps: Write the two numbers one above the other, digits aligned by place value, longer number on top.
Multiply the top number by the units digit of the bottom number, carrying tens into the next column as you go, and write the result as the first partial-product row.
Place a zero in the units column of the next row to record the shift, then multiply the top number by the tens digit of the bottom number, again carrying, and write this second row.
For each further digit of the bottom number, add one more placeholder zero and write another shifted partial-product row.
Add all the partial-product rows together, column by column from the right, carrying as needed, to obtain the final product.
Check the result with an estimate: round each factor and confirm the answer is close to the rounded product.

sections.heading: Alternative Multiplication Algorithms
sections.body:
The standard algorithm is efficient but opaque, and several alternative methods make the underlying structure visible or suit different temperaments and technologies. The grid, box, or area method draws a rectangle partitioned according to the place value of each factor. To multiply forty-three by twenty-six you split forty-three into forty and three and twenty-six into twenty and six, forming a two-by-two grid whose four cells hold the products eight hundred, one hundred and twenty, sixty, and eighteen. Adding the four cells gives one thousand one hundred and eighteen. The grid is nothing but the distributive property drawn as a picture, and because it names every partial product it is an excellent teaching bridge to both the standard algorithm and later algebraic multiplication of expressions.

Lattice or gelosia multiplication, used across the medieval Islamic world and in Renaissance Europe, arranges single-digit products in a grid of diagonally split cells. Each cell holds the product of one digit of each factor, tens above the diagonal and units below, and the answer is read by adding along the diagonals with carrying. The lattice separates multiplication entirely from addition, which some learners find liberating, and it never requires holding a carry in the head during multiplication.

The Russian peasant method, also called doubling and halving or Egyptian multiplication, needs only the ability to double, halve, and add, and no times tables at all. Write the two numbers side by side, repeatedly halve one column, discarding remainders, while doubling the other, then delete every row whose halved entry is even and add the surviving doubled entries. This works because halving with truncation is really writing one factor in binary, and the surviving rows correspond to the ones in that binary expansion; the method is thus the direct ancestor of how computers multiply.

Napier's bones, a set of numbered rods invented by John Napier around 1617, mechanised the lattice idea so that multi-digit multiplication reduced to laying out rods and adding along diagonals. The various finger-multiplication tricks, such as the well-known method for the nines or the technique for numbers between six and ten, are memory aids that encode particular distributive decompositions rather than general algorithms.

None of these methods is more or less correct than the standard one; they compute the same partial products in different orders and layouts. Their value in a full education is threefold: they reveal that the standard algorithm is a choice, not a law of nature; they offer a fallback when a learner's memorised procedure fails; and several of them, especially doubling and halving, connect directly to how arithmetic is actually performed inside machines.

sections.heading: Mental Multiplication Strategies
sections.body:
Skilled mental calculators rarely visualise the written algorithm; instead they reshape a problem into pieces they can handle in the head, almost always by exploiting the distributive, associative, and commutative properties. The most fundamental move is partitioning by place value, the same idea as the grid method but performed mentally: to find twenty-three times seven, compute twenty times seven, which is one hundred and forty, and three times seven, which is twenty-one, then add to get one hundred and sixty-one. Because the larger partial product carries most of the magnitude, working from the largest place first also gives a running estimate.

Compensation adjusts a number to something convenient and then corrects. To multiply by nine, multiply by ten and subtract one copy: nineteen times nine is nineteen times ten minus nineteen, one hundred and ninety minus nineteen, one hundred and seventy-one. To multiply by ninety-nine, multiply by one hundred and subtract the number itself. Multiplying by five is often easiest as multiplying by ten and halving, and multiplying by fifty as multiplying by one hundred and halving.

Doubling and halving rebalances a product using the associative property: twice one number times half another leaves the product unchanged, so sixteen times twenty-five becomes eight times fifty, then four times one hundred, which is four hundred, computed with no effort. Factoring a factor into convenient parts uses the same law; to multiply by twelve, multiply by two, then by two again, then by three, or multiply by ten and add two more copies.

The difference of two squares gives an elegant trick for products of numbers straddling a round value. Because a number just below a round value times a number just above it equals the round value squared minus the small offset squared, nineteen times twenty-one is twenty squared minus one, that is four hundred minus one, three hundred and ninety-nine. Squares of numbers ending in five are instant: to square thirty-five, multiply the tens digit by one more than itself, three times four is twelve, and append twenty-five to get one thousand two hundred and twenty-five.

Choosing among these strategies is itself a skill, and there is rarely a single best route. The near-doubles and place-value partition suit most everyday products; compensation shines for factors near a round number; doubling and halving rescues awkward pairings; the squares tricks handle their special cases. A confident calculator glances at the numbers, notices a feature to exploit, and picks accordingly. This estimating, feature-spotting habit is worth cultivating not because mental arithmetic often beats a calculator in speed but because it keeps a person's number sense alive and provides an immediate check on whatever a machine reports.

sections.heading: Division Meaning and the Long Division Algorithm
sections.body:
Long division is the written algorithm most feared and least understood, yet it is a straightforward application of place value and repeated estimation once its logic is exposed. The task is to divide a dividend by a divisor, producing a quotient and possibly a remainder. Unlike the other written algorithms, long division works from the left, the most significant place, because we want the leading digit of the answer first and because each digit of the quotient depends on the remainder carried down from the place above.

Consider seven hundred and forty-one divided by three. We ask how many threes fit into the leading seven hundreds; two hundreds, since two threes are six hundreds and three would be nine hundreds, too many. We write two in the hundreds place of the quotient, subtract six hundred from seven hundred and forty-one to leave one hundred and forty-one, and continue. How many threes in one hundred and forty; forty, because forty threes are one hundred and twenty. Write four in the tens place, subtract one hundred and twenty from one hundred and forty-one, leaving twenty-one. Finally, how many threes in twenty-one; exactly seven. Write seven in the units place, subtract, and the remainder is zero. The quotient is two hundred and forty-seven.

The mantra sometimes taught, divide, multiply, subtract, bring down, describes the four repeated actions but hides their meaning. What actually happens is that at each place we make the best estimate of how many divisors fit, record it in the correct place of the quotient, remove that many divisors, and then combine what is left with the next place of the dividend. The subtraction removes the counted groups; the bringing down simply re-attaches the next smaller place so the leftover can be shared further.

The genuine difficulty of the standard method is that each quotient digit must be guessed correctly in one go, and with multi-digit divisors that guess involves its own estimation, which is why long division with a two-digit divisor feels so much harder than with a single digit. A learner who understands the method as repeated best-estimate subtraction, rather than a four-word chant, can slow down, take smaller bites, and still reach the correct answer even when a first guess proves too large.

Two situations trip up beginners and deserve rehearsal. The first is a leading place too small to hold one divisor, as when dividing a three-digit number by a divisor larger than its first digit; you then look at the first two digits, and the quotient simply has no digit in that leading place. The second is a place inside the dividend into which the divisor will not go after a subtraction: there you must write a zero in the quotient and bring down the next digit, because omitting that zero shortens the answer by a whole place. When the dividend runs out and a non-zero remainder is left, the calculation may stop there, or a decimal point and trailing zeros may be appended to continue dividing into tenths and hundredths, depending on whether an exact whole-number remainder or a decimal quotient is wanted.
steps: Set up the dividend under the long-division bracket with the divisor to its left.
Look at the leading digits of the dividend and find the largest multiple of the divisor that fits; write that quotient digit above the correct place.
Multiply the quotient digit by the divisor and write the product beneath the digits you used.
Subtract to find what remains at that place.
Bring down the next digit of the dividend and join it to the remainder.
Repeat the find, multiply, subtract, bring-down cycle for each remaining digit; whatever is left after the last digit is the remainder.
Check by multiplying the quotient by the divisor and adding the remainder, which must reproduce the dividend.

sections.heading: Alternative Division Methods
sections.body:
Because the standard long division algorithm demands a correct quotient digit in a single guess, several gentler methods trade some efficiency for reliability and transparency, and one of them, short division, trades the other way for speed. The partial-quotients method, sometimes called chunking, removes the requirement to guess the exact digit. Instead of asking how many divisors fit into a place all at once, you subtract any convenient multiple of the divisor, record how many you took in a running tally beside the work, and repeat until nothing usable remains. To divide seven hundred and forty-one by three you might subtract two hundred threes, six hundred, leaving one hundred and forty-one, then forty threes, one hundred and twenty, leaving twenty-one, then seven threes, leaving zero, and finally add the tally, two hundred plus forty plus seven, to get two hundred and forty-seven. The answer is identical to long division, but you may take the divisor away in whatever comfortable lumps you like, so a wrong estimate merely costs an extra step rather than forcing an erasure.

Chunking is really long division with the estimation relaxed, and it makes the meaning of division as repeated subtraction unmistakable. Its cousin, plain repeated subtraction, subtracts one divisor at a time and is impractical for large dividends but valuable for cementing the concept and for programming, where it is the simplest possible division loop.

Short division is the compact opposite. When the divisor is a single digit, the subtractions are small enough to do mentally, so the intermediate working is not written; instead each remainder is carried as a small superscript to the next digit of the dividend. Dividing seven hundred and forty-one by three, you say three into seven is two remainder one, carry the one to make fourteen, three into fourteen is four remainder two, carry the two to make twenty-one, three into twenty-one is seven, giving two hundred and forty-seven directly on one line. Short division is quick and clean but only comfortable with small divisors, because the carried remainder combined with the next digit must stay within a range you can divide in your head.

These methods coexist rather than compete. Beginners often start with chunking to see what division means and to build confidence without the pressure of a single correct guess, then compress to short division for one-digit divisors and reserve full long division for larger ones. Understanding all three means a calculator can always fall back to a slower but surer route when a quick method stalls, and can recognise that every one of them is answering the same question: how many of the divisor are contained in the dividend, and how much is left over.

sections.heading: Remainders, Divisibility, and Interpreting Quotients
sections.body:
Division of whole numbers does not always come out evenly, and the leftover, the remainder, is not a nuisance to be discarded but information that must be interpreted in light of the problem. The division algorithm, a theorem rather than a procedure despite its name, states precisely that for any dividend and any non-zero divisor there exist a unique quotient and a unique remainder with the remainder at least zero and strictly less than the divisor. So thirty divided by seven is four remainder two, because four sevens are twenty-eight and the leftover two is smaller than seven. If a remainder ever reached or exceeded the divisor, another whole divisor could still be taken out, so the quotient was too small.

How a remainder should be handled depends entirely on the situation, and mishandling it is a classic source of wrong answers even when the arithmetic is perfect. If twenty-nine children must travel in buses holding eight, twenty-nine divided by eight is three remainder five, but you cannot leave five children behind, so you round the quotient up to four buses. If instead you are sharing twenty-nine pounds among eight people, the remainder is carried into a fraction or decimal, giving three pounds sixty-two and a half pence each. Sometimes the remainder itself is the answer, as when you ask what day of the week falls a hundred days from now and only the remainder after dividing by seven matters. The same calculation, three remainder five, thus yields four, three and a bit, or five depending on the question.

Divisibility, the case of a zero remainder, has memorable tests that follow from place value. A number is divisible by two if its last digit is even, and by five if its last digit is zero or five, because ten is a multiple of both. It is divisible by ten only if it ends in zero. Divisibility by four depends on the last two digits, and by eight on the last three, because a hundred is a multiple of four and a thousand of eight. The rule for three, and likewise for nine, is subtler: add the digits, and if the digit sum is divisible by three, or nine, so is the whole number, a consequence of every power of ten being one more than a multiple of nine. Divisibility by six combines the tests for two and three. These tests let you simplify fractions, spot factors, and check calculations quickly. Understanding remainders and divisibility also opens the door to modular arithmetic, the mathematics of cyclic quantities such as clock times and calendar days, and to the number theory that underlies modern cryptography.

sections.heading: Multiplying and Dividing Fractions, Decimals, and Negatives
sections.body:
The same two operations extend beyond whole numbers, and the extensions are governed by the demand that the familiar properties keep holding. Multiplying fractions is, surprisingly to beginners, simpler than adding them: multiply the numerators together and the denominators together, so two-thirds times four-fifths is eight-fifteenths. The area picture justifies this, since two-thirds of four-fifths of a unit square is the overlap of a horizontal and a vertical strip. Dividing by a fraction is defined so as to remain the inverse of multiplying, and the rule invert and multiply follows: dividing by four-fifths is multiplying by its reciprocal, five-fourths. This explains the counter-intuitive result that dividing by a number smaller than one makes a quantity larger, because you are asking how many small pieces fit, and many do.

Decimals inherit the whole-number algorithms with one extra bookkeeping rule about the decimal point. To multiply decimals, ignore the points, multiply as whole numbers, and then place the point so that the answer has as many decimal places as the two factors together; so one point two times zero point three, with one decimal place each, gives thirty-six with two decimal places, zero point three six. To divide by a decimal, shift the point in both divisor and dividend by the same number of places until the divisor becomes a whole number, which does not change the quotient because it multiplies top and bottom equally, then divide normally.

Signed numbers obey the rule that like signs give a positive product and unlike signs a negative one, so negative three times negative four is positive twelve while negative three times four is negative twelve. The positive-times-positive case is ordinary. The negative-times-positive case is repeated addition of a negative, clearly negative. The negative-times-negative case is the one that puzzles people, and it is best defended by insisting the distributive property must survive: since negative three times zero is zero, and zero is four plus negative four, expanding forces negative three times negative four to be the opposite of negative three times four, hence positive twelve. Division of signed numbers follows the identical sign rule because it is the inverse of multiplication.

Two facts about zero deserve emphasis. Multiplying by zero always gives zero, but dividing by zero is undefined, not infinite: there is no number that, multiplied by zero, yields a non-zero dividend, and zero divided by zero could be anything, so the operation is simply forbidden. These extensions matter because real problems involve parts, measurements, and debts, and because algebra, which treats numbers of every kind uniformly, cannot proceed until multiplication and division are understood to work consistently across them all.

sections.heading: Estimation, Checking, and Catching Errors
sections.body:
A calculation is worthless if it is wrong, and the habit of estimating before and checking after is what separates reliable arithmetic from lucky arithmetic.
