Estimation means replacing the actual numbers with nearby round ones and computing quickly to get the order of magnitude of the answer. Before multiplying forty-three by twenty-six, round to forty and thirty and note the product should be near one thousand two hundred; the exact answer, one thousand one hundred and eighteen, sits comfortably close, whereas an answer of a hundred or of ten thousand would betray a misplaced digit or a forgotten place. Estimation is especially valuable with a calculator, because a machine faithfully computes whatever was keyed, including the consequences of a slipped finger, and only a human sense of the expected size will catch such blunders.

Several structural checks catch errors that estimation misses. The inverse-operation check verifies a product by dividing it back, or a quotient by multiplying it and adding the remainder, and should reproduce the original. Because multiplication is commutative, redoing a product with the factors swapped is a genuinely independent check that will usually expose a carrying slip, since the intermediate steps differ. For division, confirming that the remainder is smaller than the divisor is a free sanity check that costs nothing and catches a common class of mistake.

Casting out nines is an old and elegant check that exploits divisibility by nine. Replace each number by its digit sum, reduced repeatedly to a single digit, then perform the same operation on those digit roots; the digit root of the true answer must match. If two numbers with digit roots five and seven are multiplied, the product's digit root should equal the digit root of thirty-five, which is eight, and any answer whose digit root differs is certainly wrong. Casting out nines cannot catch every error, notably it misses digit transpositions and any mistake that is itself a multiple of nine, but it is quick and catches most arithmetic slips.

The most common errors have recognisable signatures. Misaligned columns in long multiplication produce answers that are wrong by a factor of ten in one partial product. Forgotten carries make answers slightly too small. Losing a placeholder zero when multiplying by a tens digit shrinks a partial product tenfold. In division, forgetting to write a zero in the quotient when the divisor does not fit into a brought-down place is a frequent and serious slip that leaves the quotient with too few digits, which estimation immediately flags. Building in the double discipline of a rough estimate first and an independent check afterward makes these mistakes visible, and turns arithmetic from a source of anxiety into something a person can trust their own hand to do.

sections.heading: Historical Algorithms and Connections Onward
sections.body:
The written algorithms taught today are the survivors of a long competition among calculating methods, and seeing that history clarifies why they took their present form and where they lead. Ancient Egyptians multiplied by doubling and adding, exactly the peasant method, and had no general multiplication table. Babylonians, working in base sixty, relied on extensive tables of products and reciprocals baked into clay. The Greeks and Romans, hampered by additive numerals with no positional structure, found multiplication laborious and often used counting boards or the abacus, whose beads embody place value physically.

The decisive advance was the Hindu-Arabic positional system with a symbol for zero, developed in India in the first millennium and transmitted through the medieval Islamic world, where mathematicians such as al-Khwarizmi, whose Latinised name gives us the word algorithm, wrote influential treatises on calculating with these numerals. Fibonacci's Liber Abaci of 1202 helped carry the methods into Europe, where they slowly displaced the abacus over the following centuries. The lattice method, Napier's bones of 1617, and eventually mechanical calculators and the electronic computer are all points on this same trajectory toward faster, more automatic multiplication and division.

The operations connect forward as much as backward. In algebra, multiplying two binomials such as x plus three by x plus two is the grid method with letters in place of digits, and the distributive property that justified long multiplication justifies expanding brackets and multiplying polynomials. The area model becomes the standard picture for completing the square and for integration. Long division of numbers has a direct analogue in polynomial long division, used to factor expressions and to analyse rational functions, and the remainder theorem is the polynomial echo of the whole-number division algorithm.

Inside computers, multiplication and division reduce to the doubling-and-halving idea because machines store numbers in binary, where multiplying by two is a shift of the digits and any multiplication is a sum of shifted copies, precisely the Russian peasant method mechanised. For very large numbers the schoolbook algorithm, whose effort grows with the square of the number of digits, becomes too slow, and faster methods matter. Karatsuba's algorithm, discovered in 1960, multiplies large numbers with fewer digit multiplications by a clever splitting, and later methods based on the fast Fourier transform, culminating in a 2019 algorithm by Harvey and van der Hoeven, are faster still. These advanced algorithms power the arithmetic behind cryptography, scientific computation, and every calculation too large for a person. The humble times table thus sits at the head of a chain that runs, unbroken, from a child's counters to the fastest known ways of multiplying.

sections.heading: Common Misconceptions and Pitfalls
sections.body:
A cluster of tenacious misconceptions surrounds multiplication and division, and naming them is the surest way to inoculate a learner against them. The most damaging is the belief that multiplication always makes numbers bigger and division always makes them smaller. This is true only for factors and divisors greater than one; multiplying by a half or by zero point two shrinks a number, and dividing by a half doubles it. The belief is planted innocently by the repeated-addition picture, which cannot represent multiplying by a fraction, and it later obstructs work with decimals, ratios, and rates, where a student who knows that division makes things smaller will reject a correct answer because it grew.

A related error treats multiplication as only repeated addition and never as scaling or area, leaving a learner stranded the moment the factors stop being whole counts of objects. Insisting on the array and scaling pictures from the start prevents this.

In the written algorithms, the frequent slips are mechanical but revealing. Forgetting the placeholder zero when multiplying by a tens or hundreds digit is endemic and shrinks that partial product tenfold or hundredfold. Misremembering carrying, either dropping a carry or adding it before rather than after the next multiplication, corrupts long multiplication quietly. In long division, the single most consequential mistake is failing to write a zero in the quotient when the divisor will not go into a particular brought-down place; omitting it silently drops a place and makes the answer ten times too small, a mistake an estimate would catch at once.

Language causes its own confusion. Because multiplication is commutative the order of factors does not matter for the answer, but the two orders can model different situations, and reading divided by carelessly is a common trap, since six divided by two is three but two divided by six is a third. The words dividend, divisor, and quotient are worth learning precisely so that instructions are unambiguous.

Two special-number pitfalls recur. Learners sometimes think that dividing by zero gives zero or infinity; it is simply undefined, because no number times zero can equal a non-zero dividend. Others treat multiplying by one or dividing by one as somehow doing nothing worth noting, when recognising the identity is exactly what makes equivalent fractions and unit conversions work. Finally, the sign rule that negative times negative is positive is accepted grudgingly and then misapplied to addition; keeping the multiplication rule distinct from the addition rule for signs prevents this. Every one of these pitfalls yields to the same remedy: understanding why each procedure works, estimating the expected answer, and checking the result independently, so that a wrong answer announces itself rather than passing unnoticed.

guides.title: Addition and Subtraction: Algorithms and Strategies
guides.summary: A comprehensive guide to the two most fundamental arithmetic operations, covering their meanings, mental strategies, the standard and alternative written algorithms, and their extension to negative numbers, decimals, and fractions.

sections.heading: What Addition and Subtraction Mean
sections.body:
Addition and subtraction are the first arithmetic operations a person meets, and understanding what they mean matters more than memorising rules. Addition combines quantities: if you have three apples and gather two more, you have five. Subtraction reverses this: from five apples, giving two away leaves three. These operations are inverses of one another, a fact that runs through everything that follows. Because they are inverses, every subtraction can be rewritten as an addition with an unknown, and every addition implies two subtractions.

Mathematicians and teachers distinguish several real-world situations that all lead to the same arithmetic. Addition models joining, or putting sets together, and part-part-whole reasoning, in which two parts make a whole. Subtraction models at least three distinct situations: taking away, or removing part of a set; comparison, or finding how much more one quantity is than another; and the missing addend, or how much must be added to reach a target. Recognising that "How many more does Ana have than Ben?" and "How many did I lose?" both call for subtraction, despite feeling different, is a genuine conceptual step for young learners and a source of confusion when it is missed.

The operations obey structural laws that make computation flexible. Addition is commutative, meaning the order of the numbers does not change the sum: 4 + 7 equals 7 + 4. It is also associative, so when adding several numbers the grouping does not matter: two plus three, then plus five, equals two plus the sum of three and five. Zero is the identity element for addition, because adding zero changes nothing. Subtraction, by contrast, is neither commutative nor associative: 7 minus 4 is not 4 minus 7, and this asymmetry is exactly why it needs its own careful treatment.

The formal relationship is captured by a single statement: a minus b equals c precisely when c plus b equals a. This is not a trick but the definition of subtraction in terms of addition, and it is the reason a subtraction fact such as 12 minus 5 can be found by asking, "5 plus what makes 12?" Skilled arithmetic exploits this constantly.

It helps to picture both operations on a number line. Addition moves you to the right by the second quantity; subtraction moves you to the left. Comparison appears as the gap between two points. This single image unifies whole numbers, negative numbers, decimals, and fractions, all of which live on the same line. Everything in this guide, from a child counting on fingers to a clerk balancing accounts, is ultimately about combining or separating positions on that line, and the many algorithms are simply reliable procedures for doing so quickly and without error. Holding onto the meaning behind the symbols keeps the procedures sensible rather than mysterious.

sections.heading: The Place-Value Foundation
sections.body:
Every efficient method for adding and subtracting multi-digit numbers rests on place value, the idea that a digit's meaning depends on its position. In the decimal, or base-ten, system there are ten symbols, 0 through 9, and each position to the left is worth ten times the position to its right. The number 3,482 means three thousands, four hundreds, eight tens, and two ones. Written as an expanded sum it is 3000 + 400 + 80 + 2. This positional principle, inherited from Indian mathematics and transmitted through the Arabic-speaking world, is what makes columns line up and what makes carrying and borrowing possible.

Because each column represents a power of ten, adding within a column can produce a result of ten or more, which must be exchanged for one unit of the next column up. Ten ones become one ten; ten tens become one hundred. This exchange is the heart of carrying, also called regrouping or trading, and it is nothing more than the place-value exchange applied on paper. Subtraction works the reverse exchange: when a column has too few to take from, one unit of the higher column is unbundled into ten of the lower, which is borrowing. Neither operation is arbitrary; both are direct consequences of what the positions mean.

Understanding place value explains why written algorithms require the digits to be aligned by position rather than by the left edge. When adding 47 and 5, the 5 must sit beneath the 7, in the ones, not beneath the 4, because only quantities of the same kind may be combined directly. A great many student errors come from misalignment, especially with decimals, where the decimal point marks the boundary between whole and fractional positions and must be kept in a straight vertical line.

Place value also reveals the deep similarity between whole numbers and decimals. To the right of the ones column, positions continue as tenths, hundredths, and thousandths, each one-tenth of the position to its left. The same carrying and borrowing rules apply without modification; only the labels change. A number such as 12.75 is one ten, two ones, seven tenths, and five hundredths. Money, being decimal, uses exactly this structure, which is why arithmetic with currency is arithmetic with decimals.

It is worth remembering that base ten is a human convention, not a mathematical necessity. Computers use base two, where the only digits are 0 and 1 and each position doubles; the ancient Babylonians used base sixty, whose traces survive in our sixty-minute hour and 360-degree circle. Addition and subtraction algorithms transfer to any base, with carrying occurring whenever a column reaches the base value. Seeing this generality helps demystify the standard procedures: they are not magic recipes but the logical machinery of positional counting, applied one column at a time from right to left.

sections.heading: Number Facts and Fluency
sections.body:
Beneath every large calculation lie the single-digit sums, the roughly one hundred combinations from 0 + 0 to 9 + 9, together with their related differences. Fluency with these basic facts is the bedrock of arithmetic. A person who must reconstruct 8 + 6 laboriously each time will make more errors and lose the thread of longer problems; one who knows it instantly can devote attention to the structure of the task. Fluency does not mean rote parroting alone, however. The strongest arithmetic combines quick recall with the ability to derive a forgotten fact from a known one.

Educators organise the facts into families that support derivation. Doubles, such as 6 + 6 = 12, are learned early and used as anchors: 6 + 7 is then just one more than the double, and 6 + 5 one less. The combinations that make ten, such as 3 + 7 and 4 + 6, deserve special attention because base ten pivots on them; knowing them instantly enables the powerful making-ten strategy. Adding zero and adding one are trivial once understood as identity and successor. The commutative law immediately halves the burden, since knowing 9 + 4 gives 4 + 9 for free.

Subtraction facts are best learned not as a separate hundred items but as the inverses of the addition facts. Because 8 + 5 = 13, the learner already possesses 13 − 5 = 8 and 13 − 8 = 5. Framing subtraction as the missing addend, asking what must be added to the smaller number to reach the larger, turns recall of differences into recall of sums, a substantial efficiency. This is why fact families are usually taught as triples: 7, 6, and 13 generate two additions and two subtractions.

Practice that builds genuine fluency is spaced and varied rather than massed and mechanical. Short, frequent sessions outperform long cramming, and mixing fact families prevents the false fluency of a predictable worksheet. Games, number-bond diagrams, and ten-frames give the facts a visual and physical grounding that pure flashcards lack. The goal is automaticity: the answer arriving without conscious effort, freeing working memory for the demands of multi-digit computation.

Research in cognitive science supports this emphasis. Working memory is sharply limited, holding only a few items at once, so any capacity spent recomputing basic facts is capacity unavailable for tracking carries, aligning columns, or reasoning about a word problem. This is the practical case for fluency: not that memorisation is virtuous in itself, but that fluent facts are a prerequisite for higher mathematics, from long multiplication and division to fractions and algebra, where arithmetic slips quietly derail otherwise sound reasoning. A learner secure in the basic facts approaches the algorithms that follow with confidence rather than dread, and can turn attention to meaning rather than mechanics.

sections.heading: Mental Strategies for Addition
sections.body:
Long before reaching for a written algorithm, skilled calculators manipulate numbers in their heads using a small toolkit of strategies. These are not tricks to memorise but flexible ways of exploiting the structure of the number system, and teaching them builds number sense that pure procedure cannot.

Counting on is the earliest strategy: to add 8 + 3, start at eight and count three more, nine, ten, eleven. It is efficient only when the second number is small, so learners graduate from it, but it establishes addition as forward motion. Making ten is far more powerful. To compute 8 + 5, notice that eight needs two to reach ten; split the five into two and three, giving 8 + 2 + 3, which is 10 + 3, or thirteen. Because working with tens is easy, decomposing one addend to complete a ten turns an awkward sum into a trivial one. This strategy generalises to larger numbers: 47 + 6 becomes 47 + 3 + 3, reaching fifty then fifty-three.

Using doubles and near-doubles leans on facts already secure. Faced with 7 + 8, a calculator who knows 7 + 7 = 14 simply adds one more. Compensation adjusts a number to a friendlier value and corrects afterwards: to add 39 + 26, round 39 up to 40, add to get 66, then subtract the borrowed one for 65. The mental cost of the adjustment is small compared with the ease of adding a round number.

For multi-digit sums, partial sums, or adding by place, is the most transparent mental method and mirrors how the written algorithm works. To add 348 + 275, add the hundreds, three hundred plus two hundred is five hundred, then the tens, forty plus seventy is one hundred and ten, then the ones, eight plus five is thirteen, and finally combine: five hundred plus one hundred and ten plus thirteen is 623. Because each part is held separately, the method is easy to follow and to check, though it demands holding several partial results in mind at once.

Many mental calculators work left to right rather than right to left, contrary to the written convention. Left-to-right addition gives an early sense of the answer's size and suits estimation, which is itself a vital skill. A quick estimate, that 348 + 275 is roughly 350 + 275, or about 625, guards against gross errors before the exact figure is found. The habit of estimating first, computing second, and checking the exact answer against the estimate is one of the most valuable in all of arithmetic. Fluent adults switch among these strategies automatically, choosing whichever fits the particular numbers, and this adaptive expertise, not the memorisation of any single procedure, is the true mark of arithmetic competence.

sections.heading: Mental Strategies for Subtraction
sections.body:
Subtraction feels harder than addition to most people, and the mental strategies for it deserve their own treatment. The single most liberating idea is that subtraction can be performed by adding up rather than taking away. To find 83 − 76, instead of removing seventy-six from eighty-three, ask how far it is from 76 to 83: four gets you to 80, three more to 83, so the difference is seven. This counting-up or complementary-addition method, sometimes called the shopkeeper's method because it is how change was once counted out, is especially fast when the two numbers are close together, exactly the case where taking away is most tedious.

When the numbers are far apart, counting back may be quicker. To compute 62 − 5, step back five from sixty-two. As with addition, decomposing to cross a ten smooths the path: 62 − 5 becomes 62 − 2 − 3, dropping to sixty then fifty-seven. Taking from ten handles facts like 15 − 8 by subtracting from the ten and adjusting: 10 − 8 = 2, plus the leftover 5, gives seven.

Compensation works for subtraction as it does for addition, but the correction rule differs and is a common stumbling point. If you round the number being subtracted, you must correct in the opposite direction. To find 74 − 29, subtract 30 to get 44, then add back the one you over-subtracted, giving 45. A related and powerful idea is the constant-difference principle: adding the same amount to both numbers leaves the difference unchanged, because the gap between them does not move. Thus 74 − 29 equals 75 − 30, which is forty-five, computed with no borrowing at all. This transformation, adjusting both numbers to make the subtrahend round, underlies the equal-additions written algorithm discussed later.

Subtracting by place, the partial-differences method, mirrors partial sums but must handle the possibility that a column difference is negative. To compute 452 − 176: hundreds give four hundred minus one hundred, three hundred; tens give fifty minus seventy, negative twenty; ones give two minus six, negative four; and combining yields three hundred minus twenty minus four, which is 276. Managing the negative partials takes care, which is why many prefer the counting-up approach for mental work.

Estimation remains essential. Rounding 452 − 176 to 450 − 175 gives about 275, close to the exact 276 and enough to catch a wild error. The recurring theme is choice: fluent subtractors do not apply one fixed routine but select counting up for near numbers, counting back or taking from ten for small subtrahends, and constant difference to eliminate borrowing entirely. Building this repertoire, and the judgement to deploy it, transforms subtraction from a dreaded chore into a flexible, often mental, operation that no longer depends on paper.

sections.heading: The Standard Addition Algorithm
sections.body:
The standard written algorithm for addition, taught in classrooms across the world, is a compact procedure for adding numbers of any size reliably. Its power lies in reducing a large problem to a sequence of single-digit additions, handled one column at a time. Because it is systematic, it works the same whether the numbers have two digits or twenty, and it leaves a clear record that can be checked.

To use it, write the numbers one above another with their place-value columns aligned: ones beneath ones, tens beneath tens, and so on. Work from the rightmost column leftward. Add the digits in each column. If the total is nine or less, write it beneath the column and move on. If the total is ten or more, write the ones digit of that total beneath the column and carry the tens digit into the next column to the left, where it joins the digits already there. This carrying is the algorithm's essential move, and it is nothing more than the place-value exchange of ten units for one unit of the next rank.

A worked example makes the rhythm clear. To add 487 and 356, align them and begin with the ones: 7 + 6 = 13. Write 3, carry 1 into the tens column. The tens now hold 8 + 5 plus the carried 1, which is 14. Write 4, carry 1 into the hundreds. The hundreds hold 4 + 3 plus the carried 1, which is 8. Write 8. The sum is 843. Notice that at no point did the calculator add anything harder than two single digits plus a small carry; the algorithm's genius is this decomposition.

The method extends without change to more than two addends, though a column may then carry two into the next. Adding 8 + 7 + 9 in a column gives 24, so 4 is written and 2 carried. It also extends to decimals: align the decimal points, which automatically aligns the place-value columns, and proceed exactly as with whole numbers, placing a decimal point in the answer directly below the others. Adding 3.7 and 12.45 requires only that the columns line up, filling the empty hundredths of 3.7 with an understood zero.

Common errors are instructive. Forgetting to carry, or writing the whole two-digit column total instead of carrying, corrupts the answer; so does misaligning the columns, which is why neat vertical writing matters. A prudent calculator checks the result, either by re-adding in the opposite direction or by estimating first: 487 + 356 is roughly 490 + 360, about 850, which agrees with 843. The standard algorithm is fast and universal, but it should be taught alongside the mental strategies and place-value understanding that explain why each carry is legitimate, so that it never becomes a ritual performed without comprehension.

sections.heading: The Standard Subtraction Algorithm
sections.body:
The standard written subtraction algorithm mirrors its addition counterpart, reducing a multi-digit difference to a series of single-digit subtractions worked column by column from right to left. The complication it must handle is that a column's top digit may be smaller than the digit below it, so there is not enough to subtract from. The resolution is borrowing, more precisely called decomposition or regrouping: one unit of the next higher column is unbundled into ten of the current column, giving enough to complete the subtraction.

Write the larger number, the minuend, above the number being subtracted, the subtrahend, aligned by place value. Begin at the ones column. If the top digit is at least as large as the bottom, subtract and record the difference. If it is smaller, borrow: reduce the digit in the next column to the left by one and add ten to the current column, then subtract. Continue leftward, borrowing whenever a column falls short.

Consider 502 − 267. In the ones column, 2 is less than 7, so borrow. But the tens digit is 0, with nothing to lend, so the borrowing must reach into the hundreds first: the 5 hundreds become 4 hundreds and the 0 tens become 10 tens; then one of those tens is lent to the ones, making the tens 9 and the ones 12. Now 12 − 7 = 5 in the ones, 9 − 6 = 3 in the tens, and 4 − 2 = 2 in the hundreds. The difference is 235. The chained borrow across a zero is the classic hard case and the source of many errors.

This procedure, the decomposition method, is the one most widely taught today because it makes the place-value logic visible: you can see the top number being physically re-expressed. An older alternative, the equal-additions method, avoids emptying a zero column by instead adding ten to the top digit and adding one to the bottom digit of the next column, relying on the constant-difference principle that adding the same amount to both numbers preserves the difference. Both methods give identical answers; they differ only in bookkeeping, and equal additions was favoured before the reasons behind the steps became a teaching priority.

Subtraction with decimals again requires only that the decimal points, and hence the columns, be aligned, filling missing places with zeros so that every column has a digit to work with. To compute 8 − 3.6, treat the 8 as 8.0. Checking is straightforward and strongly advised because subtraction errors are common: add the answer to the subtrahend and confirm it reproduces the minuend, since 235 + 267 should return 502. A quick estimate, that 502 − 267 is about 500 − 270, roughly 230, provides a further guard against the borrowing slips to which this algorithm is prone.

sections.heading: Alternative Written Algorithms
sections.body:
The standard algorithms are not the only reliable written methods, and several alternatives are taught either as stepping stones to understanding or as ends in themselves. Knowing more than one method deepens comprehension and offers a fallback when the standard procedure fails a learner. Each alternative trades some compactness for greater transparency about place value.

Partial sums writes out each column's contribution in full before combining. To add 348 + 275, record 500 from the hundreds, 110 from the tens, and 13 from the ones, then add these partial sums to reach 623. Nothing is carried; the place-value structure is laid bare. Its subtraction analogue, partial differences, records 300, then negative 20, then negative 4 for 452 − 176, and combines them to 276, though the negative partials demand care. These methods are slower but far clearer about why the answer is what it is, which is why many curricula introduce them before the compact standard form.

Expanded notation, or the expanded algorithm, writes each number as a sum of its place values before operating: 348 becomes 300 + 40 + 8. Adding the two expanded forms and then recombining makes every carry an explicit act of regrouping tens into hundreds, so the learner performs the exchange consciously rather than mechanically. This bridges directly to the standard algorithm, which is simply the same work compressed.

Left-to-right addition, favoured by many mental calculators, can also be written down. Beginning with the largest place gives an early estimate of the answer and suits situations where an approximate result arrives before an exact one is needed. It requires adjusting earlier columns when a later column carries back into them, which is its chief awkwardness on paper.

For subtraction, the equal-additions algorithm mentioned earlier remains in use in some countries and was standard in many before the mid-twentieth century. Instead of decomposing the minuend, it adds ten to a top digit and compensates by adding one to the next lower digit of the subtrahend, exploiting the constant-difference principle. It is efficient and avoids the troublesome borrow across zeros, but it hides its justification, which is why decomposition displaced it in classrooms that prioritise understanding over speed.

The Austrian method, or additions method, computes subtraction by counting up, writing the complement rather than taking away, and is essentially the shopkeeper's mental strategy formalised on paper. There are also historical curiosities such as scratch or galley arithmetic, once used with dust boards, where intermediate digits were crossed out and replaced. The enduring lesson is that no single algorithm is uniquely correct; each is a route through the same place-value landscape. A confident arithmetician understands several, appreciates their trade-offs between transparency and compactness, and can move fluidly between them according to the demands of the moment and the numbers at hand.

sections.heading: Extending to Negative Numbers
sections.body:
Whole-number arithmetic answers many questions, but not all. What is 4 − 9? Within the counting numbers the question has no answer, yet it arises constantly: temperatures fall below zero, bank accounts run into debt, elevations dip below sea level. The integers, the whole numbers together with their negatives and zero, extend the number line indefinitely to the left, and once they are admitted, subtraction can always be carried out. This closure, the guarantee that every subtraction has a result, is a chief reason the negatives are indispensable.

On the number line, a negative number is a position to the left of zero, and its magnitude, or absolute value, is its distance from zero regardless of direction. Addition still means moving right and subtraction moving left, but now these movements can carry you past zero. To compute 4 − 9, start at four and move nine to the left, landing on negative five. To compute negative three plus five, start at negative three and move five right, reaching two. Keeping the number line in mind makes signed arithmetic concrete rather than a set of arbitrary sign rules.

The rules themselves can be derived from this picture and from a single, elegant reformulation: subtracting a number is the same as adding its opposite. Thus a minus b equals a plus the opposite of b, for any numbers whatsoever. This unifies addition and subtraction into one operation with signs, so that 7 − 10 is read as seven plus negative ten, which is negative three. Subtracting a negative reverses direction twice and therefore adds: five minus negative three equals five plus three, or eight. The often-memorised phrase that two minuses make a plus is really this fact about opposites, and it becomes obvious once subtraction is seen as adding the opposite.

Adding two numbers of the same sign combines their magnitudes and keeps the sign: negative four plus negative six is negative ten, as two debts combine into a larger debt. Adding numbers of opposite signs finds the difference of their magnitudes and takes the sign of the larger: negative eight plus five is negative three, because the eight-step leftward move outweighs the five-step rightward one. These are not new laws but consequences of movement along the line.

Models beyond the number line help intuition. The debt-and-credit metaphor treats negatives as amounts owed and positives as amounts held; the charged-particle model pairs each positive with a negative that cancels it to zero, so that adding a positive and a negative annihilates a matching pair. All these pictures agree with the formal rules and with each other. Mastery of signed addition and subtraction is a gateway skill: it is prerequisite to solving equations, to reading graphs with all four quadrants, and to the whole of algebra, where quantities routinely change sign and the fluent handling of opposites separates confident students from struggling ones.

sections.heading: Decimals, Fractions, and Other Quantities
sections.body:
Addition and subtraction reach far beyond whole numbers, and the same underlying ideas govern their application to decimals, fractions, measurements, and other kinds of quantity. The unifying principle is that only like quantities may be combined directly: you can add tenths to tenths and metres to metres, but not tenths to hundredths or metres to litres, until the quantities are expressed in comparable units.

Decimals extend the place-value system rightward, so adding and subtracting them requires nothing new beyond aligning the decimal points, which automatically aligns the columns of tenths, hundredths, and thousandths. Filling short numbers with trailing zeros makes every column complete: to add 3.7 and 12.45, treat 3.7 as 3.70. The standard algorithms then proceed unchanged, carrying and borrowing exactly as for integers. The single most common error is misalignment, adding by the right-hand edge instead of by the decimal point, which the discipline of writing the points in a vertical line prevents.

Fractions demand more, because a fraction's value depends on both its numerator and its denominator, and only fractions with the same denominator represent parts of the same size. To add one-half and one-third, the halves and thirds must first be re-expressed with a common denominator, here sixths: one-half is three-sixths, one-third is two-sixths, and their sum is five-sixths. The general rule is to find a common denominator, for which the least common multiple of the denominators is most efficient, rewrite each fraction, add or subtract the numerators, and simplify. Mixed numbers such as two and three-quarters are handled either by converting to improper fractions or by adding whole parts and fractional parts separately, borrowing a whole as needed when a subtraction of the fractional parts falls short.

Measurement introduces units that may not be purely decimal. Time is a mixed-base quantity: sixty seconds make a minute and sixty minutes an hour, so adding 45 minutes to 40 minutes gives 85 minutes, which regroups to 1 hour 25 minutes, a carry, but at sixty rather than ten. Traditional units of length and weight behave similarly, with twelve inches to a foot or sixteen ounces to a pound, and arithmetic with them requires regrouping at the appropriate conversion value rather than at ten. The logic of carrying and borrowing is identical; only the exchange rate changes.

The same is true of any positional system. In base two, columns carry when they reach two; in the base sixty of Babylonian astronomy, at sixty. Even abstract objects that can be combined and separated, such as vectors added tip to tail or polynomials added term by like term, echo the rule that like combines with like. Recognising this common thread turns a scattering of special cases into a single coherent competence: identify the units, make them comparable, then add or subtract, regrouping whenever a column overflows or comes up short.

sections.heading: A Brief History and the Tools of Calculation
sections.body:
The way people add and subtract has changed profoundly over millennia, and the modern algorithms are a late and hard-won achievement. The earliest arithmetic left no columns to carry because early number systems were not positional. Egyptian numerals repeated symbols for units, tens, and hundreds; Roman numerals likewise combined letters, and adding them meant gathering symbols and simplifying, a workable but clumsy scheme with no place value and no zero. Serious computation was therefore done not on the page but on the counting board or abacus, where beads or pebbles in grooves represented place values physically and carrying meant moving a bead to the next wire.

The decisive advance was the Hindu-Arabic positional system, developed in India in the first millennium and crucially including a symbol for zero as a placeholder. Zero is what allows 502 to be distinguished from 52 and makes columnar arithmetic possible. Indian mathematicians such as Brahmagupta, writing in the seventh century, set out rules for computing with zero and with negative numbers. The system passed to the Islamic world, where the ninth-century scholar al-Khwarizmi wrote an influential treatise on calculation with these numerals; the Latinised form of his name gives us the word algorithm, and the word algebra comes from another of his works.

Europe adopted the new numerals slowly. Leonardo of Pisa, known as Fibonacci, promoted them in his 1202 book Liber Abaci, showing merchants how much faster written calculation could be than the counting board. For centuries the abacists, who computed with counters, competed with the algorists, who computed with pen and Hindu-Arabic figures, and only gradually did the written methods win out as paper became cheaper and the advantages of a permanent, checkable record became clear. The specific carrying and borrowing procedures taught today crystallised over this long period.

Mechanical aids continued to evolve. In the seventeenth century Blaise Pascal built a geared adding machine, the Pascaline, that performed carries automatically, and Gottfried Leibniz extended such devices. The nineteenth and twentieth centuries brought commercial mechanical calculators, then electromechanical and electronic ones, culminating in the pocket calculator and the computer, which perform billions of additions per second using binary place value and hardware carry logic that is a direct descendant of the pencil-and-paper method.

This history carries a lesson for learners. Written addition and subtraction can feel like timeless, obvious procedures, but they are cultural inventions refined over thousands of years, dependent on the profound ideas of place value and zero. Calculators and computers have not made the algorithms obsolete; understanding why they work remains essential for estimation, for catching machine errors, and for the more advanced mathematics built upon them. The tools change, from pebble to microchip, but the underlying arithmetic of combining and separating quantities endures unchanged.

sections.heading: Common Errors, Misconceptions, and Where This Leads
sections.body:
Recognising the typical errors in addition and subtraction is as valuable as knowing the correct procedures, because most mistakes follow predictable patterns rooted in shallow understanding rather than carelessness. Cataloguing them helps learners self-correct and helps teachers diagnose.

In addition, the commonest slips are forgetting to carry, or writing the full two-digit total of a column instead of carrying its tens digit, so that 8 + 5 in a column is recorded as 13 rather than as three-carry-one. Misaligning the columns, adding 47 and 5 as though the 5 were tens, corrupts everything and is especially frequent with decimals, where ignoring the decimal point and aligning by the right edge produces nonsense. In subtraction, the notorious error is subtracting the smaller digit from the larger regardless of which is on top, so that a column of 3 over 7 is wrongly recorded as 4; the learner treats subtraction as if it were commutative, which it is not. Borrowing across a zero, as in 502 − 267, defeats many because the empty column has nothing to lend and the borrow must chain leftward.

Deeper misconceptions lie beneath these surface errors. Some learners never grasp that the digits in a column represent different place values, so carrying and borrowing feel like arbitrary rituals; when the ritual is misremembered, there is no understanding to fall back on. Others believe that you cannot take a bigger number from a smaller one, a belief harmless within whole numbers but a genuine obstacle to accepting negative numbers later. Still others over-generalise the commutativity of addition to subtraction. The remedy in each case is to reconnect the procedure to its meaning, using place-value materials, number lines, and the inverse relationship between the two operations.

Estimation is the single most effective safeguard. A calculator who first judges that 487 + 356 should be around 850 will notice at once if the algorithm yields 743 or 8,430. Cultivating the habit of estimating before computing, and checking the exact answer against the estimate, catches the majority of gross errors and costs little. Checking by the inverse operation, confirming a difference by adding it back, catches the rest.

These humble operations open onto the whole of mathematics. Multiplication is repeated addition, and the multiplication algorithm is built from additions of partial products; division is repeated subtraction. Fractions, decimals, and negative numbers all rest on addition and subtraction extended to new quantities. In algebra, combining like terms is addition wearing symbolic clothing, and solving equations depends on adding or subtracting the same quantity from both sides. Fluency and understanding here are therefore not merely useful in daily life, though they are that; they are the foundation on which every later mathematical structure is raised, and time invested in securing them repays itself many times over.

guides.title: Counting, Place Value and Positional Number Systems
guides.summary: A complete introduction to how humans count, how position gives digits their value, and how the decimal, binary and other positional systems work and connect.

sections.heading: What Counting Is: Number, Numeral and Enumeration
sections.body:
Counting is the act of putting the objects in a collection into a one-to-one correspondence with a fixed, ordered sequence of tags, and reporting the last tag reached. When a child touches four apples in turn while saying "one, two, three, four," the word four is doing two different jobs at once, and separating them is the first step toward understanding number systems. The word names a quantity in the abstract, a property shared by every collection of four things whether they are apples, sounds or days. That abstract property is a number. The written or spoken symbol used to record it, such as the mark 4 or the word four, is a numeral. The number is the idea; the numeral is the label. Many different numerals can name the same number: 4, IV, four, quatre and the binary 100 all point to the same quantity.

Enumeration, the process itself, rests on principles that psychologists and mathematicians have made explicit. The stable-order principle says the tags must be recited in the same fixed sequence every time. The one-to-one principle says each object is tagged exactly once, none skipped and none double-counted. The cardinality principle says the final tag names the size of the whole collection, not merely the last object. The abstraction principle says anything can be counted, tangible or not. The order-irrelevance principle says the answer does not depend on which object you start with. Together these turn a recitation of sounds into a reliable measurement of quantity.

Two roles of number then follow. A cardinal number answers "how many," as in five sheep. An ordinal number answers "which position," as in the fifth sheep or the third day. English marks the difference with distinct words, one against first, and the two roles behave differently under operations: you may add cardinals but the sum of positions is meaningless. A nominal use, a third role, treats numerals merely as names, as with a bus route or a jersey; here arithmetic is simply inappropriate.

Counting also presupposes a starting point and a direction. Most traditions begin with one and proceed without end, which already contains a deep idea: for any number reached, there is always a successor, so the counting numbers never run out. This unbounded sequence of one, two, three and onward is called the natural numbers, and it is the raw material from which every richer system is built. Before any base, place value or written notation appears, the essential achievement is this: humans learned to detach quantity from the particular things possessing it, to name that quantity, and to compare collections precisely by matching rather than by vague impressions of more and less. Every later refinement is a more efficient way to record and manipulate what plain counting already establishes.

sections.heading: Tallies, Body-Counting and the Origins of Number
sections.body:
Long before written numerals, people kept count with physical tokens and marks, and traces of these methods survive in museums and in living languages. The oldest surviving evidence includes notched bones such as the Lebombo bone from southern Africa, roughly 42,000 years old, bearing twenty-nine cut marks, and the Ishango bone from central Africa, some 20,000 years old, whose grouped notches have prompted much speculation about early arithmetic. Whatever their exact purpose, such artefacts show the tally idea at work: to record a quantity, make one mark per item, so the marks stand in one-to-one correspondence with the things counted. A tally needs no names for large numbers; it only needs the discipline of one stroke each.

The pure tally soon acquires structure because unstructured strokes become impossible to read at a glance. The familiar five-bar gate, four uprights crossed by a fifth diagonal, is a grouping device: the eye reads groups of five almost instantly, so a fence of gates is counted by fives and singles rather than one by one. This instinct to bundle is the seed of the idea of a base, developed fully in later sections. Tally sticks were serious instruments of commerce and government. English medieval exchequer tallies, split lengthwise so that creditor and debtor each held a matching half, recorded debts to the Crown for centuries; their notches encoded pounds, shillings and pence by width. The system ended only in 1826, and burning the obsolete sticks in 1834 accidentally set fire to the Houses of Parliament.

Body-counting supplied another primitive method and another source of bases. Many peoples counted on the fingers, giving the near-universal preference for ten, the number of human fingers, as a natural grouping. Others used more of the body: certain languages of highland New Guinea count up one arm, across the head and down the other, reaching totals of twenty-seven or more, with each body point serving as a numeral. The Yuki people of California are reported to have counted the gaps between fingers rather than the fingers, yielding a base of eight. Counting on the twelve finger-bones of one hand, using the thumb as pointer, plausibly underlies the recurring importance of twelve and sixty in trade and timekeeping.

These origins explain features of number that otherwise look arbitrary. Ten dominates because of anatomy, not logic; a species with eight fingers would likely favour eight. Words for numbers often preserve the fossilised structure of old bases: French quatre-vingts, literally four-twenties for eighty, and English survivals like dozen, score and gross, point back to grouping by twelve and twenty. Understanding tallies and body-counting therefore does more than recount history. It reveals that the abstract systems taught in school grew directly out of concrete, physical acts of matching and grouping, and that the choice of base was a cultural and biological accident later frozen into notation.

sections.heading: The Idea of a Base: Grouping and Bundling
sections.body:
A base is the size of the bundle a number system uses to package quantities. Instead of writing forty-seven strokes, we group them, and the base fixes how many strokes make one group. In base ten we bundle by tens: forty-seven is four full tens and seven left over. In base five we would bundle by fives: the same quantity is nine fives, but nine is itself too big for a single base-five digit, so we bundle again, giving one twenty-five, four fives and two ones. The base determines both the size of each bundle and how many distinct single symbols, or digits, the system needs. Base ten uses ten digits, 0 through 9; base five uses five, 0 through 4; base two needs only two, 0 and 1. In general a base b system uses exactly b digits, from 0 up to b minus one, and never a digit as large as the base itself.

The power of grouping is that bundles can themselves be bundled. Ten ones make a ten; ten tens make a hundred; ten hundreds make a thousand. Each level is the base multiplied by the level below it, so the values grow as successive powers of the base: one, b, b squared, b cubed and so on. This is why a handful of digits can name astronomically large numbers compactly. Three decimal digits reach into the hundreds, six into the hundred-thousands, and each extra digit multiplies the reach by ten. The economy is dramatic compared with tallying, where the length of the record grows in direct proportion to the quantity.

Choosing a base is a genuine trade-off. A small base like two uses very few symbols, which is ideal for machines that distinguish only two states, but it makes representations long: the number two hundred needs eight binary digits but only three decimal ones. A large base like sixty, used by the Babylonians, keeps representations short and has the arithmetic advantage that sixty divides evenly by two, three, four, five and six, easing fractions, but it demands many distinct symbols and a heavier memory burden. Twelve has been proposed as an optimum because it too divides cleanly by two, three, four and six, and traces of a base-twelve habit persist in clocks, dozens and inches to the foot.

Crucially, the base is a feature of the representation, not of the number itself. The quantity we call forty-seven is one and the same whether written 47 in decimal, 132 in base five or 101111 in binary; only the packaging differs, as a length is the same whether measured in metres or feet. Recognising this separation between an abstract quantity and its base-dependent numeral dissolves much confusion and is the conceptual key to converting between systems, a procedure taken up later once place value has been made precise.

sections.heading: Place Value: How Position Encodes Magnitude
sections.body:
Place value, also called positional notation, is the rule that a digit's contribution depends on where it stands, not only on which digit it is. In the numeral 3,333 the same symbol 3 appears four times yet means, from left to right, three thousand, three hundred, thirty and three. Its value is multiplied by a power of the base according to its column. This single idea is arguably the most important invention in the history of arithmetic, because it makes writing and calculating with large numbers routine rather than the preserve of specialists.

The mechanism is precise. Reading a whole number from right to left, the rightmost column is the units, worth the base to the power zero, which is one. The next column is worth the base itself, the next the base squared, and so on, each column worth the base times the one to its right. A digit's actual contribution is the digit multiplied by its column's value. So in base ten the numeral 4,062 means four times one thousand, plus zero times one hundred, plus six times ten, plus two times one, that is 4000 plus 0 plus 60 plus 2. Rewriting a numeral as this sum of digit-times-place-value is called its expanded form, and it makes the hidden multiplication explicit.

Contrast this with an additive, non-positional system such as Roman numerals, where each symbol carries a fixed value regardless of position, so that XXX simply means ten plus ten plus ten. Additive systems need new symbols for each new order of magnitude and make multiplication and long division extremely awkward, which is why Roman arithmetic relied on the counting board. Positional systems, by reusing the same few digits across unlimited columns, allow the compact algorithms of column addition, carrying, borrowing and long multiplication that schoolchildren still learn. The efficiency is not cosmetic; it changed what ordinary people could compute.

Two subtleties give place value its full power. First, the columns extend without limit to the left, so any number, however large, has a place; there is never a quantity too big to write. Second, the same scheme extends to the right of a separating mark, the decimal point, into columns worth one tenth, one hundredth and so on, allowing fractions to be written in the very same notation as whole numbers, a point developed in a later section. Together these make one uniform system that spans the very large and the very small.

Place value also imposes a duty on notation: every column must be accounted for, even an empty one, or the columns to its left shift and the value changes. The numeral 402 differs from 42 precisely because the empty tens column is held open. Marking that emptiness reliably requires a special symbol, and the invention of that symbol, zero, is the subject of the next section.

sections.heading: Zero: The Placeholder and the Number
sections.body:
Zero plays two distinct roles, and much of its history is the story of these roles being recognised one at a time. The first role is as a placeholder: a mark that holds a column open so that the digits around it keep their proper places. Without it, positional notation is ambiguous, because the numeral for two hundred and five and the numeral for twenty-five would both look like a two and a five with a gap, and a gap is easy to misread. A dedicated symbol for the empty column removes the ambiguity: 205 cannot be confused with 25. The second role is as a genuine number, a quantity in its own right, the size of a collection with nothing in it, obeying arithmetic laws such as any number plus zero equals that number, and any number times zero equals zero.

Historically the placeholder came first, and separately, in more than one culture. Babylonian scribes, writing in base sixty from the second millennium BCE, at first left a blank for an empty position and later used a pair of slanted wedges as a separating mark, though they never treated it as a number and rarely placed it at the end of a numeral. The Maya of Mesoamerica, working in a largely base-twenty system for their calendars, used a shell-shaped glyph for zero, again chiefly as a placeholder. The decisive step, treating zero as a number to be reckoned with, is credited to Indian mathematicians. The astronomer Brahmagupta, in 628 CE, set out rules for arithmetic with zero and with negative numbers, defining how zero behaves under addition, subtraction and multiplication, though his treatment of division by zero was, understandably, unsettled.

Division by zero remains the point where zero refuses to behave. Dividing a nonzero quantity by zero has no meaningful answer within ordinary arithmetic, because no number multiplied by zero gives back the original quantity; the operation is left undefined rather than assigned a value. The expression zero divided by zero is worse, being not merely undefined but indeterminate, since any number satisfies the corresponding multiplication. These are not gaps to be patched but genuine limits marking where the rules stop.

The concept travelled westward through the Islamic world, where scholars such as al-Khwarizmi in the ninth century transmitted the Indian numerals and methods; the very word algorithm derives from his name, and cipher and zero both descend from the Arabic sifr, meaning empty. Medieval Europe adopted the system slowly, with resistance from those wedded to Roman numerals and the abacus, before it prevailed by the Renaissance. The lesson for a modern reader is that zero is not a trivial nothing but a hard-won abstraction: the small circle that makes positional notation unambiguous and turns the number line into a complete, symmetric object with a true centre.

sections.heading: The Hindu-Arabic Decimal System and Its History
sections.body:
The number system now used almost everywhere on Earth is the Hindu-Arabic decimal system: ten digits, 0 through 9, arranged by place value in powers of ten, with zero as both placeholder and number. Its name records its journey. The digits and the positional principle were developed in India over several centuries in the first millennium CE, refined by mathematicians and astronomers who needed to handle very large numbers for calendrical and astronomical work. The forms of the digits themselves evolved from the Brahmi numerals, and the crucial combination of a small fixed set of digits with strict place value and a working zero was in place in Indian mathematics by around the sixth or seventh century.

From India the system passed into the Islamic world, whose scholars both preserved and extended it. In the early ninth century al-Khwarizmi, working in Baghdad, wrote an influential treatise on calculation with the Indian numerals, and his contemporary al-Kindi wrote on their use; through such works the numerals became known in Arabic as the Indian figures. Two related digit styles developed, the Eastern Arabic numerals still used in parts of the Middle East and the Western or Maghrebi forms that fed into Europe. The Arabic term sifr for the empty placeholder became, through Latin, the European cipher and zero.

Europe received the system mainly through trade and translation. The pivotal popular text was the Liber Abaci of Leonardo of Pisa, known as Fibonacci, published in 1202, which showed merchants how the new numerals made commercial arithmetic, interest, currency conversion and bookkeeping far easier than the Roman numerals and counting boards then in use. Adoption was nonetheless gradual and sometimes resisted; some authorities distrusted the numerals as easy to forge or alter, and the abacists and algorists argued for generations. By the sixteenth century, aided by printing, the Hindu-Arabic system had won decisively across Europe and, through European expansion, most of the world.

Several features explain its triumph. It is economical, naming any quantity with only ten symbols. It is uniform, using one scheme for units, tens, hundreds and, past the decimal point, for tenths and hundredths, so the same algorithms serve integers and fractions alike. It is efficient for calculation, supporting compact written procedures for the four operations that require no physical apparatus. And it is unbounded and unambiguous, thanks to place value and zero. These qualities made pencil-and-paper arithmetic accessible to ordinary literate people rather than to a trained caste of reckoners.

It is worth stressing that decimal is base ten only by the accident of human anatomy, ten fingers, not by mathematical necessity. The deep invention is not the number ten but the marriage of positional notation with zero, which works equally in any base. Recognising this prepares the way to see binary, octal and hexadecimal not as alien codes but as the same idea wearing a different base.

sections.heading: Reading and Writing Numbers: Digits, Grouping and Expanded Form
sections.body:
Turning a quantity into a written numeral, and reading a numeral aloud correctly, both depend on handling place value systematically. To write a whole number, one places its digits in columns from the units at the right, filling every intervening column, using zero to hold any column that would otherwise be empty. A long numeral is broken into groups to aid the eye. English-speaking convention groups the digits in threes from the right, separating the groups with commas or thin spaces, so that 1,000,000 is read at a glance as one million. The groups correspond to the words used in speech: the first group is ones, the next thousands, then millions, billions and trillions, each group a further thousand times larger.

Reading aloud follows these groups. The numeral 42,507 is read as forty-two thousand, five hundred and seven, naming each group with its scale word. Within a group of three, the hundreds digit is named, then the tens and units are read as a two-digit combination, with the irregular English words for eleven through nineteen and the tens ending in -ty. A zero within a group is not spoken but must still hold its column: 4,027 is four thousand and twenty-seven, the empty hundreds place silent yet essential. Practices differ across languages and even within English; American usage often omits the and, saying four thousand twenty-seven.

Expanded form makes the internal structure explicit and is the bridge between reading a numeral and understanding it. To expand a number is to write it as the sum of each digit multiplied by its place value. Thus 3,405 in expanded form is three thousand plus four hundred plus zero tens plus five, or more formally three times one thousand plus four times one hundred plus zero times ten plus five times one. Expansion exposes exactly why the value is what it is and is invaluable when teaching the standard algorithms, since carrying and borrowing are just the regrouping of these place-value sums.

Care is needed with the naming of very large numbers, where two conventions collide. On the short scale, now standard in English, a billion is a thousand million, a trillion a thousand billion, and each named number is a thousand times the last. On the long scale, historically used in much of continental Europe, a billion meant a million million. The same word can therefore denote different quantities, and precise contexts, especially scientific and financial, often prefer unambiguous powers of ten or scientific notation to avoid the clash.

Finally, writing extends leftward without limit and, past the decimal point, rightward as well. There is no largest whole number that can be written, since one may always append another group. This open-endedness, together with the discipline of filling every column, gives the decimal system its combination of unlimited reach and complete precision, and it is the same discipline, transferred to other bases, that governs binary and hexadecimal notation.

sections.heading: Non-Decimal Bases: Binary, Octal and Hexadecimal
sections.body:
Because place value works in any base, the same positional machinery produces number systems built on grouping sizes other than ten. The most important in the modern world is binary, base two, which uses only the digits 0 and 1. Each column is worth twice the one to its right, giving place values of one, two, four, eight, sixteen and onward as powers of two. The binary numeral 1011 therefore means one eight, no four, one two and one one, that is eleven in decimal. Binary matters because digital electronics distinguishes reliably between just two states, on and off, high and low voltage, so a binary digit, or bit, maps directly onto a physical switch. Every number, letter and instruction inside a computer is ultimately a pattern of bits.

Binary's drawback is length: quantities that are compact in decimal sprawl across many bits, and long strings of ones and zeros are hard for humans to read and easy to mistranscribe. Octal, base eight, and hexadecimal, base sixteen, exist largely to compress binary for human eyes. Their special convenience is that eight and sixteen are themselves powers of two, so each octal digit corresponds exactly to three bits and each hexadecimal digit to four bits, with no arithmetic across the boundary. A binary string can thus be translated to octal or hexadecimal simply by chunking it into groups and reading each group, and back again by expanding each digit, which is why programmers reach for these bases constantly.

Hexadecimal needs sixteen distinct digits, but the decimal system supplies only ten symbols, so hexadecimal borrows the first six letters of the alphabet: A stands for ten, B for eleven, C for twelve, D for thirteen, E for fourteen and F for fifteen. The hexadecimal numeral 2F means two sixteens plus fifteen, that is forty-seven in decimal. Because one hexadecimal digit encodes four bits, a byte of eight bits is written neatly as exactly two hex digits, from 00 to FF, spanning zero to two hundred and fifty-five. This is why colours, memory addresses and machine data are so often shown in hexadecimal.

To prevent confusion when several bases appear together, notation marks which base is meant. A subscript is the clearest mathematical convention, so that the same quantity might be written with a small ten, two or sixteen after the numeral. In computing, prefixes are common: 0b for binary, 0o or a leading zero for octal, and 0x for hexadecimal, so 0x2F unmistakably means hexadecimal forty-seven. Without such a marker a bare string like 101 is genuinely ambiguous, being one hundred and one in decimal, five in binary or sixty-five in hexadecimal.

Other bases appear in specialised settings, from base sixty in timekeeping and angles to base twelve in advocacy for a duodecimal reform, but binary, octal and hexadecimal dominate technology. Understanding them is not a separate skill but the recognition that the familiar decimal habits transfer wholesale once the base is changed.

sections.heading: Converting Between Bases
sections.body:
Converting a number from one base to another is a mechanical procedure that follows directly from place value, and it splits naturally into two directions: from another base into decimal, and from decimal into another base. Both rest on the fact that a numeral is a sum of digits multiplied by powers of the base, so no new mathematics is required, only careful bookkeeping. The worked examples below use small numbers so the arithmetic can be checked by hand, but the methods scale to any size.

Converting into decimal is the easier direction and uses expansion. Write down the place value of each column as the appropriate power of the source base, multiply each digit by its place value, and add the results. To convert the binary numeral 1101 to decimal, the columns from the right are worth one, two, four and eight; the digits are 1, 0, 1, 1, giving one eight plus one four plus no two plus one one, that is 8 plus 4 plus 0 plus 1, which totals thirteen. To convert the hexadecimal 1A to decimal, the columns are worth sixteen and one, the digit A means ten, so the value is one sixteen plus ten, that is twenty-six.

Converting a decimal number into another base uses repeated division by the target base, reading the remainders. The remainders, collected from last to first, are the digits of the answer. This works because each division peels off one place value at a time: dividing by the base separates the units digit, which appears as the remainder, from everything worth a whole bundle or more, which stays in the quotient. To convert decimal thirteen to binary, divide thirteen by two to get quotient six remainder one; divide six by two to get quotient three remainder zero; divide three by two to get quotient one remainder one; divide one by two to get quotient zero remainder one. Reading the remainders from last to first spells 1101, and expanding 1101 back gives thirteen, confirming the answer. The same method converts thirteen to base five: thirteen divided by five is quotient two remainder three, and two divided by five is quotient zero remainder two, so the digits read from last to first are 23, meaning two fives and three ones, which is indeed thirteen.

The reverse direction, decimal to base, and the forward direction, base to decimal, can be chained to convert between two non-decimal bases: pass through decimal as an intermediate, converting the source numeral to decimal by expansion and then the decimal value to the target base by repeated division. For bases that are powers of two, however, a shortcut avoids arithmetic entirely by grouping bits directly, because each hexadecimal digit is worth exactly four bits and each octal digit exactly three. Thus the binary string 11010110 splits into 1101 and 0110, reading as hexadecimal D6, while the same string split into 11, 010 and 110 from the right reads as octal 326. These shortcuts, and the general division method, are set out step by step below.
ingredients: The number to be converted and its current base
The target base you want to convert into
The digit set for the target base (for hexadecimal, remember A=10 through F=15)
Paper for recording remainders or partial sums
steps: To go from any base to decimal: write each digit's place value as the base raised to 0, 1, 2, and so on from the right.
Multiply each digit by its place value and add all the products; the sum is the decimal value.
To go from decimal to base b: divide the decimal number by b and record the whole-number quotient and the remainder.
Divide that quotient by b again, recording the new quotient and remainder; repeat until the quotient is 0.
Read the remainders from the last one obtained to the first; this string of remainders is the numeral in base b.
For binary-to-hex, group the bits into fours from the right (pad the left with zeros) and replace each group of four bits with its single hex digit.
For binary-to-octal, group the bits into threes from the right instead, and replace each group with its octal digit; reverse the grouping to convert back.
Check your answer by expanding it back into decimal and confirming it matches the original.

sections.heading: Arithmetic in Place Value: Carrying and Borrowing
sections.body:
The standard written algorithms for adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing are not arbitrary rituals but direct consequences of place value, and they work identically in any base once the base of grouping is respected. The two mechanisms that make them work, carrying and borrowing, are both acts of regrouping between adjacent columns, exchanging a bundle at one level for the equivalent number of units at the level below, or the reverse.

Column addition proceeds from the units rightmost column leftward. Within each column the digits are added; if the total is less than the base it is written directly, but if it reaches or exceeds the base, the column overflows and must be regrouped. In decimal, adding 7 and 5 gives 12, which is one ten and two ones; the two is written and the one ten is carried into the tens column, where it is added to whatever is there. The carry is simply the recognition that ten units make one bundle at the next place. In binary the same thing happens sooner: 1 plus 1 is two, which is one bundle of two and no units, so 0 is written and 1 is carried, giving the rule that 1 plus 1 equals 10 in base two.

Subtraction reverses this with borrowing. When a column's top digit is too small to subtract the digit below it, a bundle is borrowed from the column to the left. In decimal, to subtract 8 from the units of a number whose units digit is 3, one borrows a ten from the tens column, turning the 3 into 13 and reducing the tens digit by one; then 13 minus 8 is 5. Borrowing is the exact inverse of carrying: it exchanges one bundle at a higher place for the base's worth of units at the lower place. The same procedure works in every base, borrowing the base itself rather than always ten.

Multiplication builds on these by distributing over place value. Long multiplication multiplies the whole top number by each digit of the bottom number in turn, shifting each partial product one place further left to reflect the place value of the digit doing the multiplying, then adds the partial products with ordinary carrying. Multiplying by ten, or by the base generally, is therefore trivial: it shifts every digit one column left and drops a zero into the units place, because every place value is multiplied by the base. In binary, multiplying by two shifts left by one bit, a fact heavily exploited in computing.

Long division inverts multiplication, repeatedly asking how many times the divisor fits into the leading portion of the dividend, subtracting, and bringing down the next digit. Because the answer is built one place at a time, division too respects place value at every step. Understanding all four operations as regrouping within a positional system, rather than as memorised moves, makes them transferable to any base and demystifies the shortcuts.

sections.heading: Fractions, the Decimal Point and Extending Place Value Rightward
sections.body:
Place value does not stop at the units column. The same rule, that each column is worth the base times the column to its right, run in reverse means each column to the right is worth the previous one divided by the base. Placing a separating mark, the decimal point in base ten, after the units column opens an unlimited sequence of fractional columns worth one tenth, one hundredth, one thousandth and onward. The numeral 3.142 therefore means three units plus one tenth plus four hundredths plus two thousandths. Fractions and whole numbers are thus written in one uniform notation, and the four arithmetic algorithms apply unchanged, provided the points are kept aligned.

This extension makes many fractions easy to write and compute. A half is five tenths, written 0.5; three quarters is 0.75; a fifth is 0.2. These are terminating decimals, ending after finitely many columns, and they occur precisely when the fraction, in lowest terms, has a denominator whose only prime factors are those of the base. In base ten the base factorises as two times five, so only denominators built from twos and fives terminate; a quarter, an eighth, a twentieth all terminate, but a third does not.

When a fraction does not terminate, its decimal expansion repeats. One third is 0.333 recurring, the digit three continuing without end; one seventh is 0.142857 repeating in a block of six digits; one eleventh is 0.09 repeating. The repetition is guaranteed for any fraction of whole numbers because the long-division remainders can take only finitely many values, so eventually one recurs and the pattern from there on must cycle. Every fraction of integers therefore has a decimal expansion that either terminates or eventually repeats, and conversely every terminating or repeating decimal represents such a fraction. Numbers whose expansions neither terminate nor repeat, such as pi or the square root of two, cannot be written as a fraction of whole numbers and are called irrational.

The uniformity of positional fractions is what makes decimals so convenient for measurement and money, where they largely displaced the older habit of expressing quantities in mixed units and vulgar fractions. It also underlies scientific notation, in which a number is written as a value between one and ten multiplied by a power of ten, compactly recording both very large and very small quantities and making their orders of magnitude explicit.

The same rightward extension works in any base. In binary a point, sometimes called a radix point, introduces columns worth a half, a quarter, an eighth and so on as reciprocal powers of two, so the binary 0.101 means a half plus an eighth, that is five eighths. This is how computers store fractional values, and it explains a common surprise: a simple decimal such as one tenth does not terminate in binary, so it cannot be stored exactly, which is the root of small rounding errors in digital arithmetic. Understanding fractional place value thus reaches directly into everyday computing.

sections.heading: Historical and Alternative Systems: Roman, Babylonian, Mayan and Chinese
sections.body:
The positional decimal system is only one of many number notations humans have devised, and surveying the alternatives sharpens understanding of what positional notation contributes. The systems differ chiefly along two axes: whether they are additive or positional, and what base they use. Comparing them shows that place value and zero, not any particular base, are the decisive innovations.

Roman numerals form an additive and partly subtractive system with no place value and no zero. Fixed symbols, I for one, V for five, X for ten, L for fifty, C for a hundred, D for five hundred and M for a thousand, are combined by adding their values, with a smaller symbol before a larger one signalling subtraction, as in IV for four and IX for nine. The value of a symbol never depends on its position, so XXX is simply three tens. The system is adequate for labelling and for recording results but poorly suited to calculation, since it lacks columns to align and offers no easy multiplication; Roman reckoners computed on the abacus and merely wrote the answers in numerals.

Babylonian mathematics used a genuinely positional system, remarkably early, but in base sixty, called sexagesimal. Two cuneiform wedge shapes, one for units and one for tens, built the sixty digit-values, and these composite digits were then arranged by place value in powers of sixty. This was the first positional system in history, yet for most of its life it lacked a symbol for an empty place, so numerals could be ambiguous, a gap later partly filled by a placeholder mark. The choice of sixty, with its many divisors, survives today in the sixty seconds of a minute, sixty minutes of an hour, and three hundred and sixty degrees of a circle.

Mayan numerals were positional in a mainly base-twenty, or vigesimal, system, written vertically, using a dot for one, a bar for five, and a shell glyph for zero, an independent invention of the placeholder in the Americas.
