Draw a line through one vertex parallel to the opposite side, and the two outer angles at that vertex equal two of the triangle's angles by the alternate-angle rule, while the three together make a straight line, which is 180 degrees. This proof holds only on a flat plane. On the curved surface of a sphere the angles of a triangle sum to more than 180, which is why long-distance navigation on the Earth cannot use flat geometry without correction.
Triangles classify two independent ways. By sides: equilateral has all three sides equal and therefore all three angles equal at 60 degrees each; isosceles has two equal sides and, necessarily, two equal base angles opposite them; scalene has all three sides different and so all three angles different. By angles: acute has all three angles under 90 degrees, right has exactly one at 90, and obtuse has exactly one above 90. A triangle can have at most one angle of 90 or more, since two would already consume the whole 180-degree budget.
The exterior-angle rule is a useful shortcut: extend one side and the exterior angle you create equals the sum of the two interior angles it does not touch. It saves a subtraction and it makes many proofs shorter.
Two triangles are congruent — identical in both size and shape, so one could be picked up and laid exactly onto the other — if they match on any of four criteria. Side-side-side means all three pairs of sides are equal. Side-angle-side means two pairs of sides and the angle trapped between them. Angle-side-angle means two pairs of angles and the side between them, and angle-angle-side means two angles and a side not between them. There is deliberately no angle-angle-angle criterion, because equal angles fix shape but say nothing whatever about size; triangles matching on all three angles are similar, meaning same shape with sides in a constant ratio called the scale factor.
Worked example: a triangle has angles of 90 and 35 degrees, so the third is 180 minus 90 minus 35, which is 55 degrees. Similar triangles solve a genuinely useful field problem — if a one-metre stick casts a 1.5-metre shadow at the same moment a tree casts a 12-metre shadow, the sun's rays strike both at the same angle, the two triangles are similar, and the tree stands 12 multiplied by 1 divided by 1.5, which is 8 metres tall. The measurement fails if the two shadows are taken minutes apart, because the sun has moved.

sections.heading: The Pythagorean theorem
sections.body:
In any right triangle, the square built on the hypotenuse — the side opposite the right angle, which is always the longest — has exactly the same area as the two squares built on the other two sides added together. Written with a and b as the leg lengths and c as the hypotenuse, all measured in the same unit, this is a squared plus b squared equals c squared. The relationship is genuinely about areas, which is why the classic proofs work by cutting and rearranging square regions rather than by manipulating symbols. It was known in practice to Babylonian and Egyptian builders long before Pythagoras, whose school is credited with the general proof around 500 BCE.
The forward calculation is direct. A right triangle with legs of 3 and 4 has c squared equal to 9 plus 16, which is 25, so c is the square root of 25, which is 5. Whole-number sets like this are called Pythagorean triples, and (3, 4, 5) is the most famous; any multiple of a triple is also a triple, so (6, 8, 10) and (9, 12, 15) work, and other primitive triples include (5, 12, 13), (8, 15, 17) and (7, 24, 25).
To find a missing leg rather than the hypotenuse, rearrange: b equals the square root of (c squared minus a squared). If the hypotenuse is 13 and one leg is 5, the other is the square root of (169 minus 25), which is the square root of 144, which is 12. Note the subtraction — using addition here is the commonest slip, and it produces an impossible answer in which a leg exceeds the hypotenuse, so the error announces itself if you check.
The practical applications are everywhere in building and layout. Carpenters and bricklayers square a corner by the three-four-five method: measure three units along one wall, four along the other, and adjust until the diagonal between those marks is exactly five. Larger multiples such as 6-8-10 or 12-16-20 give better accuracy over long runs, because a small angular error shows up as a bigger, easier-to-detect length error. The same theorem defines straight-line distance on a coordinate grid: the distance between two points is the square root of the squared horizontal gap plus the squared vertical gap.
The honest limitation is that the theorem holds only when one angle is exactly 90 degrees. Applied to a triangle that is merely close to right, it gives an answer that is merely close, and for a genuinely oblique triangle you need the Law of Cosines instead, which is the same statement with a correction term. The converse is equally useful and often overlooked: if you measure three sides and find that the two shorter squares do add to the longest square, the triangle is necessarily right-angled. That is what makes the three-four-five check a proof rather than an approximation, and it is why a builder can trust a tape measure to establish a true right angle without ever owning a square.

sections.heading: Circles and their measurements
sections.body:
A circle is the set of all points lying at one fixed distance, the radius, from a chosen centre point. The diameter, twice the radius, is any straight line through the centre with both ends on the circle, and it is the widest measurement the circle has. The constant pi, approximately 3.14159, is defined as the ratio of any circle's circumference to its diameter — and the remarkable content of that definition is the word any. Every circle in the universe, from a bacterium to a planetary orbit, has the same ratio, which is what makes a single constant possible. Pi is irrational, so no fraction gives it exactly; 22/7 is accurate to about one part in 2,500 and 355/113 to about one part in ten million, which is more than any hand measurement will ever justify.
The two headline formulas are circumference equals pi times diameter, equivalently two times pi times radius, and area equals pi times radius squared. A wheel of diameter 0.7 metres has circumference pi times 0.7, about 2.20 metres, so it advances 2.20 metres per full rotation — which is exactly how a measuring wheel or a car's odometer converts turns into distance. A circular pizza of radius 15 centimetres has area pi times 225, about 706.9 square centimetres.
Portions of a circle follow the same logic scaled by the fraction of the full turn. Arc length for a central angle measured in degrees is that angle over 360 times the full circumference. Sector area, the pizza-slice region, is that angle over 360 times the full area. A 90-degree sector of a circle of radius 4 has area one quarter of pi times 16, which is 4 pi, about 12.57 square units.
Radians are the alternative angle unit, defined so that a full circle is 2 pi radians and therefore 180 degrees equals pi radians. Their advantage is that the fraction disappears: arc length becomes simply radius times angle, and sector area becomes half of radius squared times angle, but only when the angle is in radians. Using a degree value in those simplified formulas produces an answer wrong by a factor of about 57.
The single most frequent circle error is confusing radius with diameter. Given a 10-centimetre pizza, the radius is 5, so the area is 25 pi, about 78.5 square centimetres — not 100 pi. Because the radius is squared, that mistake does not merely double the answer, it quadruples it. Whenever a problem hands you a diameter, halve it in writing before you substitute anything into an area formula. Pipes, drills, wire and tubing are almost always specified by diameter while flow and strength calculations need radius, so this conversion is a daily one in trades: doubling a pipe's diameter multiplies its cross-sectional area, and roughly its carrying capacity, by four rather than by two.

sections.heading: Perimeter and area of polygons
sections.body:
Perimeter is the total distance around the outside of a two-dimensional shape, found by adding every side length, and it is measured in ordinary length units. Area is the amount of surface the shape encloses, measured in square units such as square centimetres or square metres. The distinction matters practically: you buy skirting board, fencing and edging by perimeter, and flooring, paint and turf by area, and confusing the two is an expensive way to learn the difference.
The core formulas each rest on one idea. A rectangle's area is length times width because you can tile it with unit squares in rows, giving width rows of length squares each; its perimeter is twice the sum of length and width. A square is the special case, with area equal to the side squared and perimeter four times the side. A triangle's area is half the base times the height, because any triangle is exactly half of a parallelogram built by copying and rotating it. A parallelogram's area is base times perpendicular height, because shearing a rectangle sideways moves area around without creating or destroying any. A trapezoid's area is half the sum of the two parallel sides times the height, which is simply the average of the two parallel sides treated as an effective width.
The word perpendicular in those formulas is the trap. Height must be measured at 90 degrees to the base, not along a slanted side. A parallelogram with a base of 10 and a slanted side of 6 does not have area 60; if the perpendicular height is 5, the area is 50. Using the slant always overstates the area, and the steeper the lean, the worse the error grows.
Composite shapes are handled by decomposition. Split an awkward outline into rectangles and triangles, compute each piece, and add — or, when it is easier, enclose the shape in one big rectangle and subtract the missing corner. An L-shaped room divides into two rectangles either way you cut it, and computing it both ways is a free check that you measured consistently.
A worked example with real money attached: a room measuring 4 metres by 3 metres needs flooring, so the area is 12 square metres. At $18 per square metre the material comes to $216, but ordering exactly 12 square metres will leave you short. Cuts, offcuts at the walls and pattern matching typically waste 5 to 10 per cent of the material, and more like 15 per cent for diagonal layouts or strongly patterned tile, so ordering about 13.2 square metres and paying roughly $238 is the realistic figure. Trade practice is to add the waste allowance before ordering, never after discovering the shortfall mid-job.

sections.heading: Surface area and volume of solids
sections.body:
Volume measures how much space a three-dimensional solid occupies and is expressed in cubic units such as cubic centimetres or cubic metres. Surface area measures the total area of all the faces enclosing that space and is expressed in square units. They answer different questions: volume tells you how much a tank holds or how much concrete to pour, surface area tells you how much paint, sheet metal or insulation to buy.
For a rectangular box the volume is length times width times height, and the surface area is twice the sum of the three distinct face areas, that is 2(lw + lh + wh). A cube is the special case with volume equal to the side cubed and surface area six times the side squared. A cylinder holds pi times radius squared times height, since it is a circular base extruded straight up, and its surface area is two circular ends plus the wrapped rectangular side, giving 2 pi r squared plus 2 pi r h — the side term is the circumference multiplied by the height, which is exactly what unrolling the label off a tin reveals. A sphere has volume four-thirds pi r cubed and surface area 4 pi r squared. A cone has volume one-third pi r squared h and surface area pi r squared plus pi r L, where L is the slant height measured along the sloping surface rather than the vertical axis.
The general rules underneath are worth more than the individual formulas. Any prism, meaning any solid with a constant cross-section, has volume equal to the base area times the height. Any pyramid or cone tapering to a point has exactly one-third the volume of the prism or cylinder sharing its base and height. That one-third factor is not approximate and not a convention; it is exact, and forgetting it triples the answer.
A worked example: a cylindrical water tank of radius 0.5 metres and height 1.2 metres has volume pi times 0.25 times 1.2, which is about 0.942 cubic metres. Since one cubic metre is exactly 1,000 litres, the tank holds roughly 942 litres, which at one kilogram per litre is nearly a tonne of water — a figure worth knowing before deciding what it stands on.
Mixed units are the most destructive error here. A radius given in centimetres alongside a height in metres must be converted before anything is multiplied, because the mismatch does not produce a slightly wrong answer, it produces one wrong by a factor of 10,000. Write the units through every line of the calculation and confirm they combine into cubic units at the end; if they do not, stop rather than round.

sections.heading: Units of measurement and converting between them
sections.body:
The metric system, formally the International System of Units, is built on powers of ten, which reduces most conversions to shifting a decimal point. For length, one kilometre is 1,000 metres, one metre is 100 centimetres, and one centimetre is 10 millimetres. For mass, one kilogram is 1,000 grams, one gram is 1,000 milligrams, and one tonne is 1,000 kilograms. For volume, one litre is 1,000 millilitres, one cubic metre is 1,000 litres, and — the bridge worth memorising — one millilitre is exactly one cubic centimetre. That last equivalence is what lets you convert between a container's measured dimensions and its capacity without any lookup table.
Bridges to US customary units are all approximate except one: an inch is exactly 2.54 centimetres by international definition since 1959, which makes a foot exactly 30.48 centimetres. A mile is about 1.609 kilometres, a kilogram about 2.205 pounds, and a US gallon about 3.785 litres. Be careful with the imperial gallon still used in some countries, which is about 4.546 litres, roughly 20 per cent larger — a difference that has caused real fuel-loading incidents. Temperature converts by degrees Celsius equals degrees Fahrenheit minus 32, times five ninths, and back the other way by degrees Fahrenheit equals degrees Celsius times nine fifths, plus 32. So 25 degrees Celsius is 77 Fahrenheit, and normal body temperature of 37 Celsius is 98.6 Fahrenheit.
The reliable method for any conversion is dimensional analysis: multiply by fractions that equal one, arranged so the unwanted units cancel. Converting 5 miles to kilometres, multiply 5 miles by 1.609 kilometres per mile; the word miles appears once on top and once on the bottom and cancels, leaving 8.05 kilometres. Converting 90 kilometres per hour to metres per second, multiply by 1,000 metres per kilometre and by one hour per 3,600 seconds, leaving 25 metres per second. Writing the units out and watching them cancel is not pedantry; it is the only check that catches a conversion applied upside down, which otherwise produces a plausible-looking number.
Area and volume do not scale by the linear factor. Because one metre is 100 centimetres, one square metre is 100 squared, that is 10,000 square centimetres, and one cubic metre is 100 cubed, that is 1,000,000 cubic centimetres. Writing one square metre as 100 square centimetres understates the true area by a factor of a hundred, and the equivalent mistake in volume is off by ten thousand. This is the single most common unit error in practical work, and it is worth a deliberate pause every time a conversion involves squared or cubed units. The hectare exists precisely because of this awkwardness: it is 10,000 square metres, or a square 100 metres on a side, chosen as a human-sized land unit sitting between the square metre and the square kilometre, which is a full million square metres.

sections.heading: Equipment You'll Actually Need
sections.body:
Geometry rewards actually drawing and measuring things. A good compass and protractor will do more for your intuition than any printed diagram, because a diagram shows you a finished result while a construction shows you why the result had to come out that way. The moment you bisect an angle with nothing but a compass and a straightedge, the abstract claim that the bisector is equidistant from both arms stops being a memorised sentence and becomes something you watched happen.
Each tool below earns its place for a specific reason. The drawing compass is not interchangeable with tracing round a cup: it holds a chosen radius fixed while you swing it, which is precisely the property every classical construction depends on. Buy one with a locking screw on the hinge, because a compass that drifts open mid-arc will quietly ruin every construction you attempt and you will blame yourself rather than the tool. The protractor should be the transparent semicircular kind with the centre point clearly marked; opaque ones force you to guess where the vertex sits under the plastic, which is the source of most one- to two-degree reading errors. A ruler marked in both inches and millimetres is worth having specifically because it makes unit conversion a thing you can read off directly rather than compute.
Graph paper matters more than it looks. Coordinate work done freehand produces axes with unequal scales, and unequal scales make circles look like ellipses and right angles look wrong, which corrupts the very intuition you are trying to build. String and a tape measure move geometry outdoors, where distances exceed any ruler and where the similar-triangle and shadow methods actually pay off; twine also serves as an improvised compass at any radius by pinning one end.
Nesting measuring cups or a graduated cylinder let you test volume claims physically. Pouring a cone's worth of water into a cylinder of the same base and height, and watching it fill exactly one third, converts a formula into a fact you have personally verified. The bubble level is optional but genuinely useful outdoors: field measurements that assume a stake is vertical are wrong by the amount it leans, and a stake that looks upright on sloping ground routinely is not. Expect the whole kit to cost less than a textbook, and expect it to be more use.
ingredients: A compass (the drawing kind with a pivot point and pencil, from an office- or school-supply store), for constructing accurate circles and arcs
A protractor, for measuring and drawing angles to the degree
A clear plastic ruler marked in both inches and centimeters/millimeters
Graph paper, for coordinate-plane work
A roll of string or twine and a tape measure, for field measurements and large-scale constructions outdoors
A set of nesting measuring cups or a graduated cylinder (from a kitchen drawer or a school science kit), for hands-on volume comparisons
Optional: a small bubble level (from a hardware store), to confirm a stick or stake you've set up is truly vertical before taking an outdoor measurement

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: Measuring a Real Height You Can't Reach
sections.body:
The Greek scholar Thales of Miletus is said to have measured the height of the Great Pyramid at Giza around 600 BCE using nothing but a stick and its shadow, without ever climbing it. The reasoning is available to anyone. Sunlight arriving at any one place and moment is effectively parallel, because the sun is so distant that the spread of its rays across a garden is negligible. Parallel rays strike a vertical stick and a vertical tree at the same angle, so the stick with its shadow and the tree with its shadow form two triangles that have all three angles equal — a right angle at the ground, the shared sun angle, and therefore a shared third angle. Triangles with equal angles are similar, and similar triangles have sides in a constant ratio, so the ratio of height to shadow is the same for both. Knowing three of the four numbers gives you the fourth.
Three conditions decide whether the measurement is any good. Both shadows must be measured within a couple of minutes of each other, because the sun moves roughly a quarter of a degree per minute and the shadow lengths drift measurably. Both objects must stand on ground that is level relative to each other; a shadow falling downhill reads longer than it should and inflates the computed height. And the object must be genuinely vertical, which for a leaning tree it is not — measure to the point directly beneath the top rather than to the trunk's base if the lean is noticeable.
Expect accuracy of a few per cent from careful work, which is entirely adequate for deciding whether a tree can reach a roof.
steps: Choose a sunny day and a tall object you can't easily measure directly — a tree, a flagpole, a building — plus a plain straight stick or yardstick of known height (exactly 1 meter is convenient).
Push the stick vertically into open ground nearby, checking it's truly upright with a bubble level if you have one, somewhere both the stick and the object are catching full sun.

Measure the length of the stick's shadow with your tape measure, then immediately measure the length of the object's shadow — both within a couple of minutes of each other, since the sun keeps moving.

Set up the similar-triangles proportion: (stick height) ÷ (stick's shadow) = (object height) ÷ (object's shadow), then solve for the unknown. Example: a 1 m stick casts a 0.6 m shadow, and the tree's shadow measures 7.2 m; object height = 1 × (7.2 ÷ 0.6) = 12 m.

Cross-check with a second method if you can: stand at a known distance from the object, sight the angle up to its top with a protractor, and use the tangent ratio (this bridges directly into trigonometry) to see whether the two methods agree.

Record the date, time, and both shadow lengths, then repeat on a different day — the ratio method should give you a consistent height regardless of when you measure, as long as both shadows are taken at the same moment.

sections.heading: Similar Figures and Scale Factors
sections.body:
Two figures are similar when they share exactly the same shape without necessarily sharing the same size. Formally, every pair of corresponding angles is equal and every pair of corresponding sides is in one fixed ratio, called the scale factor and usually written k. Congruence is the special case where k equals exactly one, so congruent figures are similar figures that happen not to have been resized.
The rule that trips up nearly everyone the first time concerns how the different kinds of measurement scale. If every length is multiplied by k, then every area is multiplied by k squared, and every volume is multiplied by k cubed. Areas and volumes never scale by k itself. The reason is structural rather than mysterious: an area is fundamentally a length multiplied by a length, so scaling both factors scales the product twice over, and a volume multiplies three lengths.
Work it through on a scale model. A 1:24 model of a car that is 4.5 metres long is 4.5 divided by 24, which is 0.1875 metres, about 18.75 centimetres. That part is straightforward because length scales by k. But if the real windshield has an area of 1.2 square metres, the model's windshield is not 1.2 divided by 24. It is 1.2 divided by 24 squared, that is 1.2 divided by 576, roughly 0.00208 square metres or about 20.8 square centimetres. And if the real fuel tank holds 60 litres, the model's equivalent cavity holds 60 divided by 24 cubed, which is 60 divided by 13,824, a mere 4.3 millilitres.
The consequences of this reach well beyond model-making. Doubling every dimension of a cooking pot multiplies its capacity by 2 cubed, which is eight, so a pot that looks twice the size holds eight times as much and takes correspondingly longer to heat. Photographic enlargement to twice the width uses four times the paper. Doubling a pizza's diameter quadruples the amount of pizza, which is why the larger size is usually better value despite looking only modestly bigger.
The same arithmetic underlies the square-cube law that constrains living things and structures alike. As an animal gets smaller, its surface area shrinks as k squared while its volume, and therefore its heat-producing mass, shrinks faster as k cubed. Small animals therefore carry proportionally more skin per unit of body and lose heat faster, which is why a shrew must eat almost continuously while an elephant faces the opposite problem of shedding heat. The same law explains why a scaled-up insect could not support its own weight: its cross-sectional strength would grow as k squared while its weight grew as k cubed. The practical lesson for anyone building or specifying anything is that a design verified at one size is not verified at another, and scaling drawings up without recalculating loads is how structures fail.

sections.heading: Coordinate Geometry: Locating and Measuring Points on a Plane
sections.body:
Attaching coordinates to points turns geometry into something you can compute rather than only construct. The plane is ruled by two perpendicular number lines, the horizontal x-axis and the vertical y-axis, meeting at the origin, and every point is named by an ordered pair giving its horizontal position first and its vertical position second. Order matters: (2, 5) and (5, 2) are different places, and reversing them is the single commonest coordinate slip.
Once points have coordinates, the Pythagorean theorem becomes a distance-measuring tool anywhere on the grid. The distance formula, d equals the square root of the horizontal gap squared plus the vertical gap squared, is not a new result at all — it is the Pythagorean theorem applied to the right triangle whose two legs are the horizontal and vertical separations between the points and whose hypotenuse is the straight segment joining them. Because both gaps are squared, it makes no difference which point you subtract from which; a negative gap squares to the same positive number, so the formula cannot produce a negative distance.
The midpoint formula finds the point exactly halfway between two others by averaging their coordinates separately: the midpoint of two points has x equal to the mean of the two x-values and y equal to the mean of the two y-values. Averaging is the right operation because moving halfway along a straight segment means covering half the horizontal change and half the vertical change.
Picture a city laid out on a grid where each block measures 0.1 mile. The straight-line distance between the intersections at (2, 3) and (7, 15) is the square root of 5 squared plus 12 squared, which is the square root of 169, exactly 13 blocks, or 1.3 miles — a clean 5-12-13 Pythagorean triple hiding in the street plan. The midpoint of those same two intersections is at (4.5, 9), which is the calculation a mapping application performs whenever it proposes a meeting place halfway between two addresses.
The honest caveat is that this straight-line figure is rarely the distance you will actually travel. On a street grid you cannot cut diagonally through buildings, so the walking distance is the sum of the horizontal and vertical legs, here 5 plus 12, which is 17 blocks or 1.7 miles — noticeably further than the 13-block direct line. That sum-of-legs measure is known as taxicab or Manhattan distance, and it is what routing software actually optimises. Straight-line distance remains the right measure for anything that travels unobstructed, such as radio signals, aircraft or line of sight, and for quickly bounding how far apart two things can possibly be. A further caveat applies over long distances on the Earth: the flat distance formula assumes a plane, and beyond roughly a hundred kilometres the planet's curvature makes it read short, at which point great-circle calculations replace it.

sections.heading: Transformations: Sliding, Flipping, Turning, and Symmetry
sections.body:
Four operations describe every way a figure can be moved or resized on the plane, and knowing which of them preserve measurement is the practical point.
A translation slides a figure without turning or flipping it: each point moves by the same horizontal and vertical amount, so the point (x, y) becomes (x + a, y + b). Nothing about the figure changes except where it sits. A reflection flips the figure across a mirror line. Reflecting across the x-axis sends (x, y) to (x, minus y); across the y-axis it sends (x, y) to (minus x, y); across the line y = x it swaps the coordinates entirely. A rotation turns the figure about a fixed centre by a given angle — rotating 90 degrees counterclockwise about the origin sends (x, y) to (minus y, x), 180 degrees sends it to (minus x, minus y), and 270 degrees counterclockwise sends it to (y, minus x).
Translations, reflections and rotations are collectively called rigid transformations or isometries, because they preserve every length and every angle, changing only position and orientation. A figure and its image under any of them are congruent. Reflection differs from the other two in one respect worth naming: it reverses orientation, turning a clockwise-labelled figure into a counterclockwise one, which is why a reflected shape cannot generally be slid into place over the original without lifting it off the plane. Your left and right hands are the three-dimensional version of exactly that fact.
A dilation is the fourth operation and the odd one out. It multiplies every distance from a chosen centre by a scale factor, so it changes size while preserving shape. It is not rigid, it produces a similar rather than congruent figure, and it is the transformation underlying every scale drawing, map and photographic enlargement.
Symmetry is what happens when a transformation maps a figure exactly onto itself. Line symmetry means some reflection leaves the figure looking unchanged; rotational symmetry means some rotation of less than a full turn does the same. A regular pentagon has five-fold rotational symmetry, mapping onto itself every 360 divided by 5, that is every 72 degrees, and it also has five lines of reflective symmetry.
None of this is decorative. The hexagonal cells of a honeycomb exploit the fact that regular hexagons are one of only three regular polygons — with equilateral triangles and squares — that tile a flat plane leaving no gaps and no overlaps, because their interior angle of 120 degrees divides evenly into 360. Of those three, the hexagon encloses the most area for the least perimeter, so bees obtain maximum storage from minimum wax.

guides.title: Trigonometry
guides.summary: The mathematics of triangles and angles — how the sine, cosine, and tangent ratios link a triangle's angles to its side lengths, letting you find unknown distances and heights you cannot measure directly. Covers the unit circle, the Laws of Sines and Cosines, radians, and real-world navigation and construction uses.

sections.heading: What trigonometry is and why it exists
sections.body:
Trigonometry takes its name from the Greek trigonon, meaning triangle, and metron, meaning measure. It studies the fixed relationships between the angles of a triangle and the lengths of its sides. The central discovery, and the reason the whole subject exists, is this: in a right triangle, once you fix one of the two non-right angles, the ratios between the sides are locked in permanently, no matter how large or small you draw the triangle. A right triangle with a 30-degree angle has the same side ratios whether it spans a page, a building site or the distance to a star.
That single fact is what converts an angle into a distance. If ratios depend only on the angle, then measuring an angle — which you can do from where you stand — tells you a ratio, and one known length converts that ratio into an unknown length you cannot reach. This is how the height of a mountain, the width of a river, the distance to a ship and the position of a planet were all determined long before anyone could travel to them. The Greek astronomer Hipparchus is credited with compiling the first table of these ratios around 150 BCE for exactly this purpose, and the method has been continuously in use ever since.
The vocabulary is defined relative to whichever acute angle you have chosen to work from, conventionally labelled with the Greek letter theta. The hypotenuse is the side opposite the right angle; it is always the longest side and it never changes identity regardless of which acute angle you pick. The opposite side is the one facing the angle theta across the triangle, not touching it at all. The adjacent side is the remaining one, which touches theta and is not the hypotenuse.
The point most worth grasping early is that opposite and adjacent are not properties of the sides themselves; they are roles assigned relative to your chosen angle. Switch your attention to the other acute angle and the two legs swap roles entirely — what was opposite becomes adjacent and vice versa — while the hypotenuse stays put. A great many beginner errors are simply this relabelling done carelessly, and the reliable defence is to sketch the triangle, mark theta with an arc, and physically label the three sides before writing any equation. Everything else in basic trigonometry is built from three ratios formed out of these three sides, and every one of those ratios inherits the same property: it depends on the angle alone and not at all on the size of the triangle. The reason that property holds is worth stating outright, because it is the load-bearing fact of the whole subject: two right triangles that share an acute angle necessarily share all three angles, since the right angle is common and the remaining angles must make up the 180-degree total. Triangles with identical angles are similar, and similar triangles have proportional sides. Scaling a triangle therefore multiplies both terms of every ratio by the same factor, which cancels and leaves the ratio untouched.

sections.heading: The three primary ratios: SOH-CAH-TOA
sections.body:
For an acute angle theta inside a right triangle, three ratios carry almost all of practical trigonometry. The sine of theta is the opposite side divided by the hypotenuse. The cosine of theta is the adjacent side divided by the hypotenuse. The tangent of theta is the opposite side divided by the adjacent side. The standard mnemonic SOH-CAH-TOA encodes exactly these three definitions in order: Sine equals Opposite over Hypotenuse, Cosine equals Adjacent over Hypotenuse, Tangent equals Opposite over Adjacent. A useful consequence falls straight out of the definitions — dividing sine by cosine cancels the hypotenuse and leaves opposite over adjacent, so tangent equals sine divided by cosine.
These ratios are pure numbers with no units. Dividing metres by metres leaves nothing behind, which is precisely why the same value works whether you measure in millimetres or miles. What the number depends on is the angle and nothing else. The sine of 30 degrees is 0.5 always and everywhere, meaning that in any right triangle containing a 30-degree angle, the side facing that angle is exactly half the hypotenuse. Because the hypotenuse is always the longest side, sine and cosine can never exceed 1; a calculator returning 1.4 for a sine means you have divided the wrong way round.
Work an example. A right triangle has a hypotenuse of 10 and an acute angle theta of 30 degrees. The opposite side is the hypotenuse multiplied by the sine, that is 10 times 0.5, which is 5. The adjacent side is the hypotenuse multiplied by the cosine, that is 10 times the cosine of 30 degrees, which is 10 times 0.866, giving 8.66. Verify with Pythagoras: 5 squared plus 8.66 squared is 25 plus 75, which is 100, and 100 is 10 squared. The check closes, so the work is sound. Building this habit of confirming against Pythagoras costs seconds and catches almost every ratio chosen incorrectly.
The single most frequent practical error has nothing to do with the mathematics: it is using a calculator set to the wrong angle mode. If you enter the sine of 30 expecting 0.5 and receive minus 0.988, the machine has interpreted 30 as 30 radians rather than 30 degrees. Radians are the default in most programming languages, spreadsheet functions and scientific calculators after a reset, so this is not a rare misfortune but the normal state of an unchecked machine. Confirm the mode before every session by computing the sine of 30 and looking for exactly 0.5, and confirm it again after anyone else has used the device.
One further asymmetry is worth knowing. Tangent has no upper bound, unlike sine and cosine. As the angle approaches 90 degrees the adjacent side shrinks toward zero while the opposite side does not, so the ratio grows without limit: the tangent of 89 degrees is about 57, and at exactly 90 degrees it is undefined rather than infinite, because the division has no denominator left. Any calculation that produces a tangent of a near-right angle is therefore extremely sensitive to small measurement errors, which is why surveyors avoid sighting almost straight up.

sections.heading: Finding sides and finding angles
sections.body:
Right-triangle problems come in exactly two shapes, and recognising which one you are facing is most of the work.
The first is finding a side when you know an angle and one other side. The method is to choose whichever of sine, cosine or tangent connects the side you know to the side you want, then solve the resulting equation. Consider a ladder leaning against a wall at 65 degrees to the ground, reaching 4 metres up the wall. The 4 metres is the side opposite the 65-degree angle, and the ladder itself is the hypotenuse, so sine is the ratio that links them: the sine of 65 degrees equals 4 divided by the ladder length. Rearranging, the ladder length is 4 divided by the sine of 65 degrees, that is 4 divided by 0.906, giving 4.41 metres. Note that the unknown started in the denominator, which is why the final step was a division rather than a multiplication; getting this backwards produces 3.63 metres, a ladder shorter than the height it reaches, which is impossible and therefore self-announcing.
The second shape is finding an angle when you know two sides. This calls for the inverse functions — arcsine, arccosine and arctangent, marked on calculators as sin to the minus one, cos to the minus one and tan to the minus one. They answer the question: what angle has this ratio? A wheelchair ramp rising 1 metre over a horizontal run of 12 metres has a known opposite and a known adjacent, so tangent is the relevant ratio, and the angle is the arctangent of 1 divided by 12, that is the arctangent of 0.0833, which is 4.76 degrees. Accessibility codes in many jurisdictions cap ramp slope at about 1 in 12, roughly 4.8 degrees, so this example just qualifies — and a ramp rising 1 metre over only 10 metres, at 5.71 degrees, would not.
A reliable four-step procedure covers both cases. Sketch the triangle and label which side is opposite and which adjacent relative to the angle in question. Decide which ratio involves the two sides you care about. Solve the equation, taking care about whether the unknown is on the top or the bottom. Then sanity-check: any angle in a right triangle must lie strictly between 0 and 90 degrees, the hypotenuse must be the longest side, and the side opposite the larger acute angle must be the longer leg. The conceptual trap worth naming is confusing the function with its inverse. Sine takes an angle and returns a ratio; arcsine takes a ratio and returns an angle. They undo each other in the same way squaring and square-rooting do, and feeding an angle into arcsine is as meaningless as taking the square root of a square root symbol.

sections.heading: The unit circle and angles beyond 90°
sections.body:
Right-triangle definitions only reach from 0 to 90 degrees, because no right triangle can contain a larger acute angle. The unit circle removes that ceiling and extends sine and cosine to every angle, positive or negative, without limit.
Draw a circle of radius exactly 1 centred on the origin of a coordinate grid. Measure an angle theta counterclockwise from the positive x-axis, and mark the point where that radius meets the circle. That point's coordinates are, by definition, the cosine of theta and the sine of theta, in that order. Cosine is the horizontal coordinate; sine is the vertical one. This is not a new definition competing with the triangle one — for angles between 0 and 90 the radius, its horizontal shadow and its vertical shadow form a right triangle with hypotenuse 1, so opposite over hypotenuse is simply the vertical coordinate over 1. The circle definition agrees with the triangle definition everywhere they overlap and keeps working where the triangle definition gives up.
It immediately supplies values that no triangle could: the sine of 90 degrees is 1 and its cosine is 0, at the top of the circle; the sine of 180 degrees is 0 and its cosine is minus 1, at the far left; the sine of 270 degrees is minus 1, at the bottom. Because the point simply travels round and round, both functions repeat exactly every 360 degrees — they are periodic — and both stay bounded between minus 1 and plus 1, since no coordinate on a unit circle can exceed the radius.
Signs follow directly from which quadrant the point lands in, summarised by the mnemonic ASTC, often remembered as All Students Take Calculus: in the first quadrant all three ratios are positive; in the second only sine is positive; in the third only tangent; in the fourth only cosine. You need not memorise this if you can picture the coordinates, since a point up and to the left obviously has positive y and negative x.
The fundamental identity falls out of the circle for free. Any point on a circle of radius 1 satisfies x squared plus y squared equals 1, and since x is cosine and y is sine, the sine squared plus the cosine squared of any angle equals 1. Worth memorising alongside it are the exact values: at 30 degrees, sine is one half and cosine is root three over two; at 45 degrees both are root two over two, about 0.707; at 60 degrees the 30-degree pair swaps over. The practical warning is that sine and cosine turn negative past 90 degrees, so a compass bearing of 210 degrees has both negative, and code or arithmetic that assumes positivity will silently place your result in the wrong quadrant of the map.

sections.heading: Radians: the natural angle unit
sections.body:
The degree, with 360 to a full circle, is an arbitrary human convention inherited from Babylonian astronomy. It survives because 360 divides evenly by so many small numbers, which is genuinely convenient for splitting a circle by hand. But it carries no mathematical meaning, and formulas written in degrees are littered with correction factors of 180 over pi that exist purely to undo the convention.
The radian removes that. It measures an angle by the length of arc that angle cuts on a circle of radius 1 — so an angle of one radian sweeps out exactly one radius-length of arc along the rim. Since the full circumference of a unit circle is 2 pi, a full turn is 2 pi radians, and therefore a half turn of 180 degrees is exactly pi radians. Converting is mechanical: multiply degrees by pi over 180 to get radians, so 90 degrees becomes pi over 2, about 1.571; multiply radians by 180 over pi to get degrees, so one radian is about 57.3 degrees. The exact values worth memorising are 30 degrees as pi over 6, 45 as pi over 4, 60 as pi over 3, 90 as pi over 2, 180 as pi, and 270 as three pi over 2.
The payoff is that formulas simplify. Arc length equals radius times angle, and sector area equals one half of radius squared times angle — but both only when the angle is in radians. In degrees you must reinsert the fraction of the angle over 360. Angular speed in physics is quoted in radians per second for the same reason, and the derivatives of sine and cosine in calculus are clean only in radians; in degrees, differentiating sine introduces a stray factor of pi over 180 that propagates through every subsequent line.
A worked example: a wheel of radius 0.3 metres turns through 2 radians. A point on the rim travels an arc of 0.3 times 2, which is 0.6 metres. No conversion, no fraction, no pi in sight — that directness is the whole argument for the unit. Note also that 2 radians is about 114.6 degrees, so the wheel has turned less than a third of a revolution, which is a useful reality check when radian values feel unintuitively small.
The dominant practical error, and it is worth stating bluntly because it accounts for more wrong trigonometry answers than any conceptual misunderstanding, is a calculator or programming language left in the wrong angle mode. Spreadsheet trigonometric functions and essentially every programming language expect radians, while school problems and field instruments are stated in degrees. Confirm the mode matches the units in the question before you begin, and re-confirm after any reset, battery change or shared use.

sections.heading: The Laws of Sines and Cosines for any triangle
sections.body:
The sine, cosine and tangent ratios are defined on right triangles and do not apply directly to any other kind. Most real triangles — a plot of land, a truss, a triangle of three landmarks — contain no right angle at all. Two general laws handle them. Label the angles A, B and C, and label each side with the lower-case letter matching the angle it faces, so side a is opposite angle A.
The Law of Sines states that a divided by the sine of A equals b divided by the sine of B equals c divided by the sine of C. In words, each side is proportional to the sine of the angle facing it, which makes intuitive sense: bigger angles open onto longer sides. Use it when you know two angles and any side, since the third angle follows from the 180-degree sum. A worked example: angle A is 40 degrees, angle B is 60 degrees, and side a is 8. Then angle C is 80 degrees, and side b is a times the sine of B divided by the sine of A, that is 8 times 0.866 divided by 0.643, which is 10.77.
The Law of Cosines states that c squared equals a squared plus b squared minus twice a times b times the cosine of C. It is the Pythagorean theorem with a correction term attached: when C is exactly 90 degrees, its cosine is zero, the whole correction vanishes, and the statement collapses back into a squared plus b squared equals c squared. Use it when you know two sides and the angle trapped between them, or when you know all three sides and want an angle. A worked example: sides a and b are 5 and 7 with an included angle C of 60 degrees. Then c squared is 25 plus 49 minus 2 times 5 times 7 times 0.5, which is 74 minus 35, giving 39, so c is the square root of 39, about 6.24.
The genuine trap is the ambiguous case. Given two sides and an angle that is not between them, there may be two different triangles that fit the data equally well, because the sine of an angle and the sine of its supplement are identical — the sine of 30 degrees and the sine of 150 degrees are both 0.5. A calculator returns only the acute possibility. Whenever the Law of Sines hands you an angle in a side-side-angle situation, check whether 180 degrees minus that answer also produces a triangle whose angles sum correctly; if it does, both are legitimate and only physical context can decide between them. The Law of Cosines has no such ambiguity, because cosine takes a different value in the first and second quadrants, so when you know three sides it is always the safer instrument.

sections.heading: Real-world uses: heights, distances, and navigation
sections.body:
The practical payoff of trigonometry is measuring what you cannot reach. Two field terms set up almost every problem. The angle of elevation is measured upward from the horizontal to something above you; the angle of depression is measured downward from the horizontal to something below. Both are taken from a horizontal reference, never from the vertical, and mixing that up substitutes an angle for its complement — turning 32 degrees into 58 and the answer into nonsense.
Measuring a building's height: stand a measured 50 metres from its base on level ground and sight the top at an angle of elevation of 32 degrees. The height above your eye is 50 times the tangent of 32 degrees, that is 50 times 0.625, giving 31.2 metres. Add your own eye height, typically 1.5 to 1.7 metres, for the true total of about 32.8 metres. Forgetting that addition is the most common field error and always understates the answer.
Navigation works the same way with the axes exchanged. A ship sails on a bearing of 060, meaning 60 degrees clockwise from north, for 20 kilometres. Its eastward displacement is 20 times the sine of 60 degrees, which is 17.3 kilometres, and its northward displacement is 20 times the cosine of 60 degrees, which is 10 kilometres. Sine gives east and cosine gives north precisely because bearings are measured from north rather than from the positive x-axis, which reverses the usual pairing. Bearings are always written as three digits clockwise from north, from 000 to 360, so 060 rather than 60 — the leading zero exists to prevent a dropped digit going unnoticed on a radio call.
The same triangle geometry runs through surveying, where positions are fixed by triangulating angles from two known points; carpentry, where roof pitch expressed as a 6-in-12 rise-over-run corresponds to an angle of the arctangent of 6 over 12, that is 26.6 degrees, and rafter length follows from the same triangle; and satellite navigation, where a receiver solves for its position from distances to several satellites.
Three field mistakes recur. Measuring the angle from the wrong reference, as noted. Forgetting the observer's eye height, or forgetting that a target below your feet needs a subtraction instead. And confusing a compass bearing, measured clockwise from north, with a standard mathematical angle, measured counterclockwise from east; converting between them requires both a reversal of direction and a 90-degree offset. The discipline that prevents all three is to sketch the situation before touching the calculator and to write on that sketch which side is opposite and which is adjacent to the angle you actually measured. One further honest caveat applies to any long sighting: the calculation assumes the baseline is horizontal and the target vertical, and on sloping ground neither is automatically true, so the answer is only as good as those two assumptions.

sections.heading: Equipment You'll Actually Need
sections.body:
Trigonometry becomes real the moment you measure something you genuinely cannot reach and then find your answer confirmed by an independent method. Until that happens the ratios stay abstract; afterwards they are a tool you trust. A homemade clinometer is the cheapest route to that moment, because it turns the tangent ratio into a number a tape measure can check.
The calculator is the one item with a real requirement attached. It must offer sine, cosine and tangent and, just as importantly, their inverses, usually reached by a shift or second-function key. It must also let you switch between degree and radian mode deliberately, and you should locate that setting before your first calculation rather than after your first wrong answer — a machine silently left in radians is responsible for more incorrect trigonometry than any misunderstanding of the subject. A free phone application works well provided you can confirm its mode.
The clinometer parts each do one job. The straw is a sighting tube that forces your eye, the instrument and the target onto a single straight line, removing the parallax error you get from squinting along an edge. The protractor supplies the graduated scale. The string and weight form a plumb line, which finds true vertical by gravity alone and is therefore unaffected by whether you are standing on a slope; the angle between your sight line and that plumb line is what you actually read. Use a weight heavy enough to pull the string taut and hang still — a washer or a nut is ideal, while a light weight swings in any breeze and costs you a degree or two of precision. A degree of error at 50 metres shifts a height estimate by roughly a metre, so this is not fussiness.
The tape measure supplies the baseline distance, which is the known length that converts a measured ratio into a real height; a measuring wheel is better beyond about 30 metres, where tape sag and repositioning introduce their own errors. Graph paper matters for plotting sine and cosine by hand, because seeing the wave emerge point by point from the unit circle is what makes periodicity obvious rather than memorised, and a drawing compass lets you construct that circle accurately. The bubble level confirms your instrument reads true zero when held horizontally, the one calibration worth doing before any field work.
ingredients: A scientific calculator with sin/cos/tan buttons and their inverses (arcsin/arccos/arctan) — any inexpensive model from an electronics store works, or a free calculator app set to the correct angle mode
A protractor, for measuring and drawing angles
A drinking straw, a protractor, about 30 cm of string or thread, and a small weight (a washer, a nut, or a metal key) — the parts of a homemade clinometer
A tape measure or a long measuring wheel, for baseline distances
Graph paper, for plotting sine and cosine waves and the unit circle by hand
A compass, for drawing an accurate unit circle
Optional: a bubble level, for confirming your clinometer reads exactly level before you take a field measurement

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: Build a Clinometer and Measure a Real Height
sections.body:
This turns the angle of elevation from a diagram into a real number you can verify against a tape measure. The underlying mechanism is simple enough to state in one line: the tangent of the angle you sight equals the height above your eye divided by the horizontal distance to the object, so multiplying the tangent by that measured distance recovers the height, and adding your own eye height gives the total.
Three details decide whether the result is trustworthy. The plumb line, not the protractor body, defines vertical, so the reading survives a tilted instrument — but the baseline must still be measured horizontally, and on a slope that means the map distance rather than the distance you walked. Your instrument almost certainly has a small zero error, and checking it against something known to be level converts that from an unknown bias into a constant you can subtract. And the weight must be allowed to stop swinging before you pinch the string; reading a moving plumb line is the largest single source of error in this method.
Expect agreement within a few per cent between two measurements taken from different baselines. Larger disagreement usually means a baseline measured along sloping ground, an eye height guessed rather than measured, or a target whose top is not above its base.
steps: Tape the string to one end of the straw so it hangs freely, and tie the weight to its other end. Tape the straw along the flat edge of the protractor so it sights parallel to the protractor's 0°–180° baseline, with the string hanging from the protractor's center point.

Test it indoors first: sight through the straw at something you know is perfectly horizontal, like a level shelf edge across the room. The string should hang across the 90° mark; if it doesn't, note the offset as your instrument's zero-error and subtract it from every future reading.

Pick a real tall object you're curious about — a tree that might reach your roof if it fell, a flagpole, a nearby tower — and measure the straight-line distance from your feet to its base with the tape measure; call this baseline distance b.

Stand at that spot, hold the clinometer to your eye, and sight through the straw at the very top of the object. Let the weighted string settle, then pinch it against the scale to freeze the reading; the angle of elevation equals 90° minus the reading, since the string hangs from the 90° mark when level.
Measure your own eye height off the ground (call it e — typically around 1.5–1.7 m for an adult).

Compute the object's total height: height = e + b × tan(angle of elevation). Example: baseline b = 15 m, angle of elevation 32°, eye height e = 1.6 m: height = 1.6 + 15 × tan(32°) = 1.6 + 15(0.6249) ≈ 1.6 + 9.37 ≈ 11 meters.

Double-check by moving to a different baseline distance and repeating the measurement — both trials should agree closely, since you're solving the same right triangle from two different vantage points.

sections.heading: Trig Identities: The Algebra That Ties the Ratios Together
sections.body:
A trigonometric identity is an equation between trigonometric expressions that holds for every angle, not merely for particular ones. They matter because they let you convert an expression you cannot evaluate into an equivalent one you can, and because they let you recover one ratio from another without ever drawing a triangle.
The Pythagorean identity states that the sine squared of an angle plus the cosine squared of that angle equals 1. It falls straight out of the unit-circle definition: a point on the unit circle has coordinates equal to the cosine and the sine, and the equation of a circle of radius 1 is simply x squared plus y squared equals 1. Equivalently it comes from the Pythagorean theorem applied to a right triangle and then dividing every term by the hypotenuse squared, which turns the sides into ratios. Two further identities follow mechanically. Dividing the whole identity by the cosine squared gives the tangent squared plus 1 equals the secant squared. Dividing instead by the sine squared gives 1 plus the cotangent squared equals the cosecant squared. Both are the same fact in different clothing rather than three separate things to memorise.
The reciprocal identities are definitions rather than derived results: secant is 1 over cosine, cosecant is 1 over sine, and cotangent is 1 over tangent. Note the deliberately confusing pairing — cosecant partners with sine, not with cosine — which is a historical accident worth naming because it catches people every time.
A worked example shows the practical use. Given only that the sine of an acute angle is three fifths, you can find the cosine without a triangle, a protractor or a calculator: the cosine squared is 1 minus the sine squared, which is 1 minus nine twenty-fifths, that is sixteen twenty-fifths, so the cosine is four fifths. The familiar 3-4-5 right triangle has emerged from pure algebra. The caveat is the word acute: for an angle in the second quadrant the same arithmetic gives minus four fifths, because the square root has two solutions and only the quadrant tells you which to take.
This identity is what an engineer checks when resolving a force into components. A 200-newton force at 30 degrees splits into 173 newtons horizontally and 100 vertically, and squaring and adding those recovers 200 — confirmation that the decomposition conserved the force's true magnitude.
Beyond the Pythagorean family sit the angle-sum identities, which state that the sine of the sum of two angles equals the sine of the first times the cosine of the second, plus the cosine of the first times the sine of the second. Setting both angles equal turns that into the double-angle identity: the sine of twice an angle is twice the sine times the cosine. These are what let you combine two waves of the same frequency into a single wave, the backbone of noise cancellation and radio modulation alike. What they emphatically do not permit is distributing the function across the addition: the sine of a sum is not the sum of the sines, and assuming otherwise is the commonest identity error there is.

sections.heading: Graphing Sine and Cosine: Amplitude, Period, and Phase Shift
sections.body:
Plotting the sine of an angle against the angle itself produces a smooth wave, because the point tracing the unit circle rises and falls repeatedly as it goes round. The general form y equals A times the sine of B times the quantity x minus C, all plus D, packs four independent pieces of real behaviour into one equation, and each parameter has a physical meaning worth naming separately.
The amplitude is the absolute value of A, and it is half the vertical distance between the wave's peak and its trough — the size of the swing away from the middle, not the full range. The period is 360 divided by B in degrees, or 2 pi divided by B in radians, and it is the horizontal length of one complete cycle before the pattern repeats; note that a larger B means a shorter period, because B counts how many cycles are squeezed into a standard interval. The phase shift is C, sliding the entire wave left or right without changing its shape, and the sign convention catches people out — the minus sign inside the bracket means a positive C shifts the wave to the right. The vertical shift is D, moving the baseline up or down, and it is the average value about which the wave oscillates.
Picture the tides at a coastal town following roughly y equals 1.2 times the sine of 30 degrees times the quantity t minus 3, plus 1.5 metres, where t is hours after midnight. The amplitude of 1.2 metres means the water swings 1.2 metres above and below its average, giving a total tidal range of 2.4 metres between low and high water. The period is 360 divided by 30, which is 12 hours, a realistic semi-diurnal cycle producing two highs and two lows a day. The phase shift of 3 pushes high tide three hours later than a plain sine wave would place it, encoding the particular geography of that harbour. And the vertical shift of 1.5 metres is mean sea level itself. A sailor reads exactly this structure off a tide table without ever calling it trigonometry.
The same wave shape describes household electricity. Alternating-current voltage follows V of t equals the peak voltage times the sine of 2 pi f t, completing f cycles every second — 60 in North America, 50 across much of the rest of the world. The literal hum audible near transformers is that sine wave made mechanical. Worth knowing honestly: a nominal 120-volt supply has a peak of about 170 volts, because the quoted figure is a root-mean-square average rather than the amplitude, and equipment must be insulated for the peak.

sections.heading: Inverse Trig Functions: Working Backward from a Ratio to an Angle
sections.body:
Arcsine, arccosine and arctangent — commonly written as sine, cosine and tangent raised to the power minus one — undo their corresponding functions. Sine takes an angle and returns a ratio; arcsine takes a ratio and returns an angle. The superscript minus one is notation, not an exponent: it does not mean one over the sine, which is the cosecant and a completely different quantity.
There is a structural problem these functions have to solve. Sine and cosine repeat, so many different angles share the same value — the sine of 30 degrees and the sine of 150 degrees are both exactly 0.5, and so are the sines of 390 and 510 degrees, and so on forever. Asking which angle has a sine of 0.5 therefore has infinitely many correct answers, and a function is only permitted to return one. The convention is to restrict the output to a fixed principal range: arcsine returns an angle between minus 90 and plus 90 degrees, arccosine returns one between 0 and 180, and arctangent returns one strictly between minus 90 and plus 90. Those ranges are chosen so that each covers every possible output value exactly once.
In an ordinary right-triangle problem the restriction never bites, because every acute angle already lies inside all three ranges. Reading a clinometer, for instance, the tangent of the sighted angle might be 9.37 divided by 15, that is 0.6249, and the arctangent of 0.6249 returns 32.02 degrees — the field measurement confirmed, with no ambiguity to resolve.
The trap appears once angles can exceed 90 degrees, which is routine in navigation, surveying and physics. A calculator's principal answer is not always the angle you are actually standing in. If context tells you an angle must be obtuse but arcsine hands back an acute value, the angle you want is 180 degrees minus that result, since an angle and its supplement share a sine. Arccosine has the opposite virtue and does not need this correction, because cosine is negative throughout the second quadrant and so its principal range already reaches 180 degrees — which is one concrete reason to prefer the Law of Cosines when the shape of a triangle is in doubt.
The general discipline is to treat the calculator's output as one candidate rather than the answer, and to check it against a sketch. A number accepted without that check can silently place a ship, a survey point or a resultant force in the wrong quadrant altogether, and the arithmetic downstream will be flawless and entirely wrong.
Programming languages address this with a two-argument arctangent function, commonly named atan2, which takes the vertical and horizontal components separately rather than their ratio. Because it can see both signs, it returns the correct angle across the full 360 degrees without any manual quadrant correction. Wherever you are converting coordinates into a bearing in code, that function rather than plain arctangent is almost always the right choice.

guides.title: Probability & Statistics You Can Use
guides.summary: How to reason about uncertainty and make sense of data. Covers probability of events and how to combine them, summarizing data with averages and spread, reading distributions and the bell curve, correlation versus causation, and the everyday statistical traps that mislead people.

sections.heading: Probability basics: measuring chance
sections.body:
Probability puts a number on how likely something is, on a scale running from 0, meaning impossible, to 1, meaning certain. The same value can be written as a fraction, a decimal, or a percentage, and moving fluently between the three forms is worth practising, because different situations make different forms readable. When every possible outcome of a situation is equally likely, the probability of an event is the count of outcomes that qualify as the event, divided by the count of all possible outcomes.

Concrete cases make the definition solid. Rolling a 4 on a fair six-sided die has one favourable outcome out of six possibilities, so the probability is one sixth, about 0.167 or 16.7 per cent. Drawing a heart from a standard 52-card deck has thirteen favourable outcomes out of fifty-two, which is one quarter, or 25 per cent. Flipping a fair coin and getting heads is one out of two, or 50 per cent. Notice that in each case the denominator counts every outcome the situation can produce, not just the interesting ones.

The complement rule is the single most useful shortcut in the subject: the probability that an event does not happen is one minus the probability that it does. The chance of not rolling a 4 is one minus one sixth, which is five sixths. This becomes far more than a convenience when a question contains the phrase at least one, because at least one is awkward to count directly and its opposite, none at all, is usually easy. Computing the chance of at least one six across several throws is almost always fastest as one minus the chance of no sixes whatsoever.

A short vocabulary keeps discussions precise. An experiment is any repeatable process with an uncertain result, such as a die roll. An outcome is one single result of it. An event is a set of outcomes grouped by some description, so rolling an even number is the event containing 2, 4 and 6. The sample space is the set of every outcome the experiment can produce, and writing it out explicitly is the most reliable cure for a confused probability problem.

The commonest error in elementary probability is assuming outcomes are equally likely when they are not. Rolling two dice and adding them produces totals from 2 to 12, and a beginner often assumes each total is equally likely at one in eleven. It is not. A total of 2 arises from exactly one pair, double one, while a total of 7 arises from six different pairs, so 7 is six times more likely than 2. The equally likely objects here are the thirty-six ordered pairs of faces, not the eleven sums, and identifying what is genuinely equally likely is the whole difficulty in most problems of this kind.

sections.heading: Combining probabilities: AND, OR, and independence
sections.body:
Real questions rarely concern a single event, so the two combination rules deserve to be understood by their mechanism rather than memorised as formulas. The word and, meaning both events occur, calls for multiplication when the events are independent, which means the outcome of one has no effect on the probability of the other. Two heads in a row is one half times one half, which is one quarter. Two sixes on two dice is one sixth times one sixth, which is one thirty-sixth. The reasoning is that the first event splits the possibilities into halves or sixths, and the second event then splits each of those pieces again, so the fractions multiply.

The word or, meaning at least one of the events occurs, calls for addition with a correction. Add the two probabilities and then subtract the probability that both happen, because outcomes lying in both events would otherwise be counted twice. Drawing a card that is a king or a heart gives four fifty-seconds plus thirteen fifty-seconds, minus one fifty-second for the king of hearts, which belongs to both groups, giving sixteen out of fifty-two, or about 30.8 per cent. When the events cannot possibly both occur, as with rolling a 2 or rolling a 5 on one die, the overlap is zero and the correction disappears, leaving a simple sum of one sixth plus one sixth, which is one third.

Dependent events break the simple multiplication because the first event changes the situation the second faces. Drawing two aces from a deck without replacing the first card gives four fifty-seconds for the first draw, but only three fifty-firsts for the second, since one ace has been removed and the deck now holds fifty-one cards. The product is twelve over two thousand six hundred fifty-two, roughly 0.45 per cent. Whether replacement occurs is not a technicality; it changes the answer materially, and problems that omit the detail are genuinely ambiguous.

Work a complete example combining both ideas. What is the chance of getting at least one 6 in three rolls of a die? Attempting it directly means adding the cases of exactly one, exactly two, and exactly three sixes, with overlaps to police. The complement is far cleaner: the chance of no 6 on a single roll is five sixths, and the rolls are independent, so the chance of no 6 across all three is five sixths cubed, which is one hundred twenty-five over two hundred sixteen. The answer is one minus that, ninety-one over two hundred sixteen, about 42 per cent.

Two errors dominate. The first is adding when multiplication is required, which typically produces an answer well above one, and any probability exceeding one is an immediate signal that something is wrong. The second is forgetting the overlap subtraction, which inflates the result in a way that is harder to notice because the number often still looks plausible.

sections.heading: Describing data: mean, median, and mode
sections.body:
Statistics begins with the problem of summarising many numbers using very few, and the first task is describing where the data sits. Three measures of centre are standard, and they answer subtly different questions. The mean, commonly called the average, is the total of all values divided by how many there are; for the values 4, 8, 6, 10 and 2 the sum is 30 and the count is 5, so the mean is 6. The median is the middle value once the data is sorted; sorting gives 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, so the median is also 6. When the count is even there is no single middle value, and the convention is to average the two central numbers. The mode is whichever value appears most often, and a dataset can have one mode, several, or none at all.

Choosing between them is not a matter of taste, because they respond very differently to extreme values. The mean uses every observation, which makes it efficient when the data is roughly symmetric, but it is pulled towards any outlier by the full weight of that outlier's distance. The median only cares about position in the sorted order, so a single enormous value moves it by at most one place. This resistance is why the median is the honest summary for skewed quantities such as income, house prices, waiting times, and repair costs, all of which have a floor near zero and no ceiling.

The classic demonstration is worth carrying in your head. Consider five salaries: thirty thousand, thirty-five thousand, forty thousand, forty-five thousand, and three hundred thousand. The mean is ninety thousand, a figure that nobody in the group earns and that sits above four of the five people. The median is forty thousand, which genuinely describes the middle person. This is precisely why official statistics and careful journalism quote median household income rather than mean household income, and why a report quoting the mean for a skewed quantity should prompt an immediate question about the shape of the underlying data.

The mode is often dismissed but it is the only sensible centre for categorical data, where arithmetic makes no sense. The average colour of a car in a car park is meaningless; the most common colour is not. It is also the right measure when the practical question is which single value to stock, produce, or prepare for.

The habit worth building is to compute at least two of the three whenever you can and to treat a large gap between mean and median as a signal rather than a nuisance. If the mean sits far above the median, the data has a long right tail and a few large values are doing the pulling. If it sits far below, the tail runs left. Either way the distribution is not symmetric, and any later reasoning that quietly assumes symmetry is on unsafe ground.

sections.heading: Measuring spread: range, variance, and standard deviation
sections.body:
Two datasets can share an identical mean and still describe completely different realities, so any honest summary reports spread alongside centre. Spread, also called dispersion, measures how tightly the values cluster around the middle, and it is frequently the more decision-relevant of the two numbers.

The simplest measure is the range, the largest value minus the smallest. It is quick and intuitive but it is determined entirely by two observations and ignores everything in between, so a single freak reading can triple it without anything else changing. Use it for a rough sense of the extremes, never as the main summary.

Variance is the standard workhorse. Compute how far each value sits from the mean, square each of those deviations, and average the squares. The squaring does two jobs: it prevents positive and negative deviations from cancelling to zero, which they always would otherwise, and it deliberately weights large deviations more heavily than small ones, which matches the intuition that being far off matters disproportionately. The cost of squaring is that variance comes out in squared units, so a variance computed on heights in centimetres is in square centimetres, which is not a meaningful physical quantity.

The standard deviation, written SD, fixes that by taking the square root of the variance, returning the measure to the original units. It answers the plain question: typically, how far from the mean does a value sit? Work an example with the values 4, 8, 6, 10 and 2, whose mean is 6. The deviations are −2, 2, 0, 4 and −4. Squaring gives 4, 4, 0, 16 and 16, which sum to 40. Dividing by the count of 5 gives a variance of 8, and the square root of 8 is about 2.83. So values typically sit a little under three units from the mean.

Interpretation is where the number earns its keep. A small SD means consistency; a large one means variability. Two factories each averaging one hundred parts per hour, one with an SD of 2 and one with an SD of 25, are not comparable operations. The first can be scheduled around with confidence; the second will regularly deliver seventy-five or one hundred twenty-five and wreck any plan built on the average alone. For questions about risk, reliability, safety margins, or capacity planning, the spread usually matters more than the centre.

One technical caveat that trips people up in practice: when the data is a sample being used to estimate the spread of a larger population, statisticians divide the summed squares by the count minus one rather than by the count. This is Bessel's correction, and it exists because the sample mean sits, by construction, at the centre of the sample itself, which makes the deviations slightly too small on average. Dividing by a smaller number compensates. For a full population census, divide by the count. Spreadsheet functions distinguish these two cases explicitly, and picking the wrong one biases the answer.

sections.heading: Distributions and the normal (bell) curve
sections.body:
A distribution describes how values are spread across their possible range, and drawing one, usually as a histogram, is the single most informative thing you can do to a fresh dataset. The most important shape is the normal distribution, the symmetric bell curve that describes adult heights, measurement errors, manufacturing variation around a target, and countless quantities produced by many small independent influences adding together. A normal distribution is completely determined by two numbers: its mean, which locates the centre, and its standard deviation, which sets the width.

Because the shape is fixed, the proportion of data lying within a given distance of the centre is always the same, which produces the empirical rule, also called the 68–95–99.7 rule. About 68 per cent of values fall within one standard deviation either side of the mean, about 95 per cent within two, and about 99.7 per cent within three. These are approximations rounded for memory; the more exact figures are 68.27, 95.45 and 99.73 per cent, and for the commonly quoted 95 per cent interval the precise multiplier is 1.96 standard deviations rather than 2.

Work an example. Adult male heights in many populations are roughly normal with a mean near 175 centimetres and a standard deviation near 7 centimetres. The rule then says about 68 per cent of men measure between 168 and 182 centimetres, about 95 per cent between 161 and 189, and a man taller than 196 centimetres, three standard deviations up, is rarer than about one in seven hundred. A z-score converts any individual value into the number of standard deviations it sits from the mean, computed as the value minus the mean, divided by the standard deviation. A height of 189 centimetres gives a z-score of 2, placing that person near the 97.5th percentile.

The essential caveat is that not everything is normal, and applying the rule to data that is not produces confidently wrong conclusions. Income is strongly right-skewed, with a floor at zero and a long tail of large values, so the symmetric bell is simply the wrong model. Waiting times and file sizes behave similarly.
