The method worked spectacularly — it produced essentially all of eighteenth-century mathematical physics — and it was logically incoherent as stated, because an infinitesimal was treated as non-zero when dividing and as zero when discarding. **Berkeley's attack** in *The Analyst* (1734) is famous, sharp and entirely fair: the vanishing increments are "the ghosts of departed quantities", and the reasoning that manipulates them is worse-founded than the theology he was arguing against. Practitioners carried on because the answers were right, but the criticism was not answered for over a century. **The nineteenth-century response was to eliminate infinitesimals entirely.** Cauchy and Weierstrass rebuilt the whole subject on limits and the epsilon-delta definition, in which no infinitely small quantity ever appears. That is the calculus taught today, and it is why dy/dx is presented as a single symbol for a limit rather than a fraction — while simultaneously behaving like a fraction in the chain rule and in substitution, which quietly confuses generations of students. **The rehabilitation.** In 1960 Abraham Robinson developed **non-standard analysis**, using tools from mathematical logic to construct the **hyperreal numbers** — a rigorous extension of the reals containing genuine infinitesimals and their reciprocals, genuine infinite numbers. Every statement expressible in the appropriate formal language holds in one system exactly when it holds in the other (the **transfer principle**), and every finite hyperreal has a **standard part**, the nearest real number, obtained by discarding the infinitesimal remainder. **In that framework, Leibniz's original arguments become valid.** The derivative genuinely is the standard part of a ratio of infinitesimals. **Smooth infinitesimal analysis** offers a different rigorous route via category theory, at the price of abandoning the law of the excluded middle. ⚠️ **The moral is worth taking.** The infinitesimal argument was not wrong because the idea was absurd; it was wrong because it lacked a consistent foundation, and once one was supplied the idea was fine. That is a different verdict from the one usually implied, and it is a reason to be careful about calling an intuition nonsense when what is missing is a definition.

sections.heading: Infinity in Geometry, Physics and Cosmology
sections.body: Outside pure mathematics, infinity appears in three quite different roles, and they are worth separating: a useful fiction, a warning sign, and an open empirical question. **As a useful fiction: projective geometry.** In the Euclidean plane, two lines meet in a point unless they are parallel, in which case they do not — an irritating exception that clutters every theorem. **Projective geometry** adds a **point at infinity** for each direction, and a **line at infinity** containing them all. Now *every* pair of distinct lines meets in exactly one point, without exception, and a great deal of geometry becomes uniform and simpler. Parallel lines meeting "at infinity" is not mysticism; it is a deliberate extension of the space, and it is precisely what a vanishing point in a perspective drawing depicts. The **Riemann sphere** does the same for the complex plane, adding a single point at infinity so that the whole sphere is the natural home of complex functions. **As a warning sign: singularities in physics.** When a physical theory produces an infinite prediction, the near-universal interpretation is that the **theory has been pushed past its domain of validity**, not that something in nature is infinite. - Classical electromagnetism gives an electron of zero size an infinite self-energy. - General relativity predicts infinite curvature at the centre of a black hole and at the Big Bang; Penrose and Hawking's singularity theorems show these are not artefacts of symmetry assumptions. The standard expectation is that a quantum theory of gravity replaces them. - Quantum field theory produced divergent integrals so routinely that **renormalisation** was developed to extract finite predictions — a procedure that troubled its own inventors, Dirac among them, and which is now understood far better through the effective-field-theory viewpoint, in which a theory is explicitly only valid below some energy scale. **As an open question: is the universe infinite?** Genuinely unknown. The observable universe is finite — light has had finite time to reach us — but the universe as a whole may be spatially infinite or finite and unbounded, like the surface of a sphere. Measurements of the cosmic microwave background constrain the spatial curvature to be very close to flat, which is *consistent* with infinite extent but does not establish it, since a very large finite universe looks flat too. ⚠️ This is a case where the honest answer is that the data does not decide. **A speculative corollary, flagged as such.** If space is infinite and roughly uniform, then any finite configuration of matter — including one identical to you — would be repeated somewhere, an argument for a form of multiverse. It is an inference from assumptions, not an observation.

sections.heading: Paradoxes of the Infinite
sections.body: A handful of results are so counterintuitive that they function as tests of whether you have actually absorbed the theory or merely learned its vocabulary. **Gabriel's horn.** Rotate the curve y = 1/x for x ≥ 1 about the x-axis. The resulting trumpet has **finite volume** (π) and **infinite surface area**. So you could fill it with a finite amount of paint, and yet no finite amount of paint could coat its inside. The resolution is that mathematical "coating" means a layer of constant thickness, and the horn narrows below any fixed thickness — filling it *does* cover the inside, with a layer that thins toward nothing. The paradox lives in the physical analogy, not the mathematics. **The Banach–Tarski theorem.** A solid ball can be divided into finitely many pieces — five suffice — which, moved only by rotations and translations, reassemble into **two balls each identical to the original**. This is a theorem, not a trick. It depends essentially on the **axiom of choice**, which is used to select the pieces, and those pieces are **non-measurable**: so intricately scattered that no consistent notion of volume can be assigned to them. Since they have no volume, volume is not conserved, and no contradiction arises. ⚠️ It says nothing about physical matter, which is not infinitely divisible; it is a statement about the pathological subsets that the axiom of choice permits. **Russell's paradox**, which nearly destroyed the subject. Consider the set of all sets that do not contain themselves. Does it contain itself? Either answer contradicts the other. Discovered in 1901, it demolished the naive principle that any describable property defines a set, arriving as Frege's life's work was going to press. The repair was the **axiomatic** approach — Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory — where sets are built up in stages by restricted rules, and no set can be formed simply by describing a property. **The Hilbert hotel** already covered, and **Galileo's paradox**, belong here too: they are the same lesson at gentler stakes. **What the family has in common.** In each case a finite intuition — that a part is smaller than the whole, that volume is preserved by cutting and moving, that any property defines a collection — is applied where it has not been shown to hold, and fails. ⚠️ The productive response is the one mathematics actually took: not to declare infinity incoherent, but to find out **exactly which assumption breaks**, state it explicitly as an axiom, and carry on. That method — locate the hidden assumption, name it, decide deliberately whether to keep it — is the most transferable thing in this whole guide.
